If the third party cannot tell that the person acts for someone else, Section 164 II BGB disregards the agent’s hidden intent not to act personally.

Exam language: undisclosed agency generally does not bind the principal through Section 164 I; the acting person risks becoming the contractual counterparty.

No Power Of Representation

If the acting person lacks power of representation, the principal is not bound at first.

Possible routes:

  • the principal can ratify the contract under Section 177 I BGB
  • if the principal refuses ratification, the third party may claim against the unauthorized agent under Section 179 BGB

Warehouse example from the deck: S is hired only for warehouse tasks and has no sales authority. S answers a buyer call anyway and sells furniture at a good price for P. P is not bound immediately because S lacked power of representation. P can ratify if the deal is attractive. If P refuses, the buyer may turn to S under Section 179 BGB.

Sources Of Power Of Representation

Statutory Authority

Some roles have representation power by law.

Example: under Section 35 GmbHG, GmbH directors represent the company in and out of court.

This is exam-relevant because legal entities cannot act physically. They need organs or agents to make declarations.

A legal entity, such as a GmbH or AG, can own assets, conclude contracts, sue, be sued, and owe duties. But it cannot speak, sign, negotiate, send an email, or physically hand over goods by itself. A human act must therefore be attributed to the legal entity.

Route Meaning Example
Organ representation A statutory company organ acts for the legal entity by law. A GmbH managing director signs a purchase contract for the GmbH.
Agency A person is authorized to represent the legal entity in a transaction. A sales employee sells goods in the GmbH’s name under granted authority.

Exam sentence:

Because a legal entity cannot act physically, the declaration must be made through an organ or agent and then attributed to the legal entity.

Authority By Declaration

Under Section 167 I BGB, the principal can grant power of representation by declaration.

Two routes:

  • internal authorization: declaration to the agent
  • external authorization: declaration to the third party

Internal example: P tells A, “You may sell furniture for me.”

External example: P tells key buyers, “A is authorized to sell furniture for us up to EUR 10,000.”

Reliance-Based Authority

The deck distinguishes two reliance categories:

  • agency by estoppel: the principal knows someone appears to act as agent and tolerates it
  • ostensible agency: the principal does not know, but could have known with due diligence because of negligence

The deck’s key consequence is that in both cases the agent acts with real power of representation. This protects a third party who reasonably relies on the principal-created appearance.

This differs from regular authorization because regular authorization is based on P’s intentional declaration, while reliance-based authority is based on P’s responsible creation or toleration of an appearance.

Type P’s mental state Legal intuition Example
Regular authorization P intentionally gives A authority. Authority comes from P’s declaration. P says, “A may sell furniture for me.”
Agency by estoppel P knows A appears to act as agent and tolerates it. P cannot silently benefit from or tolerate the appearance and later deny it. P sees A repeatedly selling to customers in P’s name and does nothing.
Ostensible agency P does not know, but should have known and prevented the appearance. P negligently failed to control the appearance of authority. A uses P’s email, office, and forms for repeated sales; P would have noticed with proper controls.

One isolated unauthorized act is usually not enough. The exam facts should show an appearance attributable to P and reasonable good-faith reliance by T.

Termination Of Authority

Section 168 BGB governs expiry of authority.

Core rules:

  • authority usually ends with the underlying legal relationship
  • authority is generally freely revocable
  • withdrawal can be declared internally to the agent or externally to the third party

Third-party protection matters. If withdrawal is only declared to the agent, a good-faith third party may still be protected under Sections 170 and 173 BGB unless the third party knew or should have known the authority had ended.

Exam trap: ending the employment contract does not always instantly solve the external third-party problem. Ask what the third party was told and whether they were in good faith.

Limits And Abuse

Abuse Of Power Of Representation

If the agent has external power but violates internal limits, the principal may still be bound externally.

Important exceptions:

  • collusion between agent and third party can make the transaction void under Section 138 BGB
  • if the agent exceeds internal limits and the third party knows this, protection of the third party is weaker

Contracting With Oneself

Section 181 BGB restricts self-dealing and acting on both sides of a transaction.

Example: an employee with broad authority grants himself a pay raise.

The concern is conflict of interest. The agent may sacrifice the principal’s interest because the agent is also on the other side.

There are two common forms:

Form Structure Example
Self-contracting A represents P, but A is personally the counterparty. A sells P’s machine to herself.
Multiple representation A represents both sides of the same transaction. A represents seller P and buyer T in the same sale.

This is stronger than a normal internal-instruction violation. In a normal internal-instruction violation, A deals with an outside third party T and may still bind P externally. In contracting with oneself, the conflict of interest can limit A’s external power because there is no independent counterparty bargain.

The deck states that the transaction is provisionally invalid unless:

  • self-dealing was permitted in advance
  • the principal ratifies later under Section 177 BGB
  • the transaction merely performs an obligation
  • the transaction is legally advantageous only for the principal

Exam route:

1. A acts as representative.
2. A contracts with herself or represents both sides.
3. Section 181 BGB is triggered.
4. Check prior permission, later ratification, mere performance of an existing obligation, or legal advantage only.
5. If no exception applies, A cannot bind P through that self-dealing transaction.

Advantages And Risks Of Agency

Advantages:

  • division of labor
  • freeing managerial capacity
  • increasing company output
  • enabling legal entities to act
  • using specialists with better knowledge
  • reducing emotional involvement in transactions

Risks:

  • loss of direct control
  • information gaps
  • different interests of principal and agent
  • need for trust, monitoring, or limits
  • principal-agent problem

Managerial takeaway: agency creates organizational scale, but scale requires controls.

Principal-Agent Problem

The principal-agent problem is the economic version of the agency risk.

The principal hires the agent. The agent performs. Both may maximize their own interest. The principal cannot perfectly observe the agent’s qualities, actions, information, or intentions.

Main information problems from the deck:

  • hidden characteristics, adverse selection: the agent is unsuitable before hiring
  • hidden action, moral hazard: the agent behaves badly after being hired
  • hidden information, moral hazard: the agent knows more than the principal can assess
  • hidden intention: the agent’s motivation is not aligned with the principal

Solutions are agency costs:

  • signaling and screening, such as certificates or assessment centers
  • incentives, such as bonuses
  • surveillance, such as dual-control or joint-representation principles
  • limitation of authority, especially through external authorization that tells third parties the limit

Exam bridge: the legal agency rules decide who is bound. The principal-agent framework explains why businesses design authority limits, bonus systems, and monitoring in the first place.

Visual Knowledge Map

flowchart TD
    Need[Principal needs legal action at scale] --> Agent[Agent acts externally]
    Agent --> Test{Section 164 I requirements met?}
    Test --> Own[Own declaration of intent]
    Test --> Publicity[In principal's name]
    Test --> Authority[Power of representation]
    Own --> Effective{All met?}
    Publicity --> Effective
    Authority --> Effective
    Effective -->|Yes| Bind[Principal and third party bound directly]
    Effective -->|No publicity| AgentBound[Acting person may bind themselves]
    Effective -->|No authority| Pending[Contract pending ratification]
    Pending --> Ratify[Principal ratifies under Section 177]
    Pending --> Refuse[Principal refuses]
    Refuse --> Liability[Unauthorized agent liability under Section 179]
    Authority --> InternalExternal[Can do vs may do]
    InternalExternal --> Risk[Principal-agent problem]
    Risk --> Controls[Screening, incentives, monitoring, authority limits]

Subject Knowledge Graph

Node Meaning Exam Relevance
Principal Person for whom the legal effect should arise. Identifies who is bound if agency works.
Agent Person acting externally for the principal. Must make own declaration, disclose agency, and have authority.
Third Party Contract partner dealing with the agent. Protection depends on publicity and authority.
Own Declaration Of Intent Agent forms and expresses own legal will. Distinguishes agent from messenger.
Principle Of Publicity Agent acts in the principal’s name or circumstances show this. If missing, principal is not bound under Section 164 I.
Power Of Representation External authority to bind the principal. Central “can do” element.
Internal Relationship Legal relationship between principal and agent. Determines “may do” and internal recourse.
External Relationship Agency power visible to third parties. Determines whether principal is bound.
Unauthorized Agent Person acting as agent without power of representation. Triggers ratification or Section 179 liability.
Agency By Estoppel Reliance authority where principal knows and tolerates apparent agency. Protects third party reliance.
Ostensible Agency Reliance authority where principal negligently does not know. Protects third party reliance created by negligence.
Contracting With Oneself Agent transacts with self or on both sides. Conflict-of-interest limit under Section 181 BGB.
Principal-Agent Problem Information asymmetry and self-interest between principal and agent. Explains monitoring, incentives, and authority limits.
From Relationship To Why It Matters
Agent acts on behalf of Principal Creates possibility of direct legal effect for principal.
Agent declares to Third Party Agency always has an external communication side.
Section 164 I BGB requires Own Declaration Of Intent Separates agents from messengers.
Section 164 I BGB requires Principle Of Publicity Third party must know whose contract this is.
Section 164 I BGB requires Power Of Representation Principal is bound only if authority exists.
Effective Agency binds Principal And Third Party Agent normally drops out of the contract.
Internal Relationship limits Agent’s May Do Principal may have internal claims against agent.
External Relationship defines Agent’s Can Do Third-party protection depends on external authority.
Lack Of Authority creates Pending Ratification Section 177 lets principal choose whether to approve.
Refusal Of Ratification triggers Section 179 Liability Third party may claim against unauthorized agent.
Section 181 BGB limits Contracting With Oneself Prevents conflict-of-interest abuse.
Information Asymmetry creates Principal-Agent Problem Explains agency costs and governance design.

Real Business Examples

  • Sales employee: authorized to conclude standard sales contracts up to a price limit. If the limit is externally communicated to regular buyers, buyers cannot easily rely on broader authority.
  • GmbH managing director: represents the company by statutory power, so the company can act in legal transactions.
  • Warehouse employee: internal job duties alone do not create sales authority unless the principal created an appearance of authority.
  • Procurement dual-control rule: two signatures may reduce hidden action but create monitoring costs and potential collusion questions.
  • Bonus plan: aligns sales incentives, but may also create pressure to sell unprofitable or unsuitable products if badly designed.

Exam Relevance

Likely prompts:

  • State and apply the three requirements of Section 164 I BGB.
  • Distinguish agent from messenger.
  • Explain the direct binding effect between principal and third party.
  • Separate internal relationship from external authority.
  • Analyze missing publicity under Section 164 II BGB.
  • Analyze unauthorized agency under Sections 177 and 179 BGB.
  • Explain agency by estoppel versus ostensible agency.
  • Apply Section 181 BGB to self-dealing.
  • Connect legal agency to the principal-agent problem.

Common traps:

  • Saying the agent is contractually bound when effective agency exists.
  • Ignoring the publicity requirement because the agent privately intended to act for P.
  • Treating internal permission limits as automatically effective against third parties.
  • Forgetting principal ratification under Section 177 BGB.
  • Treating every bad agent action as no authority; distinguish lack of authority from abuse of existing authority.
  • Mixing the legal agency rules with the economic principal-agent problem without explaining the bridge.

High-scoring answer structure:

  1. Identify the possible principal, agent, and third party.
  2. Test Section 164 I BGB: own declaration, publicity, power of representation.
  3. State the direct effect if all elements are met.
  4. If one element is missing, name the specific consequence.
  5. Check special issues: reliance authority, termination, abuse, Section 181.
  6. If asked for managerial implications, explain information asymmetry and agency costs.

Official Exercise Case Routes

Case 1a: Fuel Purchase And Publicity

Question: did F effectively represent D when buying fuel?

Route:

  1. Own declaration: F forms and expresses his own will to buy fuel.
  2. Publicity: F does not explicitly say he acts for D. Implicit publicity is doubtful because although A sees F filling D’s car, A does not necessarily know who is the buyer.
  3. Exception: for immediate everyday cash transactions where the identity of the contracting party is irrelevant, the “transaction for whom it concerns” exception may substitute for publicity.
  4. The exercise leaves the result arguable because fuel is paid immediately and the buyer identity may be irrelevant, but tank filling can be expensive and hard to unwind.

Result: effective agency is arguable. If publicity fails, Section 164 II BGB binds F personally, not D.

Exam trap: hidden intent to act for someone else is irrelevant unless the representative capacity is evident or an exception applies.

Case 1b: Unauthorized Fuel Purchase

Question: can attendant A demand the fuel price from F?

Route:

  1. No ordinary Section 433 II BGB claim against F as buyer because F did not intend to contract for himself.
  2. Section 179 I BGB applies if F acted as agent but without power of representation and D refuses ratification.
  3. Own declaration and publicity are present because F explicitly says he refuels in D’s name.
  4. Power of representation is missing because D only authorized snacks, not fuel.
  5. D refuses ratification because fuel is cheaper after the border.
  6. A chooses performance under Section 179 I BGB, meaning payment of the purchase price rather than damages.

Result: A can demand performance/payment from F under Section 179 I BGB.

Exam trap: Section 179 is not a normal contract claim; it is liability of the unauthorized agent after the principal refuses ratification.

Case 2: Laptop Purchase Through Girlfriend And Store Manager

Questions: did G represent S, did M represent E-oHG, and did S and E-oHG conclude a purchase agreement?

Route:

  1. G represents S under Section 164 I BGB: G chooses and buys the laptop, refers to S’s letter, and acts within S’s internal and external authorization under Section 167 I BGB.
  2. M represents E-oHG: M processes the sale as store manager, the enterprise-related context satisfies publicity, and Section 56 HGB supports store authority for customary sales.
  3. Contract formation: G’s offer by taking the laptop to payment is attributed to S; M’s acceptance by processing payment is attributed to E-oHG.

Result: S and E-oHG conclude a purchase agreement.

Exam trap: when both sides act through people, solve agency on both sides before concluding the contract.

Case 3: Paradise-GmbH Apple Order

Question: did farmer F and P-GmbH conclude a contract when only director E ordered apples?

Route:

  1. P-GmbH cannot make declarations itself; it acts through organs/representatives.
  2. E makes an own declaration and acts in P-GmbH’s name.
  3. Power of representation depends on Section 35 GmbHG. With several directors, joint representation is the default unless articles provide otherwise.
  4. A and E never agreed that one director can act alone, and only E ordered.
  5. Ratification under Section 177 I BGB is refused because A is not convinced and does not approve.

Result: no effective agency by E and no contract with P-GmbH.

Exam trap: director status alone is not always sole authority when joint representation applies.

Writing Workshop: Dog Sculpture Ratification

Question: did art dealer D effectively represent collector C when buying a dog sculpture instead of the instructed wolf sculpture?

Route:

  1. Own declaration: D decides to buy the dog sculpture.
  2. Publicity: D explains the situation to artist A, so A knows D acts for C’s collection.
  3. Authority: C internally authorized D to buy the wolf sculpture, not a substitute dog sculpture. The clear instruction and availability of later approval mean D acted outside authority.
  4. Pending invalidity: without authority, the declaration is pending invalid under Section 177 I BGB.
  5. Ratification: C raises no objections and sets up the dog sculpture; this is implicit ratification.

Result: effective agency in the end because C ratified D’s unauthorized declaration.

Legal-opinion template:

  1. “D could have effectively represented C when concluding the purchase agreement with A under Section 164 I BGB.”
  2. Test own declaration, publicity, and power of representation.
  3. If authority scope fails, immediately check Section 177 I BGB ratification.
  4. Conclude whether the declaration is effective for the principal.

Retrieval Prompts

Closed-book questions:

  1. What are the three requirements for effective agency under Section 164 I BGB?
  2. What is the difference between an agent and a messenger?
  3. What does the principle of publicity require?
  4. What is the difference between internal authorization and external authorization?
  5. Explain “can do” versus “may do” in agency.
  6. What happens when an unauthorized agent concludes a contract?
  7. Why does Section 181 BGB restrict self-dealing?
  8. What are the four information problems in the principal-agent problem?

Application prompts:

  1. Employee A answers P’s business phone and sells furniture after P authorized her orally. Who is bound?
  2. Warehouse worker S has no sales authority but sells furniture at a profitable price. What can P do?
  3. Former employee A keeps acting as sales agent after termination. T does not know authority was withdrawn. Which third-party protection issue arises?
  4. Manager M signs a contract with himself for a pay raise. Which statutory limit should you check?
  5. A company uses bonuses and two-signature approval for sales contracts. Link these controls to information asymmetry.

Practice Tasks

Mini Case 1: The Messenger

P writes an offer and asks M to read it word-for-word to T. M does so without changing anything.

Short answer guide: M is likely a messenger, not an agent, because M makes no own declaration of intent. Analyze whether P’s declaration was transmitted effectively.

Mini Case 2: Undisclosed Principal

A sells a laptop to T without saying she acts for P. T thinks A is the seller. A secretly intended to act only for P.

Short answer guide: publicity is missing. Section 164 II BGB prevents A’s hidden intent from helping; P is not bound under Section 164 I on these facts.

Mini Case 3: Profitable Unauthorized Deal

S has warehouse-only duties but sells furniture for P at an excellent price. P learns immediately.

Short answer guide: no authority, so P is not bound immediately. P may ratify under Section 177 I BGB. If P refuses, T may claim against S under Section 179 BGB if requirements are met.

Mini Case 4: Internal Limit

P tells A internally not to sell over EUR 5,000, but externally tells regular customers A can sell all standard furniture. A sells to T for EUR 8,000 and T does not know the internal limit.

Short answer guide: distinguish external “can do” from internal “may do.” P may be bound externally; P’s remedy may be internal against A.

Connections

Previous notes from this lecture:

  • ../week-03-contract-law-i/week-03-contract-law-i.md: agency declarations still operate through declaration-of-intent and offer/acceptance logic.
  • ../week-06-standard-business-terms/week-06-standard-business-terms.md: after identifying who is bound, test which pre-written clauses became part of the contract.
  • ../week-05-contract-law-iii-withdrawal-cancellation-dissolution/week-05-contract-law-iii-withdrawal-cancellation-dissolution.md: agency can determine who may declare termination or withdrawal for a party.

Cross-course links:

  • Organization: delegation, authority, monitoring, and role design mirror the principal-agent problem.
  • Finance: agency costs affect governance, incentives, and valuation risk.
  • SCM: procurement agents and sales agents can bind companies in supply contracts; authority limits matter in supplier-buyer relationships.

Open Uncertainties

  • The deck labels itself “Lecture 6” while the course logistics outline places Agency after Standard Business Terms as Session 7. This note follows the topic sequence.
  • The deck uses “agency by estoppel” and “ostensible agency” as English labels for reliance-based authority. German doctrinal labels may vary; this note keeps the deck’s labels and adds the underlying distinction.

Weakness Flags

  • Active recall not yet completed.
  • First drill should start with the furniture-sales example, then switch one missing requirement at a time: messenger, no publicity, no authority, internal limit, and self-dealing.

[W07.2] Week 07 Agency Cheatsheet And Tricks

Source: business-law/wiki/week-07-agency/week-07-agency-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-07-agency.md, active-recall-session-2026-07-01.md, clarification-session-2026-07-01.md

Must-Know (exam-critical)

Rule Anchor Core content
Effective agency, three cumulative elements Section 164 I BGB Own declaration of intent, publicity (acting in the principal’s name), power of representation. All three must be met.
Legal effect if all three are met Section 164 I BGB Principal and third party become the contract parties directly; the agent normally drops out of the contract.
Agent vs. messenger No fixed section, tested through Section 164 I Agent forms their own legal declaration; a messenger only transmits someone else’s already-fixed declaration. No own declaration means no agency analysis — check transmission instead.
No publicity consequence Section 164 II BGB If T cannot recognize A is acting for P, A’s hidden intent is irrelevant; A is likely bound personally, not P.
No authority consequence Sections 177 I, 179 BGB Contract is pending until P ratifies. If P refuses, the third party may claim against the unauthorized agent under Section 179 BGB — this is agent liability, not an ordinary Section 433 claim.
Internal vs. external boundary No fixed section, framed as “can do” vs. “may do” External power of representation = can do = binds P toward T. Internal relationship (employment/mandate/service) = may do = what A is permitted internally. Violating “may do” while keeping “can do” still binds P externally.
Sources of power of representation Sections 35 GmbHG (statutory), 167 I BGB (declaration), reliance (Section 242 BGB background) Statutory (organ representation), declared (internal or external authorization), or reliance-based (estoppel/ostensible).
Reliance-based authority, two forms No fixed section, course labels: agency by estoppel, ostensible agency Estoppel: P knows and tolerates the appearance. Ostensible: P doesn’t know but should have known with due care. Both give A real power of representation if T relied in good faith.
Termination of authority Section 168 BGB, third-party protection via Sections 170, 173 BGB Authority usually ends with the underlying relationship and is freely revocable. If withdrawal is only told to the agent, a good-faith third party may still be protected unless they knew or should have known.
Self-dealing / contracting with oneself Section 181 BGB Two forms: self-contracting (A is personally the counterparty) and multiple representation (A represents both sides). Transaction is provisionally invalid unless: prior permission, later ratification, mere performance of an existing obligation, or legally advantageous only for the principal.

Nice-to-Have (depth/edge cases)

  • Legal entities (GmbH, AG) cannot physically act — a human act must be attributed to them through an organ (statutory, e.g. Section 35 GmbHG director) or an agent (authorized representative); both routes exist side by side.
  • Section 56 HGB (store/shop authority) can supply publicity and authority for customary retail-style sales made by staff, without needing an explicit declaration each time.
  • With multiple GmbH directors, joint representation is the statutory default unless the articles say otherwise — one director acting alone can fail the authority element even with clear organ status.
  • Collusion between agent and third party can void the transaction under Section 138 BGB even where the agent had formal external authority.
  • If the third party actually knows the agent is exceeding internal limits, the third party’s protection weakens even though the “can do / may do” split normally favors the third party.
  • The “transaction for whom it concerns” exception can substitute for publicity in immediate, low-stakes cash transactions (e.g., paying for fuel or a small purchase) where the buyer’s identity is economically irrelevant — but this is fact-sensitive and arguable, not automatic.
  • Advantages/risks framing (division of labor, capacity, expertise vs. loss of control, information gaps) and the principal-agent problem (hidden characteristics/action/information/intention, and the agency-cost responses: signaling, incentives, surveillance, authority limits) are the bridge from the legal rules to the “why does business design authority this way” theory question.

Nuances And Traps

Nuance/Trap Why it’s easy to get wrong Correct handling
No-publicity consequence It feels intuitive that having authority should still protect the principal, so students conclude P is bound even when A never showed the transaction was for P. Authority cannot rescue missing publicity. If A does not act recognizably in P’s name, P is not bound under Section 164 I regardless of whether A had power of representation; A is likely treated as the contracting party under Section 164 II.
Section 166 BGB misrouting When an agent breaches an internal instruction (e.g., sells below the minimum price), it is tempting to reach for Section 166 BGB because it “sounds like” the general agency-attribution section. Section 166 BGB governs attribution of knowledge or defects of intent through the representative — it is not the anchor for ordinary internal recourse after a breached instruction. The correct route is: P is bound externally (can do intact), and P’s remedy against A is based on the internal relationship (employment, mandate, service duties), not Section 166.
“Wrong declaration of intent” mislabeling Describing an internal-instruction breach as a “wrong declaration of intent” externally sounds plausible but imports a Section 119-style mistake analysis that does not apply here. The correct phrasing is that the declaration is externally effective but internally forbidden — this stays inside the agency can-do/may-do frame instead of drifting into rescission doctrine.
Section 181 exceptions, incomplete list Students often recall only “prior permission” and “later ratification” and stop there. There are four exceptions: prior permission, later ratification (Section 177 BGB), mere performance of an existing obligation, and a transaction that is legally advantageous only for the principal.
Section 181 vs. an ordinary internal-instruction violation Both look like an agent overstepping bounds, so it is tempting to treat self-dealing as just another “may do” breach that still binds P externally. Self-dealing is stronger than an ordinary internal-instruction violation: because there is no independent counterparty bargain, Section 181 can actually restrict A’s external power, not just create internal liability.
Lack of authority vs. abuse of existing authority Any bad agent action can get lumped together as “the agent had no authority.” Distinguish the two: lack of authority triggers the Section 177/179 pending-ratification route; abuse of existing authority (internal-limit violation) keeps the principal bound externally and only creates internal recourse.
Reliance-based authority requires a pattern, not one incident A single unauthorized sale can look enough like “the principal should have noticed.” The exam facts should show a pattern or appearance attributable to P (repeated conduct, use of company materials/records) plus the third party’s reasonable good-faith reliance — one isolated unauthorized act is usually not enough.
Distinguishing agency by estoppel from ostensible agency Both protect a third party who relied on an apparent agency, so the two get merged. Estoppel = P actually knew and tolerated the appearance (conscious tolerance). Ostensible = P did not know, but a careful principal would have noticed and prevented it (negligent failure to control). State which mental state the facts show.

One-Line Recall Drill

164 I = own declaration + publicity + power of representation
164 II = no publicity, hidden intent irrelevant, agent likely bound personally
177 I = pending, principal ratifies
179 I = unauthorized agent liability if ratification refused
167 I = authority by declaration (internal or external)
35 GmbHG = statutory organ representation
168 = authority ends with underlying relationship, freely revocable
170, 173 = third-party protection if withdrawal only told to agent
181 = self-contracting / multiple representation, four exceptions
can do = external, binds principal
may do = internal, breach creates internal recourse only
estoppel = P knows and tolerates
ostensible = P should have known, negligent
166 =/= internal recourse; it is knowledge/defect-of-intent attribution

[W07.3] Week 07 Agency Practice Questions And Model Answers

Source: business-law/wiki/week-07-agency/week-07-agency-practice-questions-and-model-answers.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-07-agency.md, week-07-agency-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md Format note: 26 questions — 10 short-answer/theory, 16 case/legal-opinion (schema-based). Four case questions integrate other weeks: Week 11 Trade Law (Prokura/Handlungsvollmacht), Week 12-13 Company Law (Section 181 BGB self-dealing vs. Section 37 GmbHG internal limits), Week 03 Contract Law I (modified acceptance combined with agency scope), Week 10 Transfer of Property (agency’s reach over the Section 929 agreement element vs. the real-act delivery element).

Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 1

State and apply the three requirements for effective agency under Section 164 I BGB.

Model Answer: 1. Effective agency is the legal institute that lets an agent’s own declaration of intent bind a principal directly toward a third party, defined in Section 164 I BGB. 2. Statutory anchor: Section 164 I BGB. 3. Requirements: (1) an own declaration of intent by the agent, (2) publicity — the declaration is recognizably made in the principal’s name, (3) power of representation. 4. Example: an authorized sales employee negotiates and closes a sale in the shop owner’s name. 5. Consequence/trap: if all three are met, the principal and third party become the contracting parties directly and the agent drops out of the contract; missing any single element defeats agency entirely — it does not partially bind the principal.

Question 2

Compare an agent and a messenger.

Model Answer: 1. An agent forms and declares their own legal will within their authority (Section 164 I BGB); a messenger merely transmits another person’s already-formed, fixed declaration without adding any will of their own. 2. Trigger: agent status is tested under Section 164 I BGB (own declaration, publicity, authority); messenger status is tested under the rules on transmission of a declaration (Section 120 BGB governs transmission errors). 3. Consequence: an effective agent’s declaration binds the principal directly; a messenger’s transmitted declaration is legally the principal’s own declaration, so its validity turns on whether it was transmitted correctly, not on any authority analysis. 4. Contrast example: an employee negotiating price and terms with a customer is an agent; an employee reading a pre-written letter from the owner word-for-word to a customer is a messenger. 5. Exam warning: do not run the Section 164 I agency test on a messenger — analyze transmission (Section 120) instead, since a messenger never formed an “own will” to test for publicity or authority.

Question 3

Compare agency by estoppel and ostensible agency.

Model Answer: 1. Agency by estoppel exists where the principal knows a person appears to act as their agent and tolerates it; ostensible agency exists where the principal does not know but should have known and prevented the appearance through due care. 2. Trigger: both rest on a third party’s good-faith reliance on an appearance of authority created or tolerated by the principal, rather than on an actual declaration under Section 167 I BGB. 3. Consequence: in both cases the law treats the agent as having real power of representation, protecting the good-faith third party’s reliance despite the absence of actual authorization. 4. Contrast example: a principal who watches an unauthorized helper repeatedly close sales in the shop and does nothing is bound by estoppel; a principal who never checks and would have discovered repeated unauthorized use of company letterhead and email with ordinary diligence is bound by ostensible agency. 5. Exam warning: a single isolated unauthorized act is normally not enough for either route — the facts must show a pattern or appearance attributable to the principal plus reasonable reliance; do not conflate general negligence with either specific doctrine.

Question 4

List the requirements (exceptions) that allow a self-dealing transaction to stand despite Section 181 BGB.

Model Answer: The exceptions are: 1. Prior permission — the principal authorized the self-dealing transaction in advance. 2. Later ratification — the principal ratifies the transaction after the fact under Section 177 BGB. 3. Mere performance of an existing obligation — the transaction only fulfills a debt that already exists, so no fresh conflict of interest arises. 4. Legal advantage only for the principal — the transaction brings the principal solely a legal benefit with no corresponding burden.

If none of these applies, the self-dealing or multiple-representation transaction is provisionally invalid and cannot bind the principal. Section 181 exists because an agent who is also the counterparty (or who represents both sides) has a structural conflict of interest, since there is no independent party bargaining against the principal’s interest.

Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 5 (Case)

Facts: Retailer R owns a bookstore. R’s cousin K sometimes helps out unpaid during busy weekends but has no formal employment contract or job title. One Saturday, a regular customer W asks K to order a rare first-edition book. K agrees to source it and quotes a price of EUR 400, without mentioning R or the bookstore at any point during the conversation — W has only ever met K as “R’s cousin who sometimes hangs around” and has no idea K is acting on the bookstore’s behalf. K genuinely intends the transaction to be for the bookstore. Three weeks later, R obtains the book, but W refuses to pay the EUR 400, denying she ever agreed to buy anything from R’s bookstore.

Question: Does R have a claim against W for payment of EUR 400 under Section 433 II BGB?

Model Answer:

I. R could have a claim against W for payment of EUR 400 under Section 433 II BGB if R and W concluded a valid purchase contract, which in turn depends on whether K effectively represented R under Section 164 I BGB when negotiating with W.

  1. Requirements:
  • Contract requires two matching declarations of intent (offer and acceptance).
  • If K, not R, made the relevant declaration, effective representation requires: (1) own declaration of intent, (2) publicity, (3) power of representation.
  • Legal consequence if representation fails.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration: K forms and expresses her own will to sell the book for EUR 400 to W — this is not a mere transmission of R’s pre-fixed words, so K is a candidate agent, not a messenger.
  • Publicity: Questionable is whether K acted recognizably in R’s name. This is supported by K’s genuine intent to act for the bookstore and her habit of helping out there. Against this, one could argue W had no way to recognize this from the conversation — K never mentioned R or the bookstore, and W only knew K informally, not as someone acting for the bookstore in this transaction. However, publicity requires that the third party can recognize from the circumstances that the declaration is made for someone else; a private, undisclosed intention is not enough under Section 164 II BGB. Consequently, publicity is not met.
  • Power of representation: becomes irrelevant once publicity fails, since all three elements of Section 164 I BGB are cumulative.
  1. Interim result: K did not effectively represent R under Section 164 I BGB; Section 164 II BGB applies instead, and K’s hidden intent to act for R is disregarded.

V. Final answer: As a result, no contract was concluded between R and W; K herself is likely treated as the contracting party, so R has no claim against W for the EUR 400 under Section 433 II BGB.

Question 6 (Case)

Facts: Bakery owner B employs C exclusively as a delivery driver; C has no sales authority under her employment contract. While delivering an order, C is approached by a passing café owner, D, who urgently wants to buy B’s entire remaining stock of pastries for a same-day event. C, eager to help, agrees to sell D the pastries for EUR 300, explicitly telling D “I’m selling these on behalf of the bakery.” When B learns of the sale, B is furious because the pastries were reserved for a different regular customer, and B refuses to honor the deal. D, having already promised the pastries to his own event guests, wants to know his options.

Question: Can D demand performance (delivery of the pastries) from C personally under Section 179 I BGB?

Model Answer:

I. D could have a claim against C for performance under Section 179 I BGB if C acted as an unauthorized agent for B and B has refused to ratify the transaction.

  1. Requirements:
  • C made an own declaration of intent in B’s name (candidate agency under Section 164 I BGB).
  • C lacked power of representation for this type of transaction.
  • B refused ratification under Section 177 I BGB.
  • D chooses performance (rather than damages) under Section 179 I BGB.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration and publicity: C forms her own declaration to sell the pastries and explicitly states she is selling “on behalf of the bakery,” so both own declaration and publicity are met.
  • Power of representation: Questionable is whether C’s authority as a delivery driver extends to sales. This is supported by the fact that C’s employment contract covers delivery only. Against this, one could argue any employee visibly representing the business might appear to carry some authority. However, C’s role and the circumstances (an improvised curbside sale of the entire remaining stock) give no objective indication of sales authority, and there are no facts suggesting a pattern of C making sales that B tolerated or should have noticed, so no reliance-based authority arises either. Consequently, C lacked power of representation.
  • Ratification: B refuses to ratify because the pastries were reserved for someone else, satisfying Section 177 I BGB’s refusal condition.
  • Section 179 I choice: D may choose between performance and damages; the facts show D wants the pastries themselves.
  1. Interim result: C acted as an unauthorized agent; B’s refusal to ratify triggers Section 179 I BGB liability against C personally.

V. Final answer: As a result, D can demand performance (delivery of the pastries) from C personally under Section 179 I BGB, since C, not B, is now treated as bound by the sale.

Question 7 (Case)

Facts: GmbH managing director M has broad, unrestricted power of representation for TechParts GmbH, including authority to buy and sell company equipment. M personally owns an old delivery van that the company genuinely needs. Without informing the other shareholders or seeking any prior approval, M signs a purchase contract “on behalf of TechParts GmbH” to buy his own van for EUR 15,000 — a fair market price. When the other shareholders discover the deal, they argue the contract cannot bind the company because M contracted with himself.

Question: Is the purchase contract between M (as seller) and TechParts GmbH (as buyer, represented by M) valid?

Model Answer:

I. The contract’s validity depends on whether M could effectively represent TechParts GmbH under Section 164 I BGB despite Section 181 BGB’s restriction on self-dealing.

  1. Requirements:
  • M acted as TechParts GmbH’s representative (organ representation under Section 35 GmbHG).
  • M is personally the counterparty to the transaction (self-contracting).
  • Section 181 BGB is triggered.
  • Check whether an exception applies: prior permission, later ratification, mere performance of an existing obligation, or legal advantage only for the principal.
  1. Application:
  • Representative capacity: M has organ representation power for TechParts GmbH under Section 35 GmbHG, so M can, in principle, bind the company.
  • Self-contracting: M personally sells the van while simultaneously representing the buyer (TechParts GmbH), so M stands on both sides of the same transaction — this is self-contracting, not merely an internal-instruction issue.
  • Exceptions: Questionable is whether any Section 181 exception applies. This is supported by the fact that the price was fair and the company genuinely needed the van. Against this, one could argue a fair price does not by itself amount to prior permission or later ratification, and the facts show no advance authorization from the shareholders and no subsequent approval — they only object after discovering the deal. The transaction is also not the mere performance of an existing obligation, and it is not legally advantageous only for TechParts GmbH, since the company must pay EUR 15,000. However, with no exception on the facts, Section 181 BGB applies in full.
  • Consequence: because none of the four exceptions is met, M’s self-dealing falls outside his power of representation for this specific transaction.
  1. Interim result: M lacked effective power of representation for this transaction due to Section 181 BGB, notwithstanding his general organ authority.

V. Final answer: As a result, the purchase contract is provisionally invalid; it cannot bind TechParts GmbH unless the company later ratifies it under Section 177 BGB.

Question 8 (Case — integrates Week 07 + Week 11)

Facts: HandelsWaren GmbH is a mid-size wholesale trading company (a merchant by legal form under Section 6 I HGB in conjunction with Section 13 III GmbHG). The managing director grants employee N formal Prokura, duly registered in the commercial register. Internally, the shareholders instruct N never to place single orders above EUR 50,000 without board sign-off — but this limit is never communicated to any customer or supplier. Acting under her Prokura, N signs an EUR 80,000 order with supplier Q for raw materials; Q has no knowledge of the internal EUR 50,000 limit and has dealt with N as HandelsWaren’s authorized signatory before. When the shareholders discover the order, they refuse to accept the delivery, arguing N exceeded her authority.

Question: Is HandelsWaren GmbH bound to accept and pay for the EUR 80,000 order?

Model Answer:

I. HandelsWaren GmbH is bound to Q under the purchase contract if N effectively represented the company, which requires testing both ordinary agency under Section 164 I BGB and the HGB-specific Prokura rules, since HandelsWaren GmbH is a merchant.

  1. Requirements:
  • HandelsWaren GmbH qualifies as a merchant, triggering the HGB layer on top of the BGB baseline.
  • N made an own declaration of intent in the company’s name (Section 164 I BGB elements).
  • N held Prokura, and the scope of Prokura under Sections 48-50 HGB determines whether the internal EUR 50,000 limit defeats her external power.
  • Legal consequence for the EUR 80,000 order.
  1. Application:
  • Merchant status: HandelsWaren GmbH is a GmbH, so it is a merchant by legal form under Section 6 I HGB in conjunction with Section 13 III GmbHG, without needing to run the Section 1 HGB scale test. This triggers HGB rules, including Prokura, on top of the ordinary BGB agency framework.
  • Own declaration and publicity: N forms her own declaration to place the order and signs as HandelsWaren’s registered Prokurist, so both elements of Section 164 I BGB are satisfied. This could also have been analyzed as ordinary Handlungsvollmacht under Section 54 HGB, but N’s status here is the broader, registered Prokura.
  • Power of representation — Prokura scope: Questionable is whether the internal EUR 50,000 cap limits N’s external authority. This is supported by the shareholders’ clear internal instruction. Against this, Section 50 HGB provides that internal restrictions on Prokura are generally ineffective against third parties — the near-unrestrictable statutory scope of Prokura under Section 49 HGB exists precisely so that third parties like Q can rely on a registered Prokurist’s authority without investigating internal limits. However, this protection can fail if the third party knew of the limit or the abuse was obvious; here, Q had no knowledge of the EUR 50,000 cap and had previously dealt with N as an authorized signatory, so nothing on the facts should have put Q on notice. Consequently, the internal limit does not defeat N’s external power of representation.
  1. Interim result: N’s Prokura gave her full external authority to place the EUR 80,000 order despite the internal cap, because Section 50 HGB protects Q’s good-faith reliance.

V. Final answer: As a result, HandelsWaren GmbH is bound to accept and pay for the EUR 80,000 order under the contract with Q; the shareholders’ remedy for N’s breach of the internal instruction lies only in the internal employment/mandate relationship against N, not against Q.

Question 9

List the three statutory sources of power of representation and give one example of each.

Model Answer: The three sources are: 1. Statutory authority — power of representation given directly by law, independent of any individual declaration. Example: Section 35 GmbHG gives a GmbH’s directors representation power simply by virtue of holding the office. 2. Authority by declaration (Section 167 I BGB) — the principal grants authority through a declaration, either internally to the agent or externally to the third party. Example: P orally tells A, “You may sell furniture for me” (internal authorization), or P tells key buyers “A is authorized to sell up to EUR 10,000” (external authorization). 3. Reliance-based authority — power of representation arising from the principal’s own responsible creation or toleration of an appearance of agency, protecting a third party’s good-faith reliance; it splits into agency by estoppel (principal knows and tolerates) and ostensible agency (principal negligently fails to notice and prevent). Example: a principal who watches an unauthorized helper repeatedly close sales and does nothing is bound by estoppel.

If none of these three sources is present, the acting person has no power of representation, and the principal is not bound absent ratification under Section 177 BGB — the three sources are independent routes to the same legal consequence, not cumulative requirements.

Question 10

Explain what happens when a principal revokes an agent’s authority but only tells the agent, not the third party.

Model Answer: 1. This is a third-party-protection issue arising after termination of authority, governed by Section 168 BGB together with Sections 170 and 173 BGB. 2. Statutory anchor: Section 168 BGB (authority usually ends with the underlying relationship and is freely revocable), read with Sections 170, 173 BGB (protection of a good-faith third party after withdrawal). 3. Requirements/features: (1) authority has been effectively revoked internally; (2) the revocation was communicated only to the agent, not to the third party; (3) the third party neither knew nor should have known that authority had ended. 4. Example: P internally revokes A’s authority but never tells regular client Z; A, still holding old business materials, confirms an order with Z, who has dealt with A before and has no reason to suspect anything changed — Z remains protected and P is bound. 5. Trap: ending the underlying relationship (e.g., terminating A’s employment) does not by itself solve the external third-party problem — always ask specifically what the third party was told and whether the third party was in good faith, rather than assuming termination alone cuts off external effect.

Question 11

Compare “lack of authority” and “abuse of existing authority” as agency-law problems.

Model Answer (Compare Schema): Lack of authority exists where the agent never had power of representation for the transaction at all, tested through Sections 177 and 179 BGB: the contract is pending until the principal ratifies, and if the principal refuses, the third party may claim against the unauthorized agent personally under Section 179 BGB. Abuse of existing authority exists where the agent does hold valid external power of representation but violates an internal instruction on how to use it (the “may do” boundary), while the “can do” boundary toward the third party remains intact. Contrast example: a warehouse worker with no sales authority who sells furniture is a lack-of-authority case (pending ratification); a sales manager told internally never to sell below EUR 10,000 who nonetheless sells to an unaware buyer for EUR 8,000 is an abuse-of-authority case (principal is bound externally, remedy is internal against the agent). Exam trap: do not lump every “bad” agent action into “no authority” — abuse of existing authority keeps the principal bound externally, and the correct remedy lies in the internal relationship (employment, mandate, service duties), not in Sections 177/179 or in Section 166 BGB.

Question 12

List the four hidden information problems in the principal-agent problem, with the corresponding agency-cost response for each.

Model Answer: 1. Hidden characteristics (adverse selection) — the agent is unsuitable for the role before hiring; addressed by signaling and screening (e.g., certificates, assessment centers). 2. Hidden action (moral hazard) — the agent behaves badly after being hired, where the principal cannot fully observe conduct; addressed by incentives (e.g., performance-linked bonuses). 3. Hidden information (moral hazard) — the agent knows more than the principal can assess about the situation; addressed by surveillance (e.g., dual-control or joint-representation requirements). 4. Hidden intention — the agent’s underlying motivation is not aligned with the principal’s interest; addressed by limitation of authority, particularly external authorization that tells third parties the boundary of what the agent may do.

Trap: these are information/motivation problems from economics, not separate legal doctrines — the legal agency rules (Section 164 I BGB requirements, Section 181 BGB, ratification) determine who is bound, while the principal-agent framework explains why businesses design authority limits, bonus systems, and monitoring in the first place; don’t present the four categories as if they were statutory requirements.

Question 13 (Case)

Facts: Print shop owner O never explicitly authorizes intern I to sign contracts. Over several months, I repeatedly uses O’s letterhead and O’s business email account to confirm print orders with regular client X, signing “on behalf of PrintShop O.” O has easy access to the outgoing email folder and multiple opportunities to notice this but never checks it. X, relying on this established pattern, places a large order with I for a batch of prints worth EUR 2,000. O refuses to fulfill it, claiming I was never authorized to sign anything.

Question: Is O bound to X for the EUR 2,000 order?

Model Answer:

I. O could be bound to X under a purchase/service contract for EUR 2,000 if I effectively represented O, which turns on whether ostensible agency supplies the power of representation I otherwise lacks.

  1. Requirements:
  • I made an own declaration of intent in O’s name (publicity via letterhead/email).
  • I lacked actual statutory or declared authority.
  • Ostensible agency requires: an appearance of authority attributable to O (pattern/negligent failure to control) plus X’s good-faith reasonable reliance.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration and publicity: I forms and signs order confirmations “on behalf of PrintShop O” using O’s own letterhead and email account — clearly recognizable to X as acting for O.
  • Actual authority: no facts show O ever declared authority to I under Section 167 I BGB, and no statutory route applies, so actual power of representation is absent.
  • Ostensible agency: Questionable is whether O’s negligent failure to monitor creates reliance-based authority. This is supported by the repeated, months-long pattern of I using O’s official channels — not an isolated act — combined with O’s easy ability to check outgoing correspondence and consistent failure to do so. Against this, one could argue O never affirmatively created the appearance and merely stayed passive. However, ostensible agency’s essence is exactly this kind of negligent failure to prevent an appearance the principal could and should have discovered with due care; O’s access to the account and the repeated conduct meet that bar. Consequently, the appearance is attributable to O.
  • X’s reliance: X is a regular client who has observed this pattern and had no reason to doubt I’s authority; nothing on the facts suggests X knew or should have known I lacked authority, so X’s reliance is in good faith.
  1. Interim result: Ostensible agency supplies I with real power of representation for this transaction.

V. Final answer: As a result, O is bound to X for the EUR 2,000 order; O’s remedy, if any, lies internally against I.

Question 14 (Case)

Facts: Boutique owner B never assigns anyone a formal cashier or sales title. Sales assistant J, hired under a contract covering stock organizing only (no customer-facing sales duties), steps behind the register during a rush and sells customer Y a jacket at the marked price, processing payment through the store’s standard till and handing over a receipt. B later argues that J had no authority to sell anything, since her job was stock-keeping only.

Question: Did the boutique conclude a valid sale to Y?

Model Answer:

I. B’s boutique could be bound to Y under Section 433 BGB if J effectively represented B, which requires testing Section 164 I BGB together with whether Section 56 HGB’s shop-authority rule supplies the needed power of representation despite J’s contractually limited role.

  1. Requirements:
  • J’s own declaration and publicity (acting within the store, at the register).
  • Power of representation: check actual/declared authority first, then Section 56 HGB customary-shop-sale authority.
  • Any facts cutting against Y’s good-faith reliance.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration and publicity: J rings up the sale and hands over the jacket at the register inside B’s boutique — an ordinary retail transaction recognizably made for the shop, satisfying own declaration and publicity.
  • Actual/declared authority: J’s employment contract covers stock organizing only, so no explicit declared authority under Section 167 I BGB covers sales.
  • Section 56 HGB: Questionable is whether Section 56 HGB nonetheless supplies authority because J was employed and acting within a commercial shop for a customary, everyday retail-type transaction. This is supported by the boutique being a typical retail business where a staff member processing a routine register sale is the customary appearance presented to any customer, and Y has no way to know J’s internal job title is stock-only. Against this, one could argue J was never assigned register duties and B never intended her to sell. However, Section 56 HGB authority attaches to the objective appearance of an employee acting in a shop for a customary sale, not to the employee’s internal job description, and Y could not be expected to inquire about internal titles before buying a jacket at a marked price. Consequently, Section 56 HGB authority applies.
  1. Interim result: J had power of representation under Section 56 HGB despite lacking sales duties under her employment contract.

V. Final answer: As a result, the boutique concluded a valid sale to Y; B cannot rely on J’s internal job limitation to defeat the contract, though B may address the situation internally with J.

Question 15 (Case)

Facts: P revokes A’s authority to negotiate deals after A leaves the company but only tells A internally, never informing longtime client Z, who has ordered goods through A many times before. Two weeks after leaving, A — still holding old business cards and P’s former letterhead — visits Z and “confirms” a new order in P’s name for EUR 5,000. Z, unaware anything changed, agrees. P refuses to honor the order, arguing A’s authority had already ended.

Question: Is P bound to Z for the EUR 5,000 order?

Model Answer:

I. P could be bound to Z if A still had effective power of representation at the time of the order despite the internal revocation, which turns on third-party protection under Sections 168, 170, 173 BGB.

  1. Requirements:
  • A’s own declaration and publicity.
  • Authority formally ended (Section 168 BGB revocation).
  • Whether Z is nonetheless protected because withdrawal was only declared to A, not to Z, and Z neither knew nor should have known (Sections 170, 173 BGB).
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration/publicity: A confirms the order in P’s name using P’s old letterhead, so both elements are met.
  • Revocation: P validly revoked A’s authority under Section 168 BGB; internally, A no longer has authority.
  • Third-party protection: Questionable is whether Z is protected despite the revocation. This is supported by the fact that P only communicated the withdrawal internally to A and never informed Z, a longtime client who had dealt with A many times before and had every reason to expect A still represented P. Against this, one could argue A’s departure and the passage of two weeks should have prompted Z to double-check. However, Sections 170 and 173 BGB place the burden on the principal to notify third parties who relied on a previously-exercised authority; Z had no actual knowledge of the revocation and nothing on the facts suggests Z should have known, since P made no external announcement. Consequently, Z remains protected.
  1. Interim result: A’s authority, though internally revoked, remains effective against P in relation to Z under Sections 170, 173 BGB.

V. Final answer: As a result, P is bound to Z for the EUR 5,000 order; P’s recourse is only against A internally for acting after authority had ended.

Question 16 (Case — integrates Week 07 + Week 12-13)

Facts: Bau-Tech GmbH’s managing director L has statutory representation power under Section 35 GmbHG. The articles of association internally cap L’s authority to sign purchase contracts at EUR 20,000 without shareholder approval — this cap is not publicly disclosed and is unknown to the company’s regular steel supplier, ST GmbH. Separately, L signs a contract “on behalf of Bau-Tech GmbH” to buy a used company car from himself personally for EUR 12,000, a fair price, without first asking the other shareholders. When the shareholders find out, they object to both: (a) the car purchase, and (b) a EUR 35,000 steel order L signed with ST GmbH that exceeds the internal EUR 20,000 cap.

Question: Is Bau-Tech GmbH bound to (a) buy L’s car, and (b) pay ST GmbH for the steel order?

Model Answer:

I. Bau-Tech GmbH’s liability for each transaction depends on whether L had effective power of representation under Section 164 I BGB and, for organ representation, Sections 35, 37 GmbHG, with transaction (a) additionally engaging Section 181 BGB self-dealing.

  1. Requirements:
  • L acts as organ representative under Section 35 GmbHG (statutory power).
  • Section 37 GmbHG: internal limits generally do not bind externally.
  • Transaction (a): Section 181 BGB self-dealing and its four exceptions.
  • Transaction (b): whether the EUR 20,000 internal cap defeats ST GmbH’s reliance.
  1. Application:
    1. Car purchase: L represents Bau-Tech GmbH under Section 35 GmbHG while also being personally the seller — this is self-contracting, triggering Section 181 BGB. Questionable is whether an exception applies. This is supported only by the fair market price of EUR 12,000. Against this, there is no prior shareholder permission, no later ratification (the shareholders are objecting, not approving), the transaction is not the mere performance of an existing obligation, and it is not legally advantageous to Bau-Tech GmbH alone since the GmbH must pay EUR 12,000. However, a fair price alone does not satisfy any of the four Section 181 exceptions. Consequently, L lacked effective power of representation for the car purchase.
    1. Steel order: L represents Bau-Tech GmbH under Section 35 GmbHG for an ordinary transaction with ST GmbH, an independent counterparty — no self-dealing issue arises here. Questionable is whether the internal EUR 20,000 cap defeats L’s authority toward ST GmbH. This is supported by the shareholders’ clear internal restriction in the articles. Against this, Section 37 GmbHG provides that internal limitations on a director’s representation power generally do not affect its external effect — mirroring the agency-law can-do/may-do split under Section 164 I BGB — and nothing on the facts shows ST GmbH knew or should have known of the unpublished cap. However, since ST GmbH is an ordinary independent third party dealing at arm’s length with no facts suggesting bad faith, Section 37 GmbHG protects the transaction’s external validity despite the internal breach. Consequently, the internal cap does not defeat L’s authority toward ST GmbH.
  1. Interim results: (a) L’s self-dealing car purchase fell outside his power of representation absent any Section 181 exception; (b) L’s steel order remains within his external power of representation despite breaching the internal cap.

V. Final answer: As a result, Bau-Tech GmbH is not bound to buy L’s car (provisionally invalid unless later ratified under Section 177 BGB), but Bau-Tech GmbH is bound to pay ST GmbH for the EUR 35,000 steel order; the shareholders’ remedy against L for exceeding the internal cap lies only internally, e.g. under Section 43 I GmbHG duty-of-care/loyalty liability, not against ST GmbH.

Question 17 (Case — integrates Week 07 + Week 03)

Facts: Furniture retailer R authorizes sales agent A, by declaration under Section 167 I BGB, to accept offers for the “Nordic” sofa line strictly at the listed catalog price of EUR 900, with no discretion over delivery terms. Customer C sends R’s shop a written offer to buy a Nordic sofa for EUR 900 “with free delivery included.” A, eager to close the sale and clearly stating “I accept on behalf of R,” replies “Agreed, EUR 900, but delivery costs EUR 50 extra.” C never responds further. Weeks later, C arrives expecting a concluded contract with free delivery; R claims no contract was ever formed, and separately argues that even if A’s reply could be seen as forming something, A had no authority to change the delivery terms.

Question: Was a contract concluded between R and C, and is R bound by A’s reply?

Model Answer:

I. Whether R and C concluded a contract depends first on ordinary offer/acceptance analysis under Sections 145, 150 II BGB, and second — since A, not R, made the relevant declaration — on whether A effectively represented R for that declaration under Section 164 I BGB.

  1. Requirements:
  • C’s written offer must meet essentialia negotii (Section 145 BGB).
  • A’s reply must be tested under Section 150 II BGB (modified acceptance = rejection + new offer).
  • A’s reply, if a new offer, is attributed to R only if A had own declaration, publicity, and power of representation (Section 164 I BGB).
  • Power of representation is scoped by A’s actual declared authority (accept at catalog price only).
  1. Application:
  • C’s offer: naming the sofa, the EUR 900 price, and free delivery gives sufficiently definite essentialia negotii, so C made a valid offer under Section 145 BGB.
  • A’s reply as modified acceptance: A’s reply changes a term of C’s offer (adding EUR 50 for delivery instead of free delivery). Under Section 150 II BGB, any change to the offer’s terms counts as rejection of the original offer and a new counteroffer, regardless of A using the word “agreed.” So no contract formed on C’s original terms.
  • Attribution of A’s counteroffer to R: A makes an own declaration and clearly states she acts on R’s behalf, satisfying own declaration and publicity. Questionable is whether A had power of representation to make this specific counteroffer. This is supported by A’s actual declared authority extending only to accepting the EUR 900 catalog price, with no discretion over delivery terms. Against this, one could argue closing sales generally implies some flexibility on ancillary terms like delivery. However, the facts expressly limit A’s authority to accepting at the listed price, and altering delivery terms goes beyond that scope. Consequently, A acted without authority in making the counteroffer.
  • Consequence: R is not automatically bound by A’s unauthorized counteroffer; R could ratify it under Section 177 I BGB, but nothing on the facts shows ratification, and in any event C never accepted A’s counteroffer, so no contract exists on those terms either.
  1. Interim result: C’s original offer was rejected by A’s modified reply under Section 150 II BGB; A’s own counteroffer exceeded her authority and never bound R, and C never accepted it in any event.

V. Final answer: As a result, no contract was concluded between R and C — not on C’s original free-delivery terms (rejected via modified acceptance) and not on A’s EUR 50-delivery counteroffer (unauthorized, and never accepted by C); R is not bound to sell C the sofa on the facts as they stand.

Question 18 (Case)

Facts: Art broker K holds declared authority (Section 167 I BGB) from gallery owner G to sell paintings on G’s behalf, and separately holds declared authority from collector H to buy paintings on H’s behalf — two independent agency relationships, with the dual role disclosed to neither principal. K arranges the sale of one of G’s paintings to H for EUR 25,000, signing the sale-purchase contract “on behalf of G” as seller’s representative and “on behalf of H” as buyer’s representative in the same document. When G later learns K also represented H, G refuses to deliver the painting, arguing the contract cannot bind her.

Question: Is the sale-purchase contract between G and H valid?

Model Answer:

I. The contract’s validity depends on whether K could effectively represent both G and H under Section 164 I BGB despite Section 181 BGB’s restriction on multiple representation.

  1. Requirements:
  • K acts as representative for both sides of the same transaction (multiple representation).
  • Section 181 BGB is triggered.
  • Check the four exceptions: prior permission, later ratification, mere performance of an existing obligation, legal advantage only for the principal.
  1. Application:
  • Multiple representation: K signs the same contract as representative for both seller G and buyer H, so K represents both sides of one transaction — the second form of Section 181 BGB, distinct from self-contracting.
  • Exceptions: Questionable is whether any exception rescues the transaction. This is supported by nothing specific on the facts beyond the sale appearing ordinary. Against this, there is no indication G gave K prior permission to also act for H, no later ratification (G refuses once she learns of the dual role), the transaction is not the mere performance of a pre-existing obligation, and it is not legally advantageous only to G since G must actually deliver the painting. However, with none of the four exceptions met, Section 181 BGB applies in full.
  1. Interim result: K lacked effective power of representation for the sale due to unresolved multiple representation under Section 181 BGB.

V. Final answer: As a result, the sale-purchase contract is provisionally invalid; it cannot bind G (or H) unless one or both principals later ratify it under Section 177 BGB.

Question 19

Compare Section 164 II BGB and Section 179 BGB as agency-law problems.

Model Answer (Compare Schema): Section 164 II BGB is a publicity failure: the acting person never showed, expressly or by circumstances, that they intended to act in someone else’s name, so the law disregards any private intent to represent another and treats the actor as bound personally to the transaction — the analysis never reaches the question of authority at all. Section 179 BGB is an authority failure: the acting person did disclose that they were acting for a principal (publicity is satisfied), but lacked power of representation for the transaction, so the contract is provisionally ineffective pending the principal’s ratification under Section 177 I BGB, and if the principal refuses, the third party may claim performance or damages from the unauthorized agent personally under Section 179 I BGB. Contrast example: an employee who quietly intends to buy fuel “for the boss” without ever saying so is a Section 164 II case — the employee is bound personally regardless of the missing authority question. An employee who explicitly says “I’m buying this for the boss” but was only ever authorized to buy snacks, not fuel, is a Section 179 case — the disclosed representative capacity is not in doubt, only the scope of authority. Exam trap: do not skip straight to a Section 179 authority analysis without first confirming publicity is even met — if publicity fails, the case ends at Section 164 II and Section 179 liability is never reached, because Section 179 presupposes the agent’s disclosed representative capacity was already established.

Question 20

Explain what Section 166 BGB actually governs, and why it is not the answer to an internal-instruction-breach question.

Model Answer: 1. Section 166 BGB is the knowledge-attribution rule in agency law: where the legal effect of a declaration of intent depends on the presence, absence, or particular knowledge of certain circumstances, it is the agent’s — not the principal’s — knowledge or culpable ignorance that counts, since the agent is the one who actually forms and expresses the relevant declaration. 2. Statutory anchor: Section 166 BGB. 3. Requirements/features: (1) a declaration of intent was made through an agent under effective representation; (2) the legal consequence of that declaration turns on knowledge of some fact or a defect of intent (e.g., knowing about a defect, acting in bad faith); (3) it is the agent’s actual knowledge or the agent’s negligent ignorance that is imputed to the principal for that purpose, not the principal’s own state of mind — subject to the exception that a principal who gave specific instructions cannot hide behind an agent who carried them out in ignorance of facts the principal actually knew. 4. Example: a principal who has no idea a car has a hidden defect authorizes an agent to sell it; if the agent independently knows about the defect and stays silent, the agent’s knowledge is imputed to the principal for purposes of a fraudulent-concealment analysis, even though the principal personally never knew. 5. Trap: Section 166 BGB is not the anchor for an ordinary internal-instruction breach (e.g., an agent selling below an internally set minimum price) — that scenario stays inside the agency “can do” (external, binds the principal) versus “may do” (internal, recourse against the agent through the underlying employment/mandate/service relationship) framework; reaching for Section 166 there is a common misrouting error.

Question 21 (Case)

Facts: Fresh-GmbH has two managing directors, X and Y, jointly registered in the commercial register with joint representation as the default rule in the articles of association — no provision grants either director sole signing power. Supplier V, unaware of the joint-representation requirement, negotiates a EUR 40,000 delivery contract only with X, who signs “on behalf of Fresh-GmbH” alone, without consulting Y. When Y discovers the signed contract, Y refuses to approve it, believing the terms are unfavorable.

Question: Is Fresh-GmbH bound to V under the EUR 40,000 contract?

Model Answer:

I. Fresh-GmbH’s liability to V depends on whether X alone had effective power of representation under Section 164 I BGB in conjunction with Section 35 GmbHG’s organ-representation rule.

  1. Requirements:
  • X made an own declaration of intent in Fresh-GmbH’s name (publicity satisfied by signing “on behalf of” the company).
  • Power of representation for a GmbH organ is governed by Section 35 GmbHG; with several directors, joint representation is the statutory default unless the articles of association provide otherwise.
  • Consequence if X’s sole signature does not meet the applicable representation rule.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration and publicity: X forms and signs a declaration explicitly for Fresh-GmbH, so both elements are met without difficulty.
  • Power of representation: Questionable is whether X alone could bind Fresh-GmbH. This is supported by X’s status as a duly registered managing director with organ representation power in principle. Against this, the articles of association set joint representation as the default, and nothing in the facts shows any provision granting X sole signing power. However, Section 35 GmbHG’s joint-representation default means a single director’s signature does not, by itself, satisfy the power-of-representation element unless the articles depart from that default — and the facts state no such departure exists. Consequently, X lacked power of representation to bind Fresh-GmbH alone.
  1. Interim result: X’s sole signature did not meet Fresh-GmbH’s joint-representation requirement, so X lacked effective power of representation for this transaction.

V. Final answer: As a result, Fresh-GmbH is not bound to V under the EUR 40,000 contract unless Y (or both directors jointly) later ratifies it under Section 177 I BGB; since Y refuses, the contract remains provisionally ineffective, and V’s recourse, if any, lies against X personally under Section 179 BGB.

Question 22 (Case)

Facts: Procurement manager J holds broad, externally communicated authority to sign supply contracts for MetalWorks GmbH up to EUR 100,000. Supplier K secretly agrees to pay J a personal EUR 5,000 kickback if J signs an inflated EUR 90,000 order for goods actually worth EUR 60,000, and J does so, signing clearly “on behalf of MetalWorks GmbH.” MetalWorks GmbH later discovers the kickback arrangement and refuses to pay the EUR 90,000, arguing the contract cannot bind it despite J’s apparent authority.

Question: Is MetalWorks GmbH bound to pay K the EUR 90,000?

Model Answer:

I. MetalWorks GmbH’s liability depends on whether J’s formal power of representation under Section 164 I BGB is defeated by the collusive arrangement with K under Section 138 BGB.

  1. Requirements:
  • J made an own declaration of intent in MetalWorks GmbH’s name, with externally communicated power of representation covering this transaction.
  • Ordinary “can do vs. may do” analysis would treat J’s authority as intact even if J’s conduct also breaches internal duties.
  • Collusion between the agent and the third party can override formal authority and void the transaction under Section 138 BGB (violation of public policy/good morals).
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration, publicity, and formal authority: J signs explicitly for MetalWorks GmbH and holds externally communicated authority up to EUR 100,000, a limit the EUR 90,000 order does not exceed, so on an ordinary agency analysis J’s declaration would bind MetalWorks GmbH.
  • Collusion: Questionable is whether the secret kickback arrangement defeats this otherwise-valid authority. This is supported by K’s active participation in a scheme where J deliberately signs an inflated order in exchange for a personal payment — this is not a unilateral breach of an internal instruction that K is merely unaware of, but a two-sided arrangement where K knowingly helps J betray MetalWorks GmbH’s interest. Against this, one could argue the price still falls within J’s externally communicated authority limit, so the “can do” boundary is nominally intact. However, ordinary internal/external protection exists to protect good-faith third parties, not third parties who actively collude with the agent against the principal’s interest; where agent and third party collude to harm the principal, the transaction offends public policy and falls under Section 138 BGB regardless of formal authority. Consequently, the collusion defeats J’s otherwise-valid power of representation for this transaction.
  1. Interim result: The collusive kickback arrangement between J and K voids the transaction under Section 138 BGB, notwithstanding J’s formal, externally communicated authority.
