V. Final answer: As a result, MetalWorks GmbH is not bound to pay K the EUR 90,000; the contract is void, and MetalWorks GmbH’s remedies against J (internally) and potentially against K remain separate from any claim under the void supply contract.

Question 23 (Case)

Facts: At a self-service gas station, driver N fills up a company van registered to Logistics-Plus GmbH and pays cash at the counter without saying a word about who owns the van or on whose behalf she is buying the fuel. Attendant P sees the company livery on the van but has no idea whether N is buying for herself or for her employer. Two days later, N’s employer disputes the fuel bill, claiming N had no authority to buy fuel and that Logistics-Plus GmbH never contracted with the gas station at all.

Question: Did Logistics-Plus GmbH conclude the fuel purchase contract with the gas station, or is N personally bound?

Model Answer:

I. Whether Logistics-Plus GmbH or N is the contracting party for the fuel purchase depends on whether the publicity requirement of Section 164 I BGB is met or excused for this transaction.

  1. Requirements:
  • N made an own declaration of intent to buy the fuel.
  • Publicity: P must be able to recognize, expressly or by circumstances, that N acts for Logistics-Plus GmbH rather than personally.
  • Possible substitute for publicity in an immediate, low-stakes cash transaction where the buyer’s identity is economically irrelevant to the other side (“transaction for whom it concerns”).
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration: N forms her own will to buy the fuel and pay for it, so she is a candidate agent, not a mere messenger.
  • Publicity: Questionable is whether P could recognize N was acting for Logistics-Plus GmbH. This is supported by the company livery visibly displayed on the van, which gives some circumstantial indication of a business context. Against this, N says nothing at all about acting for her employer, and P has no actual way of knowing whether N is buying fuel for herself, for a personal reason, or for the company — company-liveried vehicles can still be fueled by an employee for mixed or unclear purposes. However, this is exactly the kind of immediate, fully-settled cash transaction where the identity of the contracting party is arguably economically irrelevant to the gas station, which only cares that the pump price gets paid on the spot — a point on which course materials treat the “transaction for whom it concerns” substitute for publicity as arguable rather than automatic. Consequently, whether publicity is satisfied or excused here is a genuinely close call that should be argued both ways rather than asserted outright.
  1. Interim result: If the “transaction for whom it concerns” exception applies, Logistics-Plus GmbH is bound; if not, publicity fails and N is bound personally under Section 164 II BGB.

V. Final answer: As a result, the outcome turns on which side of this arguable publicity question is taken: on the stronger reading (immediate cash transaction, identity economically irrelevant), Logistics-Plus GmbH concluded the fuel purchase; on the stricter reading (no actual words or unambiguous circumstances showing agency), N is bound personally and Logistics-Plus GmbH owes nothing to the gas station.

Question 24 (Case)

Facts: Sales manager R has externally communicated authority to sell inventory for Home-Deco GmbH, subject to an internal instruction never to sell below EUR 15,000 per unit for the “Alpine” cabinet line — an instruction R once mentioned out loud to buyer T during an earlier, unrelated negotiation where T happened to be present. Months later, R sells T an Alpine cabinet for EUR 11,000, and T, remembering the EUR 15,000 floor R had mentioned before, accepts the discounted price without asking any questions. Home-Deco GmbH refuses to honor the sale.

Question: Is Home-Deco GmbH bound to sell T the cabinet for EUR 11,000?

Model Answer:

I. Home-Deco GmbH’s liability depends on whether R’s power of representation, though formally intact under the ordinary internal/external split, is defeated here because T knew of the internal EUR 15,000 floor.

  1. Requirements:
  • R made an own declaration of intent in Home-Deco GmbH’s name with externally communicated authority to sell inventory.
  • Ordinarily, an internal-instruction breach (abuse of existing authority) still binds the principal externally, leaving only an internal remedy against the agent.
  • Exception: if the third party actually knows the agent is exceeding the internal limit, the third party’s usual protection weakens.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration, publicity, and formal external authority: R sells the cabinet explicitly for Home-Deco GmbH and holds general external authority to sell inventory, so on the ordinary “can do” analysis R’s declaration would bind Home-Deco GmbH.
  • Internal-limit breach: R’s EUR 11,000 price breaches the internal EUR 15,000 floor for the Alpine line, which is ordinarily just an internal “may do” problem that does not affect the external validity of the sale.
  • T’s knowledge: Questionable is whether T’s actual awareness of the EUR 15,000 floor changes the result. This is supported by the facts stating R had personally told T about the internal instruction on an earlier occasion, and T explicitly recalls it at the time of this sale. Against this, one could argue the internal/external split exists precisely to protect third parties from having to investigate internal limits, and T did not affirmatively investigate anything here. However, that protective purpose only extends to third parties who neither knew nor should have known of the limit; a third party with actual knowledge of the specific internal restriction cannot claim the benefit of a rule designed to protect good-faith reliance, because there is no good faith to protect. Consequently, T’s actual knowledge defeats reliance on R’s ordinarily-intact external authority for this specific transaction.
  1. Interim result: R’s external authority, though formally unaffected by an ordinary internal-instruction breach, does not protect T here because T actually knew of the EUR 15,000 floor.

V. Final answer: As a result, Home-Deco GmbH is not bound to sell T the cabinet for EUR 11,000; Home-Deco GmbH may refuse to honor the below-floor sale, and any consequence for R’s breach remains an internal matter between R and Home-Deco GmbH.

Question 25 (Case)

Facts: Antique collector Q instructs agent M, by declaration under Section 167 I BGB, to buy a specific 18th-century clock at an upcoming auction, up to EUR 8,000. At the auction, that clock is withdrawn, but M — without asking Q first — buys a different, comparable 18th-century clock instead for EUR 7,500, explaining the substitution to auctioneer S at the time of purchase. Q says nothing when M delivers the clock, displays it prominently in Q’s collection room, and shows it to visiting friends over the following weeks without ever objecting to M or S.

Question: Is Q bound to pay S the EUR 7,500 for the substitute clock?

Model Answer:

I. Q could be bound to S for the EUR 7,500 clock if M’s initially unauthorized purchase became effective through Q’s later ratification under Section 177 I BGB.

  1. Requirements:
  • M made an own declaration of intent in Q’s name (publicity satisfied via M’s explanation to S).
  • M’s declared authority was limited to the specific withdrawn clock, so the substitute purchase exceeded that authority.
  • Ratification under Section 177 I BGB can retroactively validate an unauthorized agent’s transaction through the principal’s approval, which can be given expressly or through unambiguous conduct.
  1. Application:
  • Own declaration and publicity: M forms his own declaration to buy the substitute clock and explains the situation to S, so both elements are satisfied.
  • Power of representation: Q’s declared authority under Section 167 I BGB was limited to the specific withdrawn clock up to EUR 8,000; a different, merely comparable clock falls outside that specific instruction, so M acted without authority for the substitute purchase.
  • Ratification: Questionable is whether Q’s conduct amounts to ratification. This is supported by Q accepting delivery of the clock, prominently displaying it in the collection room, and showing it to visitors over an extended period without any objection to M or S. Against this, one could argue Q never said a single word approving the purchase, so there is no express ratification. However, ratification under Section 177 I BGB does not require an express statement — unambiguous conduct consistent only with approval is sufficient, and openly integrating the clock into the collection and showcasing it to others for weeks is conduct incompatible with any intent to reject the purchase. Consequently, Q’s conduct constitutes implicit ratification.
  1. Interim result: M’s initially unauthorized substitute purchase was retroactively validated by Q’s implicit ratification.

V. Final answer: As a result, Q is bound to pay S the EUR 7,500 for the substitute clock; the ratification cures M’s lack of authority from the outset.

Question 26 (Case — integrates Week 07 + Week 10)

Facts: Warehouse operator W GmbH authorizes employee F, by declaration under Section 167 I BGB, to sell a specific forklift stored in the warehouse to buyer Z and to hand over possession on the company’s behalf. F meets Z, signs the sale agreement clearly “on behalf of W GmbH,” and separately walks Z to the warehouse bay and physically hands over the forklift’s keys. Later, W GmbH argues that F’s authority under Section 164 I BGB only covers declarations of intent, so the physical handover of the forklift needs a separate, additional showing of agency authority that the facts do not establish, meaning ownership never passed to Z.

Question: Did ownership of the forklift pass from W GmbH to Z?

Model Answer:

I. Ownership passes to Z under Section 929 sentence 1 BGB if the agreement, delivery, continued agreement at delivery, and authorization elements are met, which requires separately analyzing how agency law applies to the agreement element versus the delivery element.

  1. Requirements:
  • Section 929 sentence 1 BGB: (1) agreement between owner and acquirer that ownership shall pass, (2) delivery of the thing, (3) the agreement still existing at the time of delivery, (4) the transferor’s authorization to dispose.
  • The agreement is a declaration of intent, so Section 164 I BGB agency rules (own declaration, publicity, power of representation) apply to test whether F’s agreement bound W GmbH.
  • Delivery is a real/factual act, not a declaration of intent, so Section 164 ff. does not apply directly to the handover itself; a representative’s physical handover on the principal’s behalf is instead a question of possession through an agent in possession under Section 855 BGB, not a second agency test.
  1. Application:
  • Agreement element: F, authorized under Section 167 I BGB to sell the forklift, makes his own declaration that ownership shall pass to Z and signs clearly on W GmbH’s behalf — own declaration, publicity, and power of representation are all met, so the disposition agreement is effectively attributed to W GmbH under Section 164 I BGB.
  • Delivery element: Questionable is whether F additionally needs separate agency authority to perform the physical handover. This is supported by W GmbH’s argument that Section 164 I is agency’s only gateway and nothing else should count without it. Against this, delivery under Section 929 sentence 1 BGB is a real act of physically transferring control over the thing, not a further declaration of intent — the course materials are explicit that agency rules govern the agreement, not the handover itself, and a person handing over an item on the owner’s instruction is analyzed as holding or transferring possession on the owner’s behalf under Section 855 BGB, not as needing a fresh Section 164 I test. However, since F was already validly authorized to sell and hand over the forklift by W GmbH’s instruction, and F’s physical handover of the keys is exactly the kind of factual act Section 855 BGB accommodates without requiring separate agency formalities, the delivery element is satisfied once F physically hands the forklift over to Z. Consequently, W GmbH’s argument that a second agency showing is needed for delivery fails.
  • Remaining elements: nothing in the facts suggests the agreement lapsed before delivery or that W GmbH lacked authorization to dispose of its own forklift, so those elements are met without further issue.
  1. Interim result: All four elements of Section 929 sentence 1 BGB are satisfied — the agreement was validly attributed to W GmbH via ordinary Section 164 I agency analysis, and the delivery was validly completed as a real act without needing a separate agency test.

V. Final answer: As a result, ownership of the forklift passed from W GmbH to Z; W GmbH’s objection that delivery needed independent agency authority misapplies Section 164 I BGB to a real act it does not govern.

Quick Answer Route Summary

Question # Primary Route/Section One-line takeaway
Q1 Section 164 I BGB Three cumulative elements of effective agency.
Q2 Section 164 I BGB vs. Section 120 BGB Agent forms own will; messenger only transmits.
Q3 Reliance-based authority Estoppel = principal knew and tolerated; ostensible = principal should have known.
Q4 Section 181 BGB Four exceptions to the self-dealing bar.
Q5 (Case) Section 164 II BGB No publicity means hidden intent is irrelevant; the actor is bound personally.
Q6 (Case) Sections 177 I, 179 I BGB No authority plus refused ratification triggers unauthorized-agent liability.
Q7 (Case) Section 181 BGB Self-dealing without an exception blocks the organ’s external power.
Q8 (Case, integrates Week 11) Section 50 HGB (Prokura) Internal Prokura limits generally don’t bind a good-faith third party.
Q9 Sections 35 GmbHG, 167 I BGB, reliance Three independent sources of authority — statutory, declared, reliance-based.
Q10 Sections 168, 170, 173 BGB Revocation told only to the agent still leaves a good-faith third party protected.
Q11 Sections 177, 179 BGB vs. can do/may do Lack of authority = pending ratification; abuse of authority = bound externally, internal remedy only.
Q12 Principal-agent problem Four hidden-information problems map to four agency-cost responses.
Q13 (Case) Ostensible agency Negligent, months-long failure to control an appearance binds the principal via reliance.
Q14 (Case) Section 56 HGB Customary shop-sale authority binds despite an internal stock-only job title.
Q15 (Case) Sections 168, 170, 173 BGB Third party protected when revocation is told only to the agent, not to them.
Q16 (Case, integrates Week 12-13) Section 181 BGB vs. Section 37 GmbHG Self-dealing blocks authority; an internal cap alone does not.
Q17 (Case, integrates Week 03) Sections 150 II, 164 I BGB Modified “acceptance” is a new offer; the agent’s unauthorized counteroffer never binds the principal.
Q18 (Case) Section 181 BGB (multiple representation) Representing both sides of one deal blocks authority absent an exception.
Q19 Section 164 II BGB vs. Section 179 BGB Publicity failure ends the case before authority is ever tested — don’t skip the order.
Q20 Section 166 BGB Agent’s knowledge (not the principal’s) counts — not the anchor for internal-instruction recourse.
Q21 (Case) Section 35 GmbHG joint representation One director’s solo signature fails the default joint-representation requirement.
Q22 (Case) Section 138 BGB (collusion) Agent-third-party collusion voids the deal even within a formally intact authority limit.
Q23 (Case) Publicity / “transaction for whom it concerns” Immediate cash transactions make publicity a genuinely arguable, not automatic, question.
Q24 (Case) Internal-limit breach + actual third-party knowledge Known internal limits strip the third party’s usual can-do protection.
Q25 (Case) Section 177 I BGB ratification Unambiguous conduct (display, use, silence) can implicitly ratify an unauthorized substitute purchase.
Q26 (Case, integrates Week 10) Section 164 I BGB (agreement) vs. Section 855 BGB (delivery) Agency governs the Section 929 agreement element only; delivery is a real act, not a fresh agency test.

[W08.1] Week 08: Warranty Rights I

  • business-law/raw/moodle-export-business-law-950848573-s26-20260709/17.6. Warranty Rights I/Warranty Rights I Case facts.pdf
  • business-law/raw/moodle-export-business-law-950848573-s26-20260709/17.6. Warranty Rights I/Warranty Rights I_Slides and Solutions.pdf

Course: Business Law Processed: 2026-06-28 Wiki note: business-law/wiki/week-08-warranty-rights-i/week-08-warranty-rights-i.md

Course direction checked against business-law/wiki/_course-logistics.md: Warranty Rights I is Session 8 in the teaching outline and follows Agency. The deck labels itself “Lecture 7”; this note follows the course outline as Week 08.

External statute check: statutory anchors were cross-checked against the official Gesetze-im-Internet BGB/HGB sources on 2026-06-28. The official English BGB translation notes that English translations may lag the current German text, so use the lecture sections and the current German statute for exact wording in legal work.

80/20 Exam Summary

Warranty Rights I explains when the buyer gets special remedies because the purchased thing is defective.

  • Start with a valid purchase agreement under Section 433 BGB.
  • Ask whether the seller delivered the thing free from material and legal defects.
  • A material defect under Section 434 BGB is a deviation between actual condition and legally required condition at transfer of risk.
  • Section 434 BGB has several entry points: subjective requirements, objective requirements, assembly requirements, and aliud delivery.
  • The decisive time is transfer of risk, usually delivery under Section 446 BGB.
  • Before transfer of risk, use general impaired-performance law; after transfer of risk, use warranty law.
  • Section 437 BGB is the gateway for buyer remedies: cure, revocation, reduction, damages, and reimbursement.
  • Cure under Section 439 BGB has regular priority because the seller gets a second chance.
  • Revocation and reduction are secondary remedies. Reduction uses the Section 441 III proportional formula.
  • Warranty rights can be excluded contractually or statutorily, but exclusions have limits, especially fraud/guarantee, consumer purchases, SBT rules, buyer knowledge, commercial inspection duties, and limitation.

Contract Law Continuity Bridge

Warranty law is not a new contract-formation topic. It starts after a valid purchase contract exists.

Contract Law I: Was a contract formed?
Agency: Whose declaration counts?
SBT: Which clauses became part of the contract?
Warranty Rights: Was the purchased thing defective, and what can the buyer do?

Exam routing:

valid purchase agreement
-> defect at transfer of risk
-> no exclusion
-> correct remedy under Section 437 BGB

Case-Solving Structure

Use this structure whenever the facts mention a defective purchase item:

  1. Valid purchase agreement under Section 433 BGB.
  2. Defect at transfer of risk.
  3. No exclusion of warranty rights.
  4. Remedy under Section 437 BGB.

Why this matters: if you jump straight to damages or revocation, you may miss the gateway question. Warranty remedies only apply if the buyer can first show a relevant defect at the correct time.

Purchase Agreement Duties

Section 433 BGB gives the basic exchange:

Party Core duty Exam relevance
Seller Deliver the thing and procure ownership, free from material and legal defects. Defective performance triggers warranty analysis.
Buyer Pay the purchase price and accept delivery. Buyer breach is handled by general performance rules, not buyer warranty law.

Warranty law mainly regulates the seller’s defective performance.

Defects

The deck distinguishes material defects and legal defects.

Defect type Statutory anchor Meaning Example
Material defect Section 434 BGB The thing’s actual condition deviates from the condition legally required. Used car sold as “new”; laptop battery not suitable for the laptop.
Legal defect Section 435 BGB Third parties have rights affecting the sold thing. Sold real property is subject to another person’s lease.

Memory hook:

Material defect = something is wrong with the thing's condition.
Legal defect = someone else's right burdens the thing.

The intensity of the deviation is generally not the starting point. First ask whether there is a deviation at all; significance becomes important later, especially for revocation exclusions.

Material Defect Under Section 434 BGB

The deck uses a negative definition:

defect = actual condition differs from required condition

The required condition can come from several layers.

Subjective Requirements

Subjective requirements come from the parties’ contract.

Requirement Anchor Trigger facts Example
Agreed quality Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB Parties expressly or tacitly agree a quality. “New car” implies no micro-scratches, current unchanged model, not unused on dealer lot for more than 12 months.
Intended contractual use Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB No precise quality agreed, but seller knows the special intended use. Battery bought in shop for a specific laptop.
Agreed accessories/instructions Section 434 II 1 No. 3 BGB Contract includes agreed accessories or instructions. Device sold with required manual or agreed accessory.

Exam sentence:

The strongest defect argument is usually a subjective one, because the contract itself defines what the buyer was entitled to receive.

Objective Requirements

Objective requirements protect baseline expectations even if the contract is silent.

Requirement Anchor Trigger facts
Customary use Section 434 III 1 No. 1 BGB The thing is not fit for normal use.
Usual quality in things of the same kind Section 434 III 1 No. 2 BGB The thing falls below legitimate expectations for that product type.
Quality of sample/specimen Section 434 III 1 No. 3 BGB The delivered item differs from sample/specimen quality.
Accessories/instructions Section 434 III 1 No. 4 BGB Usual accessories or instructions are missing.

Public statements can shape legitimate expectations, especially statements by the seller or supply-chain parties.

Exam trap: do not use subjective and objective requirements as vague synonyms. Subjective = contract-specific expectation. Objective = ordinary market/product expectation.

Assembly Requirements

Assembly requirements matter only if assembly is owed or instructions matter.

If no assembly is owed, do not force an assembly analysis.

A defect can arise when assembly is faulty or when defective instructions cause bad assembly.

Aliud Delivery

Aliud delivery means delivery of a different thing.

Different thing = defect under Section 434 V BGB.

Example: the buyer orders a specific model, but the seller delivers a different model.

Transfer Of Risk

The decisive time for warranty law is transfer of risk.

contract conclusion -> before transfer of risk: general impaired-performance law
transfer of risk -> after transfer of risk: warranty law

Usually:

transfer of risk = handing over / delivery of the thing under Section 446 sentence 1 BGB

Why this matters: after transfer of risk, the buyer generally bears accidental destruction/deterioration and must pay the purchase price even if the thing later deteriorates accidentally. Therefore, the buyer must show the defect existed at transfer of risk, not merely later.

Clarification: transfer of risk is not the cure deadline.

contract concluded
-> delivery / handover = transfer of risk
-> defect must already exist here
-> buyer discovers defect later
-> buyer demands cure / sets cure period

Example: if a laptop is handed over on Monday and an internal battery defect is discovered on Wednesday, warranty law can still apply if the battery problem already existed at handover. If the buyer spills coffee on the laptop after handover, that later damage is not a seller warranty defect.

Exam wording:

Transfer of risk decides whether the defect belongs to the seller's warranty responsibility. The cure deadline decides whether the buyer may move from cure to secondary remedies.

Exclusions Of Warranty Rights

Warranty rights can fail even if there is a defect.

Contractual Exclusion

The parties may try to exclude or limit warranty rights by individual agreement or standard business terms.

Important limits:

Limit Anchor Meaning
Fraudulent concealment / guarantee Section 444 BGB Seller cannot rely on exclusion if seller concealed the defect or guaranteed quality.
New goods in SBT Section 309 No. 8 BGB SBT rules restrict warranty exclusions for newly produced goods.
Contradiction to agreed quality Section 242 BGB Seller cannot agree a quality and then exclude responsibility for that same quality.
Consumer purchase Section 476 BGB B2C rules allow only limited deviations before defect notification.

Consumer Purchase Contract

Consumer purchase contract:

trader sells a good to a consumer

Relevant protections:

  • modified general warranty rules in Sections 474-479 BGB;
  • burden-of-proof shift under Section 477 BGB;
  • limited ability to derogate from warranty rights before defect notification under Section 476 BGB;
  • easier seller recourse against supplier.

Exam trap: identify B2C status early. The same clause that might work in B2B can fail in consumer sales.

Statutory Exclusions

Exclusion Anchor Trigger facts Effect
Buyer knowledge Section 442 BGB Buyer knew the defect at contract conclusion or was grossly negligent. Warranty rights can be excluded.
Commercial inspection/notification Section 377 HGB Commercial sale between merchants; buyer fails to inspect and notify defects in time. Goods may be deemed approved; warranty rights may be lost.
Limitation Section 438 BGB Claim is time-barred. Buyer may be unable to enforce warranty rights.

Limitation examples from the deck:

  • movable thing with material defect: 2 years under Section 438 I No. 3 BGB;
  • buildings: 5 years under Section 438 I No. 2 BGB.

Legal Remedies Under Section 437 BGB

Section 437 BGB is a referral provision. It does not itself contain every requirement; it points to the remedy provisions.

Remedy Anchor Function
Cure Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB Buyer demands repair or replacement.
Revocation Sections 437 No. 2, 323/326 V BGB, plus Section 440 BGB Buyer unwinds the contract after cure priority is respected or excused.
Reduction Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB Buyer keeps the thing but lowers price.
Damages Section 437 No. 3 plus Sections 280 et seq. BGB Buyer claims compensation.
Reimbursement Section 437 No. 3 plus Section 284 BGB Buyer claims futile expenses instead of damages in lieu.

Tiered relationship:

cure first as regular second chance
-> if cure fails/refused/unreasonable or period expires
-> revocation, reduction, damages, reimbursement depending on facts

Exam trap: Section 437 is an exhaustive list. The buyer generally has no right to self-help at the seller’s expense outside the statutory route.

Cure

Cure is the primary remedy.

Core idea:

defective delivery modifies the original performance claim into a cure claim.

Buyer can generally choose:

  • re-delivery / replacement;
  • rectification / repair.

Seller’s limits:

  • refusal under Section 439 IV BGB if the chosen type of cure is possible only at disproportionate expense;
  • general impossibility limits under Section 275 BGB.

Factors for disproportion:

  • value of thing free from defect;
  • importance of the defect;
  • whether alternative cure is possible without substantial disadvantages;
  • relative versus absolute disproportion.

Costs:

  • seller bears cure costs under Section 439 II BGB;
  • seller can bear removal/installation-related cure costs under Section 439 III BGB;
  • if replacement is delivered, seller has a restitution claim for the defective thing under Section 439 V BGB.

Cure Priority, Not Negotiation

Warranty law does not require a commercial negotiation in the everyday sense. It requires a cure stage:

defect at transfer of risk
-> buyer demands cure
-> buyer chooses repair or replacement
-> seller must cure unless a valid refusal reason applies

If buyer and seller disagree about the type of cure, do not jump straight to revocation. First ask whether the seller can validly refuse the buyer’s chosen cure type under Section 439 IV BGB. If replacement is disproportionate but repair is reasonable, the buyer is usually limited to repair.

Example: a EUR 100 pair of headphones has a small button defect. A one-day repair costs EUR 20 and makes the headphones flawless. Replacement costs EUR 100 plus return and handling costs. The buyer initially may choose replacement, but the seller can likely refuse replacement as disproportionate. The buyer can still demand repair.

Opposite example: a new phone overheats unpredictably. Repair would require opening the device, replacing major components, and waiting weeks. Replacement is available quickly. Replacement is less likely to be disproportionate because the defect is serious and repair creates a substantial disadvantage for the buyer.

Exam wording:

The buyer may choose repair or replacement under Section 439 I BGB, but the seller may refuse the chosen type under Section 439 IV BGB if it is possible only at disproportionate expense. In that case, the buyer is restricted to the alternative cure type unless that too can be refused.

Revocation

Revocation is a secondary remedy.

Basic route:

defect
-> buyer demands cure / sets additional period
-> cure fails or is refused/unreasonable
-> buyer revokes
-> restitution under Sections 346-348 BGB

Important exceptions from the additional-period requirement:

Situation Anchor Exam use
Seller refuses both kinds of cure Section 439 IV BGB and Section 440 BGB logic No meaningful second chance remains.
Cure failed Section 440 sentence 1 alternative 2 BGB Generally after second failed attempt, but facts can justify more attempts.
Cure unreasonable for buyer Section 440 sentence 1 alternative 3 BGB Cure takes too long or creates serious disadvantages.

Revocation can be excluded:

Exclusion Anchor Meaning
Insignificant defect Section 323 V BGB Minor defect does not justify revocation.
Buyer responsible Section 323 VI alternative 1 BGB Buyer mainly caused the defect.
Buyer in default of acceptance Section 323 VI alternative 2 BGB Buyer caused the non-performance situation by not accepting.

Effect:

performances are returned under Sections 346-348 BGB
claim for cure and right to reduction are extinguished
damages/reimbursement may remain in principle

Warranty revocation is the purchase-defect version of general contract-law revocation. It is not rescission of a declaration of intent. The contract remains valid until it is unwound because defective performance has not been cured.

General Section 323 route:
breach -> reasonable deadline to perform -> no proper performance -> revocation

Warranty route:
defect at transfer of risk -> Section 437 gateway -> cure under Section 439
-> cure fails/refused/unreasonable or deadline expires
-> revocation via Sections 437 No. 2, 440, 323 BGB

Exam correction: mere disagreement about the preferred cure type is not enough for revocation. Revocation becomes available only if cure as such fails, is refused, is impossible, unreasonable, or the required period expires.

Reduction

Reduction is the price-lowering alternative to revocation.

Instead of revoking, the buyer declares reduction to the seller.

Basic relationship:

reduction has roughly the same requirements as revocation,
but the insignificance exclusion under Section 323 V sentence 2 BGB does not apply.

Formula under Section 441 III BGB:

reduced price = value with defect x agreed price / value without defect

Worked example:

agreed price = EUR 1000
value without defect = EUR 1000
value with defect = EUR 700

reduced price = 700 x 1000 / 1000
reduced price = EUR 700
overpayment if buyer already paid = 1000 - 700 = EUR 300

Interpretation:

Reduction preserves the contract but adjusts the price proportionally to the defect.

Before payment, the buyer can object and refuse the excessive amount. After payment, the buyer can reclaim overpayment through Section 441 IV and restitution rules.

Visual Knowledge Map

flowchart TD
    Start[Defective purchase item] --> Contract[Valid purchase agreement: Section 433]
    Contract --> Defect[Defect at transfer of risk]
    Defect --> Material[Material defect: Section 434]
    Defect --> Legal[Legal defect: Section 435]
    Material --> Subjective[Subjective requirements]
    Material --> Objective[Objective requirements]
    Material --> Assembly[Assembly requirements]
    Material --> Aliud[Different thing]
    Defect --> Risk[Transfer of risk: Section 446]
    Risk --> Exclusion[No exclusion]
    Exclusion --> Remedies[Section 437 remedies]
    Remedies --> Cure[Cure first: Section 439]
    Cure --> Revocation[Revocation]
    Cure --> Reduction[Reduction]
    Remedies --> Damages[Damages]
    Remedies --> Reimbursement[Reimbursement]

Subject Knowledge Graph

Node Meaning Exam Relevance
Purchase Agreement Contract under Section 433 BGB. Gateway to warranty rights.
Seller Duty Free From Defects Seller must deliver and transfer ownership free of material/legal defects. Breach basis for warranty law.
Material Defect Non-conformity under Section 434 BGB. Main defect category.
Legal Defect Third-party rights burden the good under Section 435 BGB. Less common but easy to miss.
Transfer Of Risk Moment that separates general performance law from warranty law. Decisive timing issue.
Contractual Exclusion Clauses or agreements limiting warranty. Must check limits.
Statutory Exclusion Buyer knowledge, HGB notification duty, limitation. Can block remedies.
Section 437 Gateway Referral provision for buyer remedies. Exam routing anchor.
Cure Primary remedy. Second-chance logic.
Revocation Secondary contract-unwinding remedy. Requires cure route unless exception.
Reduction Price adjustment. Uses proportional formula.
From Relationship To Why It Matters
Purchase Agreement creates Seller Duty Free From Defects Warranty starts from Section 433 performance duties.
Material Defect must exist at Transfer Of Risk Later deterioration is not enough.
Section 437 Gateway refers to Cure / Revocation / Reduction Section 437 is not the full test.
Cure usually precedes Revocation / Reduction / Damages Seller’s second chance is central.
Contractual Exclusion is limited by Section 444 / Section 476 / SBT rules Exclusion clauses are not always valid.
Reduction preserves Purchase Agreement Buyer keeps item but pays less.

Real Business Examples

  • A retailer sells a laptop as compatible with a specific docking station, but it is not. This is likely a subjective/intended-use defect.
  • A used car dealer advertises a car as accident-free, but it had structural accident damage. The agreed or expected quality may be missing.
  • A company buys machinery from a merchant seller and fails to inspect it after delivery. Section 377 HGB can become decisive.
  • A consumer buys a sofa online and discovers defective assembly instructions. Consumer purchase rules can limit seller-friendly exclusions.

Exam Relevance

Likely prompts:

  • Build the warranty-rights case structure for a defective purchased item.
  • Distinguish material and legal defects.
  • Identify whether the defect falls under subjective, objective, assembly, or aliud delivery rules.
  • Explain why transfer of risk matters.
  • Check whether warranty rights are excluded.
  • Explain the cure-first logic.
  • Distinguish revocation and reduction.
  • Apply the reduction formula.

Common traps:

  • Starting with Section 437 without first proving a defect.
  • Forgetting transfer of risk.
  • Treating every buyer complaint as a material defect.
  • Ignoring contractual or statutory exclusions.
  • Revoking immediately without respecting cure.
  • Confusing reduction with damages.
  • Using Section 377 HGB in non-commercial/consumer settings.

High-scoring answer structure:

  1. “There is a valid purchase agreement under Section 433 BGB.”
  2. “The item may be defective under Section 434/435 BGB at transfer of risk.”
  3. “No warranty exclusion appears / possible exclusion must be checked.”
  4. “The buyer’s remedy is routed through Section 437 BGB.”
  5. “Cure has priority unless an exception applies.”
  6. “If the requested remedy is revocation/reduction/damages, add the specific requirements.”

Official Exercise Case Routes

Case 1a: Headphones, Broken Active Noise Cancelling

Question: can C demand cure by replacement delivery?

Route:

  1. Purchase agreement: C buys headphones from O’s electronics store; employee E’s declaration is attributed to O through agency.
  2. Material defect: no special subjective agreement exists, but comparable high-priced headphones normally have working active noise cancelling. The headphones fail objective requirements under Section 434 III 1 No. 2 BGB.
  3. Transfer of risk: E handed over the headphones ten months earlier. It is unclear whether the defect existed then.
  4. Burden of proof: this is a consumer-goods sale under Section 474 I BGB: C is a consumer, O is a trader, and headphones are movable goods. Because the defect appears within one year, Section 477 BGB presumes it already existed at transfer of risk.
  5. No contractual or statutory exclusion appears.
  6. Cure: C chooses replacement delivery under Section 439 I Alt. 2 BGB.

Result: C can demand replacement headphones, against return of the old headphones under Sections 439 VI and 346 I BGB.

Exam trap: late discovery is not automatically fatal in a consumer-goods sale; check Section 477 BGB.

Case 1b: Advertising Claims About Active Noise Cancelling

Question: can C demand replacement when the normal function works but the advertised “twice as good” function does not?

Route:

  1. Purchase agreement exists.
  2. Subjective requirements are not breached because C and O made no specific individual agreement on the stronger function.
  3. Objective requirements are breached because public manufacturer advertising can shape usual quality under Section 434 III 1 No. 2 b BGB.
  4. The seller is not released under Section 434 III 3 BGB: O knew or had reason to know of the advertisement because it was displayed in O’s store; it had not been corrected; and it influenced C’s purchase.
  5. Defect existed at transfer of risk because the production defect was built in from the beginning.
  6. Cure and return route are the same as Case 1a.

Result: C can demand replacement delivery.

Exam trap: public advertising can create an objective-quality defect even without an individual agreement.

Case 1c: Replacement Delivery Versus Cheap Repair

Source status: the extracted case-facts PDF contains this subcase, but the extracted solution deck ends before an official solution. The following is an inferred answer route from the lecture framework.

Question: can C insist on replacement delivery when repair is quick, flawless, and much cheaper?

Route:

  1. C initially has the buyer’s choice under Section 439 I BGB: repair or replacement.
  2. O may refuse the selected cure type under Section 439 IV BGB if replacement is possible only at disproportionate cost.
  3. Factors favoring O: replacement creates extra return/manufacturer handling costs of EUR 60, repair costs EUR 20, repair is easy, flawless, and takes one day.
  4. Factors favoring C: C bought a new product and prefers not to receive a repaired one.
  5. Likely weighing: a one-day flawless repair creates no significant disadvantage for C compared with the disproportionate extra burden of replacement.

Likely result: C cannot insist on replacement delivery, but can still demand repair.

Exam trap: buyer’s cure choice is strong but not absolute.

Retrieval Prompts

Closed-book questions:

  1. What is the four-step structure for a warranty-rights case?
  2. What is the difference between material defect and legal defect?
  3. Why is transfer of risk decisive?
  4. What are the four material-defect routes in Section 434 BGB?
  5. Why does cure usually come before revocation?
  6. How does the Section 441 III reduction formula work?

Application prompts:

  1. Buyer purchases a “new car” with scratches and an outdated model year. Which defect route is strongest?
  2. Buyer knew about a defect before concluding the contract. Which exclusion do you check?
  3. Merchant buyer receives goods and does not inspect them for weeks. Which HGB issue arises?
  4. Seller repairs twice and the same defect remains. What remedy route opens?
  5. Defective thing worth EUR 600 instead of EUR 1000; price was EUR 900. Calculate the reduced price.

Practice Tasks

  1. Write a 10-line issue-spotting answer for a defective laptop battery sold for a known unusual laptop model.
  2. Create a defect classification table with one example each for subjective, objective, assembly, and aliud defects.
  3. Explain in plain language why the seller gets a second chance to cure.
  4. Apply Section 441 III to: agreed price EUR 500, value without defect EUR 600, value with defect EUR 300.
  5. Draft the first paragraph of an exam answer for a B2B buyer who discovers a defect after delivery but did not notify promptly.

Connections

Previous notes from this lecture:

  • Week 03 Contract Law I: contract formation and validity are prerequisites.
  • Week 05 Contract Law III: revocation and restitution logic reappear inside warranty remedies.
  • Week 06 Standard Business Terms: warranty exclusions in SBT must pass SBT control.
  • Week 07 Agency: if the purchase contract was concluded through an agent, solve agency before warranty.

Future notes:

  • Week 09 Warranty Rights II: damages, reimbursement, and work-contract warranty rights.

Cross-course links:

  • SCM/Marketing: product quality promises and after-sale service affect customer value, but Business Law asks which statutory remedy follows from the defect.

Weakness Flags

  • Pending active recall: no first-pass retrieval has been completed yet.
  • High-risk issue: distinguishing defect existence from remedy choice.
  • High-risk issue: checking transfer of risk and exclusions before Section 437 remedies.

[W08.2] Week 08 Warranty Rights I Cheatsheet And Tricks

Source: business-law/wiki/week-08-warranty-rights-i/week-08-warranty-rights-i-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-08-warranty-rights-i.md, clarification-session-2026-07-11.md

Must-Know (exam-critical)

Item Anchor Why it’s the backbone
Four-step case structure Sections 433, 434/435, 437 BGB Valid purchase agreement -> defect at transfer of risk -> no exclusion -> remedy under Section 437. Skipping straight to a remedy misses the gateway question.
Material vs legal defect Sections 434, 435 BGB Material = thing’s condition is wrong. Legal = a third party’s right burdens the thing.
Four material-defect routes Section 434 II-V BGB Subjective (contract-specific), objective (baseline market expectation), assembly, aliud (wrong thing delivered).
Transfer of risk Section 446 BGB Decisive timing checkpoint — the defect must exist at handover, not merely be discovered later. Before it: general performance law; after it: warranty law.
Section 437 as gateway, not full test Section 437 BGB It is a referral provision only — always cite the specific remedy section (439, 440/323, 441, 280 ff., 284) after invoking 437.
Cure has priority Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB Buyer chooses repair or replacement; seller gets a second chance before secondary remedies open.
Disproportionate cure refusal Section 439 IV BGB Seller can refuse the buyer’s chosen cure type (not cure altogether) if it is only possible at disproportionate expense — weigh defect-free value, defect significance, and whether the other cure type works without substantial disadvantage.
Revocation only after cure fails Sections 437 No. 2, 439, 440, 323 BGB Opens only if cure fails, is refused, is impossible, unreasonable, or the deadline expires — not merely because the parties disagree on repair vs replacement.
Reduction formula Section 441 III BGB reduced price = agreed price x actual value / defect-free value.
Buyer-knowledge exclusion Section 442 BGB Buyer knew (or was grossly negligent in missing) the defect at conclusion.
Commercial inspection/notice duty Section 377 HGB Merchant-to-merchant sale: late inspection/notice can deem goods approved and kill the whole warranty claim, independent of defect severity.

Nice-to-Have (depth/edge cases)

  • Cure cost allocation: seller bears cure costs (439 II), removal/installation costs (439 III), and gets a restitution claim for the defective thing back on replacement (439 V, via 346 I).
  • Revocation exclusions beyond failed cure: insignificant defect (323 V), buyer mainly caused the defect or is in default of acceptance (323 VI).
  • Consumer purchase layer (Sections 474-479 BGB): burden-of-proof shift under 477 (defect presumed to have existed at transfer of risk if it appears within one year), limited ability to derogate from warranty rights before notification under 476, easier seller recourse against supplier.
  • Limits on contractual exclusions: fraud/guarantee override (444), SBT restriction for newly produced goods (309 No. 8), good-faith contradiction if seller agreed a quality then tried to exclude it (242).
  • Limitation periods: 2 years for movable material defects (438 I No. 3), 5 years for buildings (438 I No. 2).
  • Public advertising/manufacturer statements can create an objective-quality defect under 434 III 1 No. 2(b) even with no individual agreement, unless the seller neither knew nor should have known of it, it was corrected, or it did not influence the purchase decision (434 III 3).
  • Reimbursement of futile expenses (Section 284) as an alternative to damages in lieu of performance, not a general cost-refund right.

Nuances And Traps

Nuance/Trap Why it’s easy to get wrong Correct handling
“Cure” sounds like negotiation Students describe cure as back-and-forth bargaining over what the buyer will accept Cure is a defined second-chance stage under Section 439, not a negotiation — the buyer picks repair or replacement, the seller can only refuse a specific type for disproportion, not haggle generally
Disagreement over cure type treated as automatic revocation It feels like a stalemate should let the buyer walk away Test Section 439 IV first: if one cure type is disproportionate, the buyer is restricted to the other type if it remains reasonable — revocation only opens once cure as such fails, is refused, is impossible, unreasonable, or the deadline expires
Warranty revocation confused with rescission (Contract Law II) Both end with the buyer “getting out,” so students merge the routes Warranty revocation unwinds a valid contract after a performance failure (Sections 437 No. 2, 440, 323); rescission attacks a flawed declaration of intent at formation (Sections 119/123) — never analyze a delivered defective good under Section 119 II
Transfer of risk confused with the cure deadline Both are “dates” in the fact pattern, easy to mix up which one to test Transfer of risk (Section 446, usually handover) tests whether the defect already existed at that moment; the cure deadline is a later, separate checkpoint that tests whether the seller’s second chance has run out
Late discovery treated as automatically fatal Students assume “found it weeks later” kills the claim In a consumer-goods sale, if the defect appears within one year of delivery, Section 477 BGB presumes it already existed at transfer of risk — the burden shifts to the seller
Treating every buyer complaint as a material defect Any dissatisfaction gets routed through 434 First confirm an actual deviation between required and actual condition exists — subjective expectation matters, but ordinary buyer disappointment without a contractual or objective baseline is not automatically a defect
Using Section 377 HGB outside merchant sales Reflexively applying “inspect and notify” logic to any purchase Section 377 only applies to a mutual commercial purchase between merchants — never apply it to a consumer buyer
Starting the answer with Section 437 Jumping straight to “buyer can revoke under 437” Prove the defect and its timing (433, 434/435, 446) before ever citing 437 — 437 is the gateway, not the starting point

One-Line Recall Drill

433 = purchase agreement duties
434 = material defect (subjective/objective/assembly/aliud)
435 = legal defect
446 = transfer of risk = handover
437 = gateway, not the full test
439 = cure (repair or replacement), buyer's choice
439 IV = seller can refuse disproportionate cure type only
440/323 = cure fails/refused/unreasonable -> revocation opens
441 III = reduced price = agreed price x actual value / defect-free value
442 = buyer knowledge exclusion
444 = fraud/guarantee overrides exclusion clauses
477 = one-year presumption in consumer sales
377 HGB = merchant inspect-and-notify, no equivalent for consumers
438 I No. 3 = 2-year limitation for movables

[W08.3] Week 08 Warranty Rights I Practice Questions And Model Answers

Source: business-law/wiki/week-08-warranty-rights-i/week-08-warranty-rights-i-practice-questions-and-model-answers.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-08-warranty-rights-i.md, week-08-warranty-rights-i-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md Format note: 25 questions — 9 short-answer/theory, 16 case/legal-opinion (schema-based). Question 8 integrates Week 11 Trade Law Section 377 HGB; Question 16 integrates Week 10 Transfer of Property; Question 17 integrates Week 09 Warranty Rights II; Question 25 integrates Week 06 Standard Business Terms.

Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 1

Explain what “transfer of risk” means in warranty law and why it functions as the decisive timing checkpoint.

Model Answer: Transfer of risk is the moment — usually handover/delivery of the thing under Section 446 sentence 1 BGB — that separates general impaired-performance law from warranty law. Before transfer of risk, any performance problem is handled under ordinary contract-breach rules; after it, the buyer bears the risk of accidental deterioration and warranty law governs whether the seller answers for a defect. The requirement matters because the buyer must show the defect already existed at transfer of risk, not merely that it was discovered later — a laptop battery defect present at handover is a seller’s problem, but coffee spilled on the laptop after handover is not. The exam trap is conflating transfer of risk with the later cure deadline: transfer of risk decides whether the defect belongs to the seller’s warranty responsibility at all, while the cure deadline decides only whether the buyer may escalate from cure to secondary remedies.

Question 2

Compare material defect and legal defect under German sales law.

Model Answer: A material defect (Section 434 BGB) exists when the thing’s actual condition deviates from its legally required condition — assessed through subjective agreement, objective baseline expectations, assembly requirements, or aliud (wrong-item) delivery — and is triggered by something being physically or functionally wrong with the thing itself. A legal defect (Section 435 BGB) exists when a third party can assert rights against the buyer in relation to the thing that were not assumed under the contract, triggered by an undisclosed encumbrance such as a lien or a lease burdening the item. Both open the same Section 437 BGB remedy gateway (cure, revocation, reduction, damages). Contrast example: a used car with a faulty transmission is a material defect; the same car secretly still subject to a bank’s registered lien is a legal defect. The exam trap is defaulting to “material defect” for every fact pattern — a problem caused by someone else’s right over the thing is a legal defect even though the same remedy provisions apply afterward.

Question 3

Explain the tiered relationship between cure, revocation, and reduction, and state the Section 441 III reduction formula.

Model Answer: The requirements are tiered: (1) cure under Section 439 BGB has priority as the seller’s second chance, because the buyer generally cannot skip straight to revocation, reduction, or damages; (2) only once cure fails, is refused, is impossible, is unreasonable for the buyer, or a set deadline expires does the buyer gain access to revocation (Sections 437 No. 2, 440, 323) or, in the alternative, reduction (Sections 437 No. 2, 441); (3) reduction differs from revocation in that the insignificance exclusion of Section 323 V sentence 2 BGB does not bar it, so even a minor defect can support a price reduction even where it could not support revocation. If reduction is chosen, the formula under Section 441 III BGB is: reduced price = agreed price × value of the thing with the defect / value of the thing without the defect. This tiering exists because warranty law is built around giving the seller a genuine second chance before the contract is disturbed further, and reduction (unlike revocation) preserves the contract entirely, only recalibrating the price.

Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 4 (Case)

Facts: K orders a specific “ThermoPro X200” espresso machine from online retailer B. B ships a similar-looking but different, cheaper “ThermoPro X100” model instead, without telling K. K notices only after unpacking. Both models function properly on their own terms, but K wants the model she actually ordered.

Question: Does K have a claim against B for delivery of the correct X200 model under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB?

Model Answer:

I. K could have a claim against B for cure by delivery of the X200 machine under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the requirements of a warranty defect claim are met.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement (Section 433 BGB); second, a defect existing at transfer of risk (Sections 434/435, 446 BGB); third, no exclusion of warranty rights; fourth, a remedy available under the Section 437 BGB gateway.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: K and B validly concluded a purchase contract for an X200 machine through K’s order and B’s confirmation; no formation obstacle is apparent.
  2. Defect: Questionable is whether receiving a different, functioning model counts as a defect. This is supported by Section 434 V BGB, under which delivery of a different thing than agreed (aliud delivery) is treated as a defect. Against this, one could argue the X100 is not “broken” and works fine on its own. However, Section 434 V BGB does not require malfunction — it protects the buyer’s contractual choice of the specific agreed item, not merely delivery of some working substitute. Consequently, a defect exists.
  3. Transfer of risk: the wrong item was itself the thing handed over at delivery, so the defect (being the wrong item) necessarily existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB.
  4. No exclusion: nothing in the facts suggests K knew of the substitution (Section 442 BGB) or that a valid exclusion clause exists; this is not a merchant-to-merchant sale, so Section 377 HGB does not apply.
  1. A material defect under Section 434 V BGB exists at transfer of risk, and no exclusion applies, so the Section 437 BGB gateway opens.
  1. Remedy: K may choose cure under Section 439 I BGB; since the correct item is what B always owed under the contract, replacement delivery of the X200 is the natural cure choice, and nothing in the facts suggests this would be disproportionately expensive for B under Section 439 IV BGB.

V. As a result, K can demand delivery of the correct X200 machine from B under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB, against return of the X100 machine under Sections 439 VI, 346 I BGB.

Question 5 (Case)

Facts: Manufacturer M advertises its “AquaFlow” garden hose nationally as “kink-resistant for its entire 20-meter length.” Retailer R sells an AquaFlow hose to buyer P without repeating or altering the claim, but had displayed M’s advertising poster in-store and never corrected or distanced itself from it. After two weeks of ordinary use, the hose kinks badly at the 12-meter mark. R and P never discussed kink-resistance specifically at the point of sale.

Question: Does P have a claim against R for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB?

Model Answer:

I. P could have a claim against R for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the hose is defective, the defect existed at transfer of risk, and no exclusion applies.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a material or legal defect at transfer of risk; third, no exclusion; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded; no issue raised on the facts.
  2. Subjective defect: no explicit individual agreement on kink-resistance was made between R and P, so a subjective-quality defect under Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB is not established on its own.
  3. Objective defect: Questionable is whether the manufacturer’s advertising creates a defect anyway. This is supported by Section 434 III 1 No. 2(b) BGB, under which public statements by the manufacturer about specific qualities of the goods can shape the buyer’s legitimate objective expectations, provided the seller knew or should have known of the statement, it was not corrected, and it was capable of influencing the purchase decision. Against this, one could argue R never personally repeated the claim to P. However, Section 434 III 3 BGB only releases the seller where the seller neither knew nor could have known of the statement, or it was corrected, or it did not influence the decision — none apply here, since R displayed the poster uncorrected in its own store. Consequently, the hose’s failure to be kink-resistant along its full length is an objective-requirement defect.
  4. Transfer of risk: the weakness in the hose’s construction was inherent from manufacture, so it existed at handover even though it only manifested after two weeks of ordinary use.
  5. No exclusion: nothing indicates P knew of the weakness or that a valid exclusion clause exists; this is a consumer sale, so Section 377 HGB is not relevant.
  1. A material (objective-requirement) defect under Section 434 III 1 No. 2(b) BGB exists at transfer of risk, unexcluded, so the Section 437 BGB gateway opens.
  1. Remedy: cure under Section 439 BGB — repair of a structural weave defect is unlikely to be practicable, so replacement is the natural cure choice, and nothing suggests it would be disproportionate for an ordinary garden hose.

V. As a result, P can demand a replacement AquaFlow hose from R under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB.

Question 6 (Case)

Facts: Buyer L purchases a designer office chair for EUR 1,200 from seller F. After delivery, L discovers one armrest has a visible manufacturing scratch that does not affect function. Repairing/refinishing the armrest costs EUR 80 and takes one day, fully restoring the chair. L instead demands a brand-new replacement chair, which would cost F EUR 1,200 plus return shipping and disposal of the scratched chair.

Question: Can L insist on replacement, or is F entitled to perform repair instead?

Model Answer:

I. L could have a claim against F for replacement under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 I BGB, unless F may validly refuse this cure type under Section 439 IV BGB.

  1. This requires: first, that L has a valid cure choice under Section 439 I BGB; second, that F’s refusal right under Section 439 IV BGB for disproportionate cost is examined; third, the resulting remedy for L.

  2. Application:

  1. Buyer’s choice: L is entitled to choose between repair and replacement under Section 439 I BGB and has chosen replacement.
  2. Disproportion: Questionable is whether F may refuse the chosen cure type. This is supported by the stark cost gap: replacement costs roughly fifteen times more than repair (EUR 1,200 plus shipping and disposal versus EUR 80), and repair fully restores the chair to a flawless, functionally unaffected condition within one day. Against this, one could argue L bought a “new, unblemished” chair and should not be forced to accept a repaired one. However, Section 439 IV BGB weighs the value of the item free of defects, the significance of the defect, and whether the alternative cure works without substantial disadvantage to the buyer — a purely cosmetic scratch, fully repairable in a day with no functional impact, does not create a disadvantage for L comparable to F’s disproportionate replacement cost. Consequently, F may refuse replacement as disproportionate.
  1. Replacement can be validly refused; repair remains available to L as the reasonable alternative cure type.

V. As a result, L cannot insist on replacement; L is restricted to demanding repair of the armrest from F under Section 439 I, IV BGB.

Question 7 (Case)

Facts: At a clearance sale, seller D expressly tells buyer Q, “this printer’s scanner unit is broken, only the printing function works,” and marks the price down accordingly. Q buys the printer anyway. A week later, Q confirms the scanner does not work and demands that D repair it under warranty.

Question: Does Q have a claim against D for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB?

Model Answer:

I. Q could have a claim against D for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the printer is defective and no exclusion applies.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a defect; third, no exclusion, in particular under Section 442 BGB; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded.
  2. Defect: a non-functioning scanner unit is a deviation from ordinary expected quality, so a material defect under Section 434 III BGB would exist in the abstract.
  3. Exclusion: Questionable is whether Section 442 BGB excludes Q’s rights for this defect. This is supported by the fact that D expressly disclosed the scanner defect before sale and Q bought the printer anyway, meaning Q positively knew of the defect at contract conclusion. Against this, one could argue Q still paid money for “a printer” generally. However, Section 442 I BGB excludes the buyer’s warranty rights precisely for defects the buyer knew of at conclusion, and the discounted price in fact confirms both parties priced the known defect into the deal. Consequently, the “no exclusion” requirement fails as to the scanner defect specifically.
  1. Warranty rights for the scanner defect are excluded under Section 442 I BGB.

V. As a result, Q has no claim against D for cure of the scanner under Sections 437, 439 BGB, because Q knew of that specific defect at contract conclusion.

Question 8 (Case — integrates Week 08 + Week 11)

Facts: Wholesaler W (a registered merchant) sells 500 packaged units of industrial-grade sealant to hardware retailer H (also a registered merchant) for H’s shop inventory. The sealant is delivered to H’s warehouse on a Monday. H’s warehouse staff sign for the delivery but do not open or inspect any cartons, simply stacking them in storage. Three weeks later, when H finally opens cartons to restock shelves, staff discover roughly a third of the units have hardened and become unusable — a defect that would have been visible immediately upon opening any carton. H immediately calls W and demands replacement units under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB.

Question: Does H have a claim against W for replacement of the defective units?

Model Answer:

I. H could have a claim against W for replacement under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the sealant is defective, the defect existed at transfer of risk, and no exclusion applies — including the Section 377 HGB commercial inspection and notice duty, since both parties are merchants.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement (Section 433 BGB); second, a material defect at transfer of risk (Sections 434, 446 BGB); third, that the sale is a mutual commercial purchase between merchants triggering Section 377 HGB; fourth, that H complied with the Section 377 HGB inspection and notice duty; fifth, no other exclusion; sixth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: W and H validly concluded a sale of 500 sealant units for H’s business; no formation issue is apparent.
  2. Defect: hardened, unusable sealant deviates from the ordinary usable quality expected of the product under Section 434 III 1 No. 1/2 BGB — a material defect — and nothing suggests the hardening happened after delivery rather than being inherent in a third of the batch, so it is treated as existing at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB absent contrary facts.
  3. Merchant/commercial-purchase gateway: Questionable is whether the ordinary BGB warranty analysis is modified here. This is supported by both W and H being registered merchants transacting for their respective businesses, making this a mutual commercial purchase under Section 343 HGB, which in turn triggers the Section 377 HGB notice regime on top of the BGB warranty gateway.
  4. Section 377 HGB inspection/notice: Section 377 HGB requires H to inspect the goods without undue delay after delivery and notify any defect without undue delay after discovery. This is supported by the fact that the defect would have been visible immediately upon opening any carton, meaning a reasonable inspection at or shortly after delivery would have caught it. Against this, one could argue three weeks is not obviously excessive for a busy warehouse. However, H’s staff did not inspect at all — they simply stacked the unopened cartons — and their conduct is attributed to H under Section 278 BGB; a multi-week delay before any inspection of a readily discoverable defect exceeds “without undue delay.” Consequently, H failed the Section 377 HGB inspection duty.
  1. Because H did not inspect and notify without undue delay, the sealant units are deemed approved under Section 377 HGB, and H’s warranty rights — including the claim for replacement under Sections 437, 439 BGB — are excluded, regardless of how serious or genuine the underlying material defect actually was.

V. As a result, H has no claim against W for replacement of the defective sealant units, because H’s own failure to timely inspect and notify under Section 377 HGB bars the Section 437 BGB warranty claim.

Additional Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 9

Explain who bears the costs of cure, and how those costs are treated if the seller cures by replacement rather than repair.

Model Answer: Section 439 II BGB places the necessary expenses of cure — transport, labour, and material costs — squarely on the seller, and Section 439 III BGB extends this to removal and reinstallation costs where the buyer has already installed or attached the defective item elsewhere, so the buyer is never required to advance or absorb the cost of the seller’s own repair or replacement. Where the seller cures by replacement rather than repair, Section 439 V BGB (via Section 346 I BGB) gives the seller a right to have the original defective item returned, mirroring the restitution logic used elsewhere when a remedy step unwinds part of the exchange. The requirement matters because it keeps cure genuinely cost-free for the buyer — a seller cannot condition free replacement on the buyer separately funding removal of the old unit. The exam trap is assuming the buyer must simply hand back the defective item without a statutory basis for that duty; Section 439 V’s cross-reference to Section 346 I is exactly that basis, and forgetting it leaves the seller’s restitution claim unsupported.

Question 10

Compare how the burden of proving a defect’s timing is allocated in an ordinary sale versus a consumer sale within one year of delivery.

Model Answer (Compare Schema): In an ordinary sale, the buyer bears the burden of proving that a defect already existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB — showing only that a problem exists today is not enough, since a defect arising after handover is not the seller’s responsibility. In a consumer sale under Sections 474-479 BGB, Section 477 BGB reverses this: if the defect becomes apparent within one year of delivery, it is presumed to have already existed at transfer of risk, and the burden shifts to the seller to disprove it. Contrast example: a self-employed carpenter buying a saw for his workshop is an ordinary sale, so he must prove the defect predates delivery; a private individual buying the same saw for home use is a consumer sale, so a fault discovered ten months later is presumed pre-existing unless the seller disproves it. Exam trap: the one-year presumption is a burden-of-proof rule inside the ordinary limitation period, not a one-year warranty extension, and it never applies outside a genuine business-to-consumer sale.

Question 11

State the main limits on a seller’s ability to contractually exclude warranty rights.

Model Answer: Sellers may in principle exclude or limit warranty rights by agreement, but several limits prevent this from swallowing buyer protection entirely. Section 444 BGB blocks reliance on an exclusion clause where the seller fraudulently concealed the defect or gave a guarantee covering it — a seller cannot both promise a quality and contract out of liability for its absence. Section 309 No. 8 BGB restricts standard-business-terms exclusions specifically for newly manufactured goods, so a blanket SBT clause cutting out warranty rights on new goods is often invalid regardless of its wording. Good faith under Section 242 BGB further bars a seller from agreeing to a specific quality and then excluding liability for exactly that quality, since the exclusion would contradict the seller’s own contractual commitment. The requirement matters because it stops exclusion clauses from stripping away protections the seller itself created through express assurances. Trap: an exclusion clause is not automatically valid merely because the parties “agreed” to it — always check fraud, guarantee, SBT rules, and good-faith contradiction before accepting it at face value.

Question 12

List the limitation periods for warranty claims relating to movable goods and buildings, and explain what they run from.

Model Answer (List-Requirements Schema): (1) For movable goods, Section 438 I No. 3 BGB sets a two-year limitation period; (2) for buildings, Section 438 I No. 2 BGB sets a five-year period, reflecting the greater complexity and cost of construction defects; (3) both periods run from delivery of the thing (movables) or the equivalent handover/acceptance event, not from when the buyer actually discovers the defect. Trap: students often assume the clock starts at discovery, by analogy to tort-law “knew or should have known” starting points — warranty limitation periods under Section 438 BGB instead start from an objective handover event regardless of when the buyer actually notices the problem, so a defect noticed at month eleven and one noticed at month twenty-three of a two-year movable-goods period face the very same cutoff measured from delivery.

Question 13

Beyond a failed or refused cure, list the other grounds on which revocation specifically can be excluded even though the general warranty gateway is open.

Model Answer (List-Requirements Schema): (1) Insignificance: Section 323 V sentence 2 BGB excludes revocation where the breach of duty is insignificant — a trivial defect cannot support unwinding the whole contract, even though it can still support a price reduction, since Section 441’s reduction route is not subject to the same insignificance bar; (2) buyer-caused defect: Section 323 VI BGB excludes revocation where the buyer is solely or predominantly responsible for the circumstance that would otherwise entitle them to revoke; (3) buyer in default of acceptance: Section 323 VI BGB also excludes revocation where the entitling circumstance occurred while the buyer was in default of accepting the goods. Trap: these exclusions attach specifically to revocation — they do not block reduction (insignificance) and do not automatically block a damages claim, which runs its own separate responsibility test under Section 280 I BGB; always identify which specific remedy is actually being excluded rather than assuming one exclusion closes every route at once.

Additional Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 14 (Case)

Facts: Buyer T tells seller S before purchase, “I need this paint to be exactly RAL 5010 gentian blue for a corporate branding job,” and S confirms in writing, “yes, this can 100% matches RAL 5010.” After delivery, independent testing shows the paint is actually RAL 5013 — a visibly different, darker blue — though S genuinely believed the match was correct.

Question: Does T have a claim for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB, even though the paint would pass ordinary market-quality expectations for “blue paint” generally?

Model Answer:

I. T could have a claim against S for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the paint is defective under the parties’ individual agreement and no exclusion applies.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a material defect at transfer of risk, tested first against the parties’ subjective agreement; third, no exclusion; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded via T’s order and S’s written confirmation.
  2. Defect: Questionable is whether ordinary “blue paint” quality suffices, given the delivered shade is an objectively normal, saleable color. This is supported instead by Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB, under which an individual agreement on quality — here S’s express written confirmation that the paint “100% matches RAL 5010” — controls ahead of any objective baseline expectation. Against this, one could argue S genuinely believed the match was accurate and acted in good faith. However, Section 434 BGB’s defect test is not fault-based; it asks only whether the delivered condition deviates from the individually agreed condition, and RAL 5013 is a distinct, visibly different shade from the agreed RAL 5010. Consequently, a subjective-quality defect exists regardless of S’s honest belief.
  3. Transfer of risk: the pigment formulation was fixed at mixing, so the mismatch existed at handover under Section 446 BGB.
  4. No exclusion: nothing indicates T knew of the mismatch or that a valid exclusion clause exists.
  1. A subjective-quality defect under Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB exists at transfer of risk and is unexcluded, so the Section 437 BGB gateway opens.
  1. Remedy: cure under Section 439 I BGB — replacement with correctly mixed RAL 5010 paint is the natural cure.

V. As a result, T can demand cure from S under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB; S’s honest belief in the match is irrelevant to whether a defect exists, since Section 434 BGB is not a fault-based test.

Question 15 (Case)

Facts: Buyer N buys a flat-pack wardrobe from furniture retailer M. The wardrobe panels themselves are flawless, but the included assembly instructions are missing a page, causing N to attach the back panel incorrectly so that the wardrobe leans and the doors do not close properly. N calls M and demands cure.

Question: Does N have a claim for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB despite the physical panels being defect-free?

Model Answer:

I. N could have a claim against M for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the wardrobe is defective on account of the faulty assembly instructions and no exclusion applies.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a material defect at transfer of risk under the assembly-requirements route; third, no exclusion; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded; M owed a flat-pack item that includes assembly by the buyer, so assembly requirements are relevant on these facts.
  2. Defect: Questionable is whether a defect exists at all, given the panels themselves are flawless. This is supported by Section 434 IV BGB, under which a defect also arises where assembly was carried out incorrectly, including where incorrect assembly resulted from defective assembly instructions supplied with the item (“IKEA clause” logic) — even though nothing is physically wrong with the components themselves. Against this, one could argue N caused the problem by assembling the wardrobe incorrectly. However, N’s assembly followed the instructions M supplied, and it was the missing page — not N’s own error — that caused the incorrect assembly. Consequently, a material defect under Section 434 IV BGB exists.
  3. Transfer of risk: the instructions were incomplete as supplied at delivery, so the defect existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB.
  4. No exclusion: nothing indicates N knew the instructions were incomplete or that a valid exclusion clause exists.
  1. A material defect under Section 434 IV BGB exists at transfer of risk and is unexcluded, so the Section 437 BGB gateway opens.
  1. Remedy: cure under Section 439 I BGB — M can cure by supplying the missing instruction page and, if needed, arranging correct reassembly; this is neither impossible nor disproportionate.

V. As a result, N can demand cure from M under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB, notwithstanding that the wardrobe’s physical panels are entirely defect-free.

Question 16 (Case — integrates Week 08 + Week 10)

Facts: A sewing machine is stolen from true owner O’s workshop. The thief sells it at a flea market to trader S, who buys it in good faith, unaware of the theft. S then sells and delivers the machine to hobbyist buyer B, who also buys and takes delivery in good faith. Two weeks later, O traces the machine to B via its serial number and demands its return under Section 985 BGB. Separately, B has discovered that the machine’s bobbin-tension mechanism was broken even before S ever possessed it, and wants cure from S.

Question: (1) Can O reclaim the machine from B despite B’s good faith? (2) Independently, does B still have a warranty claim against S for the broken mechanism?

Model Answer:

I. Two separate claims arise: O’s ownership-based recovery claim against B under Section 985 BGB, and B’s contractual warranty claim against S under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB. The separation and abstraction principles mean the outcome of one does not automatically decide the other.

  1. Requirements: for claim 1 (O v. B), O must be owner and B a possessor without a right to possess; for claim 2 (B v. S), a valid purchase agreement, a material defect at transfer of risk, no exclusion, and a remedy under Section 437 BGB — none of which require B to actually be the owner, since this is an obligation-law claim, not a property-law one.

  2. Application

Claim 1 — O v. B under Section 985 BGB. Questionable is whether O remains owner despite the chain of sales down to B. This is supported by Section 929 sentence 1 BGB, which requires the transferor’s authorization to pass ownership — the thief had no authorization from O, so the thief could not transfer ownership to S under ordinary rules. Against this, one could argue S and B nonetheless acquired ownership in good faith under Section 932 BGB despite the thief’s lack of authorization.
