However, Section 935 I BGB blocks good-faith acquisition entirely where the thing was stolen from the true owner, and this block travels through the entire chain of subsequent good-faith buyers, not merely the first one. Consequently, neither S nor B ever acquired ownership, however honestly each believed otherwise, and B currently possesses the machine with no right to possess it as against O.

Claim 2 — B v. S under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB. Questionable is whether B has any claim at all against S given that B never became owner. This is supported by the separation principle: the purchase contract between S and B (Section 433 BGB) is an obligation contract distinct from the disposition that was supposed to follow it, and under the abstraction principle the validity of the obligation contract does not depend on whether the disposition actually succeeded. Against this, one could argue that since B never became owner, “B’s purchase” was somehow void. However, nothing in the facts suggests the sales contract itself suffered any formation defect between S and B — S validly promised to sell and deliver the machine, and that promise stands regardless of S’s own defective title. Consequently, a valid purchase agreement exists between B and S; the bobbin-tension mechanism was broken before S ever possessed the machine, so a material defect under Section 434 III BGB existed at the Section 446 BGB transfer of risk from S to B, and nothing indicates an exclusion.

  1. Interim results: O remains owner and can recover the machine from B under Section 985 BGB; separately, the Section 437 BGB warranty gateway is open between B and S.

V. As a result, O can reclaim the machine from B under Section 985 BGB despite B’s good faith, because Section 935 BGB blocks good-faith acquisition for stolen goods down the whole chain of buyers — but B’s contractual warranty claim against S for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB survives entirely independently of O’s property-law claim, since the two transactions’ validity is governed separately under the separation and abstraction principles.

Question 17 (Case — integrates Week 08 + Week 09)

Facts: Buyer K orders custom-fitted industrial shelving from manufacturer P for EUR 8,000 for a warehouse expansion. On delivery, several shelf units are bent and unusable — a defect existing at transfer of risk. K demands cure and sets P a two-week deadline. P attempts a rushed repair that still leaves the units unusable and misses the deadline. K then buys equivalent replacement shelving from a competitor for EUR 9,500 to keep the project on schedule, and wants to recover the EUR 1,500 difference from P.

Question: Can K recover the EUR 1,500 price difference from P?

Model Answer:

I. K could have a claim against P for “big damages” (damages instead of the entire performance) under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB for the EUR 1,500 difference between the contract price and the substitute purchase.

  1. This requires: first, that the Section 437 BGB warranty gateway is open; second, that cure was attempted and failed, or that a reasonable additional period for cure expired without result; third, an obligation, breach of duty, responsibility (presumed), and causal damage under Section 280 I BGB; fourth, that K gave up the defective performance entirely, distinguishing big damages from small damages.

  2. Application:

  1. Gateway: the bent, unusable shelf units deviate from the ordinary usable quality required under Section 434 III BGB, and nothing suggests the bending occurred after delivery, so a material defect existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB, with no exclusion apparent.
  2. Additional period: K set a two-week deadline, a reasonable additional period under Section 281 I BGB, and P’s rushed attempt still left the units unusable within that period. Questionable is whether K needed to grant a further period. This is supported by Section 281 I BGB requiring only that a reasonable period expire without proper cure, not that the seller receive unlimited further attempts. Against this, one could argue a “rushed” attempt is not a genuine attempt and P deserves another chance. However, the facts state the deadline was missed entirely and the repair still left the units unusable, so the statutory precondition is satisfied regardless of how P characterizes its own effort. Consequently, K may proceed to damages instead of performance without granting a further period.
  3. Section 280 I elements: there is an obligation (defect-free delivery under Section 433 I 2 BGB), a breach (delivery of bent, unusable units), responsibility presumed under Section 280 I sentence 2 BGB and not rebutted on the facts, and causal damage (the EUR 1,500 extra cost incurred specifically to replace P’s failed performance).
  4. Big vs. small damages: Questionable is whether K is limited to small damages. This is supported by K’s conduct: K sourced replacement shelving from a competitor rather than keeping P’s units, meaning K gave up the defective performance entirely. Against this, one could argue K should first have to prove the returned units are worthless. However, giving up the performance for a genuine substitute purchase is exactly the fact pattern big damages is built for, and K is returning P’s defective units rather than retaining them. Consequently, K’s claim is properly analyzed as big damages, not small damages or reduction.
  1. Interim result: the warranty gateway is open, cure failed after a reasonable additional period, and the Section 280 I BGB damages requirements are met on a big-damages basis.

V. As a result, K can recover the EUR 1,500 price difference from P as big damages under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, against return of the defective shelf units to P.

Question 18 (Case)

Facts: Buyer G buys a vintage watch for EUR 5,000 from dealer V. G later discovers the watch’s movement was previously serviced with a non-original part, which is below the ordinary quality expected of an all-original vintage piece of this kind and lowers its value. An appraisal values the watch at EUR 4,000 with the non-original part and EUR 5,000 if all-original; no equivalent original replacement part is realistically available, so repair to a fully original state is impracticable. G does not want revocation and instead demands a price reduction.

Question: What is G entitled to under Section 441 III BGB?

Model Answer:

I. G could have a claim against V for a reduced price under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB if the watch is defective, cure is unavailable or dispensable, and the reduction formula is applied.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a material defect at transfer of risk; third, that the preconditions otherwise required for revocation (cure failed, impossible, or dispensable) are met, since reduction shares those preconditions but is not barred by insignificance; fourth, correct application of the Section 441 III BGB formula.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded for EUR 5,000.
  2. Defect: the non-original movement part falls below the ordinary quality customary for an all-original vintage watch of this kind, a material defect under Section 434 III BGB, and the part was fitted before the sale, so it existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB.
  3. Cure availability: Questionable is whether cure via repair could resolve this. This is supported by no equivalent original replacement part being realistically available, and further disassembly/servicing of a vintage piece risking further loss of collector value. Against this, one could argue V should still get a chance to search for a part. However, the facts state no original replacement is realistically available, so cure is impracticable. Consequently, the cure-first requirement is dispensed with and G may proceed directly to reduction.
  1. Interim result: the requirements of Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB are met.
  1. Reduction calculation: reduced price = agreed price × value with defect / value without defect = EUR 5,000 × (EUR 4,000 / EUR 5,000) = EUR 4,000.

V. As a result, G is entitled to a reduced price of EUR 4,000 — a refund of EUR 1,000 of the EUR 5,000 already paid — under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 III BGB.

Further Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 19

Explain the limit Section 476 BGB places on agreements that deviate from warranty rights in a consumer purchase, and when it applies.

Model Answer: Section 476 BGB restricts the parties’ freedom, in a consumer purchase under Sections 474 ff. BGB, to agree on terms that deviate from the buyer’s statutory warranty rights to the buyer’s disadvantage before the seller has been notified of a defect — protecting the consumer from pre-emptively signing away rights to protections the seller has not yet had to honor. The statutory anchor is Section 476 BGB, layered on top of the general warranty regime in Sections 434-441 BGB once the sale qualifies as a consumer purchase (trader selling to a consumer, Sections 13, 14, 474 I BGB). The requirement matters because it prevents traders from using standard forms or pre-sale waivers to strip away statutory protections before a consumer even knows a defect exists, closing an obvious end-run around the warranty regime. Example: a trader’s sale contract stating “buyer waives all warranty claims regardless of defect” is ineffective under Section 476 BGB against a consumer buyer, even if the consumer signed it, because it deviates from statutory warranty rights before any defect notification. The exam trap is assuming this consumer-protective limit applies to B2B sales as well — Section 476 BGB is specific to consumer purchases; between two merchants or businesses, pre-sale warranty-limiting agreements face a different, generally more permissive analysis (subject still to SBT content control and Section 444 BGB).

Further Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 20 (Case)

Facts: Buyer J tells retailer R’s sales assistant, “I need this external hard drive because I want to back up my professional video-editing files, which involve very large 4K project files.” The assistant says nothing to contradict this and completes the sale. The hard drive works perfectly for ordinary storage, but its write speed is too slow to handle the large 4K files without constant dropped frames, making it unsuitable for J’s stated purpose. A drive marketed as an “everyday backup drive” would ordinarily be expected to perform fine for typical, non-professional use.

Question: Does J have a claim for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB even though the drive works fine for ordinary backup purposes?

Model Answer:

I. J could have a claim against R for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the drive is defective measured against J’s disclosed intended use and no exclusion applies.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a material defect at transfer of risk, tested first against the parties’ subjective agreement including intended contractual use; third, no exclusion; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded via J’s purchase from R.
  2. Defect: Questionable is whether an ordinarily-functioning backup drive can be defective. This is supported by Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB, under which a defect exists where the thing is unsuitable for the use intended under the contract, where that intended use was made recognizable to the seller and not objected to. Against this, one could argue the drive works perfectly for its objectively marketed purpose as an “everyday backup drive,” so no defect exists under ordinary market expectations. However, J disclosed the specific professional 4K video-editing purpose to R’s own sales assistant before purchase, and R raised no objection or caveat about the drive’s suitability for that use — under Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB, this disclosed and unopposed intended use sets a subjective requirement that displaces the merely objective baseline. Consequently, the drive’s inability to reliably handle large 4K files without dropped frames is a defect measured against the agreed intended use, even though it performs adequately for generic backup tasks.
  3. Transfer of risk: the write-speed limitation was an inherent property of the drive from manufacture, so it existed at handover under Section 446 BGB.
  4. No exclusion: nothing indicates J knew of the speed limitation or that a valid exclusion clause exists.
  1. A material defect under Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB exists at transfer of risk and is unexcluded, so the Section 437 BGB gateway opens.
  1. Remedy: cure under Section 439 I BGB — replacement with a drive suited to J’s disclosed professional use is the natural cure, and nothing suggests disproportion.

V. As a result, J can demand cure from R under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB; the drive’s fitness for ordinary generic backup use does not defeat the claim, because Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB tests suitability against the disclosed intended use, not against generic market expectations.

Question 21 (Case)

Facts: Seller V sells buyer K a used industrial sewing machine “free of any third-party claims.” Unknown to K, V had earlier pledged the machine as security for a business loan, and the bank’s security interest was never released or disclosed to K. Two months after delivery, the bank contacts K asserting its security right and threatening to seize the machine.

Question: Does K have a claim against V for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB, even though the machine itself functions flawlessly?

Model Answer:

I. K could have a claim against V for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB if the machine suffers from a legal defect and no exclusion applies.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a legal defect at transfer of risk under Section 435 BGB; third, no exclusion; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded between V and K.
  2. Defect: Questionable is whether a fully-functioning machine can be defective. This is supported by Section 435 BGB, under which a legal defect exists where a third party can assert rights against the buyer in relation to the thing that were not assumed under the contract — the mechanical condition of the item is irrelevant to this route. Against this, one could argue the machine works perfectly and nothing is physically wrong with it. However, the bank’s undisclosed, unreleased security interest is exactly the kind of third-party right Section 435 BGB targets, and the parties’ express agreement that the machine be delivered “free of any third-party claims” confirms K never assumed this encumbrance under the contract. Consequently, a legal defect under Section 435 BGB exists.
  3. Transfer of risk: the security interest was created before the sale and never released, so it burdened the machine already at handover under Section 446 BGB.
  4. No exclusion: nothing indicates K knew of the pledge or that a valid exclusion clause exists; V’s express assurance of freedom from third-party claims cuts against any implied exclusion.
  1. A legal defect under Section 435 BGB exists at transfer of risk and is unexcluded, so the Section 437 BGB gateway opens.
  1. Remedy: cure under Section 439 I BGB — V can cure by procuring release of the bank’s security interest, clearing the machine of the third-party right; this is neither impossible nor disproportionate on the facts.

V. As a result, K can demand cure from V under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB despite the machine’s flawless physical condition, because the undisclosed bank security interest is a legal defect under Section 435 BGB, a route distinct from material defects under Section 434 BGB.

Question 22 (Case)

Facts: Buyer H inspects a used delivery van before purchase from dealer T. T invites H to “look it over as thoroughly as you like” and gives H unrestricted access for an hour. A large rust perforation is visible on the underside of the van, plainly noticeable to anyone who glances underneath, but H does not bother to look underneath at all before signing the purchase contract. After delivery, H discovers the rust damage and demands cure from T.

Question: Does H have a claim for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB?

Model Answer:

I. H could have a claim against T for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB unless H’s rights are excluded under Section 442 I BGB.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement and material defect at transfer of risk; second, examination of whether Section 442 I BGB excludes the claim, including its grossly-negligent-ignorance branch; third, a remedy under Section 437 BGB if no exclusion applies.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement and defect: validly concluded; the rust perforation deviates from the ordinary quality expected of a used van under Section 434 III BGB and existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB, since rust of that extent develops well before a single sale.
  2. Exclusion: Questionable is whether Section 442 I BGB excludes H’s rights despite H not actually knowing of the rust. This is supported by Section 442 I sentence 2 BGB, which excludes rights not only for defects the buyer actually knew of, but also for defects the buyer did not know of only as a result of gross negligence, unless the seller fraudulently concealed the defect or gave a guarantee. Against this, one could argue H never saw the rust and so cannot be treated as “knowing.” However, T expressly invited H to inspect the van as thoroughly as desired and gave H an hour of unrestricted access, and the rust perforation was plainly visible to anyone who glanced underneath — failing to perform even this basic, invited check on a highly visible defect is gross negligence, not ordinary buyer inattention. Consequently, H’s ignorance of the rust falls within the gross-negligence branch of Section 442 I BGB.
  1. Because H’s ignorance of the rust resulted from gross negligence and nothing indicates fraudulent concealment or a guarantee by T, H’s warranty rights for the rust defect are excluded under Section 442 I BGB.

V. As a result, H has no claim against T for cure of the rust damage under Sections 437, 439 BGB, because H’s failure to notice a plainly visible defect during an invited, unrestricted inspection amounts to gross negligence within Section 442 I BGB — distinct from Question 7’s scenario of actual disclosed knowledge, but producing the same exclusion.

Question 23 (Case)

Facts: Caterer C orders a custom commercial oven from manufacturer M for a new kitchen build-out, paying EUR 15,000. Before delivery, C spends EUR 2,000 having a specialized ventilation duct installed specifically to fit this oven model. The oven arrives with a defect that M cannot cure — repair is impossible and no replacement unit of that model exists. C revokes the contract and, rather than trying to prove lost profit from a working oven, wants to recover the EUR 2,000 ventilation cost as wasted expenditure.

Question: Can C recover the EUR 2,000 from M?

Model Answer:

I. C could have a claim against M for reimbursement of futile expenses under Sections 437 No. 3, 284 BGB for the EUR 2,000 ventilation cost.

  1. This requires: first, the Section 437 BGB warranty gateway is open and cure is excluded; second, C would otherwise have been entitled to damages instead of performance; third, C reasonably incurred expenses in reliance on receiving performance; fourth, the expenses’ purpose was not going to fail regardless of the breach.

  2. Application:

  1. Gateway: the oven’s defect deviates from the ordinary quality expected under Section 434 III BGB and existed at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB; cure is impossible since no replacement exists and repair cannot fix it, dispensing with the cure-first requirement under Section 440 BGB.
  2. Reliance expenditure: Questionable is whether C can recover the ventilation cost without proving lost profit. This is supported by Section 284 BGB, which allows a creditor to demand reimbursement of expenses reasonably incurred in reliance on receiving the seller’s performance, as an alternative to damages instead of performance, precisely so the creditor need not quantify a speculative profit figure. Against this, one could argue C should instead have to prove what profit the working oven would have generated. However, Section 284 BGB exists exactly to spare the creditor that speculative proof burden where reliance expenditure is easier to show, and the EUR 2,000 duct installation was reasonably incurred specifically to accommodate this oven model in reliance on M’s performance. Consequently, C may elect reimbursement under Section 284 BGB instead of proving lost profit.
  3. Purpose not otherwise doomed: nothing in the facts suggests the ventilation duct would have been wasted expenditure even if the oven had been defect-free — it was built specifically to fit this model and would have served its purpose had M performed properly.
  1. Interim result: the Section 437 BGB gateway is open, cure is impossible, and the Section 284 BGB reimbursement requirements are met.

V. As a result, C can recover the EUR 2,000 ventilation cost from M under Sections 437 No. 3, 284 BGB as reimbursement of futile expenses, without needing to prove the oven’s hypothetical lost profit.

Question 24 (Case)

Facts: Manufacturer M runs a national ad campaign claiming its “SolarMax” garden light charges “fully in two hours of sunlight.” Retailer R sells a SolarMax light to buyer P but, before the sale, R’s shop clearly displays its own printed correction stating “Note: SolarMax charging times vary; the manufacturer’s ‘two hours’ claim is not guaranteed and should be disregarded.” P notices this correction sign but buys the light anyway because he liked its design, not because of the charging-time claim, and later complains that the light actually takes four hours to charge.

Question: Does P have a claim against R for cure based on the discrepancy between the advertised and actual charging time?

Model Answer:

I. P could have a claim against R for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB only if the advertised two-hour charging claim shapes an objective-quality defect; this is questionable given R’s correction.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement; second, a material defect at transfer of risk, including whether manufacturer advertising shapes objective requirements under Section 434 III 1 No. 2(b) BGB, unless the seller is released under Section 434 III 3 BGB; third, no other exclusion; fourth, a remedy under Section 437 BGB.

  2. Application:

  1. Purchase agreement: validly concluded between R and P.
  2. Objective defect via advertising: Questionable is whether M’s “two hours” claim became part of the objectively expected quality. This is supported in principle by Section 434 III 1 No. 2(b) BGB, under which public statements by the manufacturer about specific product qualities can shape a buyer’s legitimate objective expectations. Against this, one could argue R is not the one who made the claim. However, that alone would not release R, since Section 434 III 1 No. 2(b) BGB reaches statements by manufacturers displayed by the seller too — the decisive question is instead whether R is released under Section 434 III 3 BGB, which excuses the seller where the statement was corrected in a comparable manner to how it was made, or where it did not influence the purchase decision. Both release grounds are met here: R displayed a clear, comparably prominent correction disclaiming the two-hour figure, and the facts state P bought the light for its design, not because of the charging-time claim. Consequently, R is released under Section 434 III 3 BGB, and the advertised charging time never became part of the objectively expected quality.
  1. No defect arises from the discrepancy between the advertised and actual charging time, because R’s correction and P’s independent purchase motive both satisfy the Section 434 III 3 BGB release.

V. As a result, P has no claim against R for cure based on the charging-time discrepancy — unlike Question 5, where the seller failed to correct the manufacturer’s claim and the claim did influence the buyer, here both release conditions under Section 434 III 3 BGB are met and no defect arises from the advertising.

Question 25 (Case — integrates Week 08 + Week 06)

Facts: Online furniture retailer F’s standard terms and conditions, presented to every buyer at checkout via a clearly labeled “Terms and Conditions” checkbox that must be ticked before payment, include the clause: “All items are sold with warranty rights fully excluded; the buyer accepts all goods ‘as is.’” Buyer D ticks the box and buys a newly manufactured dining table from F, which arrives with a cracked leg — a material defect existing at transfer of risk. D demands cure; F points to the clause.

Question: Can F rely on the “as is” clause to deny D’s cure claim?

Model Answer:

I. D could have a claim against F for cure under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB unless F’s “as is” clause validly excludes it — which requires both that the clause is validly incorporated and passes SBT content control, and that no overriding rule such as Section 444 BGB blocks reliance on it regardless.

  1. This requires: first, a valid purchase agreement and material defect at transfer of risk (established); second, that the clause was validly incorporated as a standard business term under Section 305 BGB; third, that the clause survives content control under Sections 307-309 BGB, in particular Section 309 No. 8 BGB for newly manufactured goods; fourth, that Section 444 BGB does not independently override even a valid exclusion.

  2. Application:

  1. Defect: the cracked leg is a material defect under Section 434 III BGB, existing at transfer of risk under Section 446 BGB; no dispute on this point.
  2. Incorporation: the clause was clearly presented and D affirmatively accepted it via the checkbox before payment, satisfying Section 305 II BGB’s incorporation requirements (clear reference, reasonable opportunity to review, agreement); it is a pre-formulated term used for a multitude of contracts, so Section 305 I BGB applies and it is a standard business term.
  3. Content control: Questionable is whether a blanket “as is” exclusion of all warranty rights survives content control. This is supported by Section 309 No. 8 BGB, part of the “black list” of clauses invalid without any room for evaluation, which specifically restricts clauses excluding or limiting warranty rights for newly manufactured goods sold as new — exactly this transaction, since the table is newly manufactured. Against this, one could argue F is free to define what it sells “as is” through ordinary contract terms. However, Section 309 No. 8 BGB exists precisely to stop blanket exclusions like this one from being imposed via standard terms on new-goods sales, and a clause that fails content control is invalid under Section 306 I, II BGB, with statutory law filling the resulting gap rather than the whole contract failing. Consequently, the “as is” exclusion clause is invalid under Section 309 No. 8 BGB.
  4. Section 444 overlay: even if the clause had somehow survived content control, nothing in the facts suggests fraud or a guarantee here, so Section 444 BGB is not independently needed to defeat the clause on these particular facts — the SBT content-control failure alone is dispositive.
  1. The “as is” exclusion clause is invalid under Section 309 No. 8 BGB; the rest of the contract remains valid under Section 306 BGB, and statutory warranty law fills the gap left by the invalid clause.

V. As a result, F cannot rely on the “as is” clause to deny D’s claim; D retains a cure claim against F under Sections 437 No. 1, 439 BGB for the cracked table leg, because the blanket warranty-exclusion clause fails SBT content control under Section 309 No. 8 BGB for newly manufactured goods.

Quick Answer Route Summary

Question # Primary Route/Section One-line takeaway
1 Section 446 BGB Transfer of risk, not discovery, is the decisive timing test.
2 Sections 434, 435 BGB Material = thing’s own condition; legal = a third party’s right over the thing.
3 Sections 439, 440/323, 441 III BGB Cure first, then revocation or reduction; reduction alone survives insignificance.
4 (Case) Section 434 V BGB Aliud delivery is a defect even if the wrong item works fine.
5 (Case) Section 434 III 1 No. 2(b) BGB Uncorrected manufacturer advertising can create an objective defect.
6 (Case) Section 439 IV BGB Seller can refuse a disproportionate cure type, buyer then limited to the other type.
7 (Case) Section 442 I BGB Buyer’s pre-conclusion knowledge of a specific defect excludes rights for that defect.
8 (Case, integrative) Section 377 HGB + Section 437 BGB Merchant buyer’s late inspection/notice bars an otherwise valid warranty claim entirely.
9 Section 439 II, III, V BGB Seller bears all cure costs, including removal/reinstallation; buyer returns the old item on replacement.
10 Section 477 BGB Consumer sale within one year: defect presumed pre-existing, burden shifts to seller.
11 Sections 444, 309 No. 8, 242 BGB Fraud, guarantee, SBT restriction, and good-faith contradiction all limit exclusion clauses.
12 Section 438 I No. 2/3 BGB Two years for movables, five for buildings; both run from delivery/handover, not discovery.
13 Section 323 V, VI BGB Insignificance and buyer-caused defect/acceptance default exclude revocation only, not reduction or damages.
14 (Case) Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB An express individual quality agreement controls even over an objectively ordinary product.
15 (Case) Section 434 IV BGB Faulty assembly instructions create a defect even when the physical components are flawless.
16 (Case, integrative) Sections 929, 932, 935, 985 BGB + Sections 437, 439 BGB Theft blocks good-faith ownership down the whole chain, but the buyer’s contractual warranty claim survives independently under separation/abstraction.
17 (Case, integrative) Sections 281, 280 I, III BGB Failed cure after a reasonable period opens big damages for the substitute-purchase price difference.
18 (Case) Section 441 III BGB Reduced price = agreed price × value with defect / value without defect.
19 Section 476 BGB Consumer purchase: cannot deviate from warranty rights to buyer’s disadvantage before defect notification.
20 (Case) Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB Disclosed, unopposed intended use sets a subjective defect standard above generic market expectations.
21 (Case) Section 435 BGB Legal defect (undisclosed third-party right) is defective regardless of the item’s flawless physical condition.
22 (Case) Section 442 I sentence 2 BGB Grossly negligent failure to notice an obvious, invited-inspection defect excludes rights just like actual knowledge.
23 (Case) Section 284 BGB Futile-expense reimbursement lets the buyer recover reliance costs without proving speculative lost profit.
24 (Case) Section 434 III 3 BGB A corrected, non-influential manufacturer claim releases the seller from an advertising-based objective defect.
25 (Case, integrative) Sections 305, 307-309 BGB + Section 437 BGB Section 309 No. 8 voids a blanket “as is” exclusion on newly manufactured goods regardless of checkbox acceptance.

80/20 Exam Summary

Warranty Rights II explains the damages side of buyer remedies and gives an overview of warranty rights in work contracts.

  • Section 437 No. 3 BGB routes warranty damages into Sections 280 et seq. BGB and reimbursement into Section 284 BGB.
  • The key exam distinction is damages in addition to performance versus damages instead of performance.
  • Use the hypothetical-performance test: would the claimed loss still exist if proper performance were rendered at the latest possible time?
  • Simple damages in addition to performance usually use Section 280 I BGB.
  • Damages instead of performance due to repairable non- or malperformance usually use Sections 280 I, III, 281 BGB and require an additional period unless an exception applies.
  • Damages instead of performance due to impossibility use Sections 280 I, III, 283 BGB when performance becomes impossible after contract conclusion.
  • Initial impossibility uses Section 311a BGB.
  • Responsibility normally means intent or negligence under Section 276 BGB; Section 280 I 2 BGB presumes fault.
  • Section 278 BGB attributes fault of persons used to perform the obligation.
  • Damage is assessed through restitution in kind, monetary compensation, and the difference hypothesis.
  • Section 284 BGB reimburses futile expenses instead of damages in lieu of performance.
  • Work-contract warranty rights under Section 634 BGB are similar to purchase warranty rights but add self-help under Section 637 BGB and use acceptance of work as the decisive timing point.

Continuity Bridge From Warranty Rights I

Week 08 gave the gateway:

valid purchase agreement
-> defect at transfer of risk
-> no exclusion
-> Section 437 remedy

Week 09 focuses on what happens when the chosen Section 437 remedy is damages or reimbursement.

Section 437 No. 3 BGB
-> damages under Sections 280 et seq.
-> reimbursement under Section 284

Legal Remedies Are Tiered

Section 437 BGB remedies remain in a tiered relationship.

cure first as the regular second chance
-> then revocation / reduction / damages / reimbursement if additional requirements are met

The damages route is not one single claim. It depends on the type of damage and the performance problem.

Distinguishing Damages Types

Core question from the deck:

Would the claimed damage still exist if performance had been hypothetically rendered correctly at the latest possible time?
Answer Damage type Typical statutory route
Yes, the loss would still exist. Damages in addition to performance. Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB.
No, proper performance would remove/avoid the loss. Damages instead of performance. Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281/283 BGB or Section 311a BGB.

Examples from the deck:

Facts Classification Route
Defective good harms buyer’s other property. Damages in addition to performance. Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB.
Defective good can be fixed; buyer claims reduced market value. Damages instead of performance. Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB.
Defective good cannot be fixed; buyer claims reduced market value. Damages instead of performance due to impossibility. Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 283 BGB.

Section 280 I BGB Basic Damages

Elements:

1. Contractual obligation.
2. Breach of duty.
3. Responsibility.
4. Causal damage.

In warranty cases:

purchase agreement
-> defective delivery
-> seller responsible unless not responsible
-> causal loss

Section 280 I 2 BGB matters because the debtor must show they are not responsible.

Responsibility

Responsibility normally covers:

  • intent;
  • negligence under Section 276 BGB;
  • strict liability if a guarantee is given;
  • attributed fault of helpers under Section 278 BGB.

Guarantee:

No intent or negligence is required if the seller assumed a guarantee.
Tacit guarantee is possible, but the threshold is high.

Third parties:

If the debtor uses another person to perform the obligation, Section 278 BGB can attribute that person's fault to the debtor.

Business example: if a seller uses an employee or another company to perform delivery/installation, the seller may be responsible for that helper within the obligation scope.

Damage

Damage is not defined directly in statutory law in the deck. The note uses this working definition:

damage = involuntary loss of material or immaterial goods/interests

Not every spending is damage. Voluntary spending in reliance on the contract can be reimbursement under Section 284 BGB instead.

Damage categories:

Category Meaning Anchor
Material damage Measurable in money. Sections 249 et seq. BGB.
Immaterial damage Not measurable in money; only compensable if statute allows. Section 253 BGB.
Lost profit Profit that would likely have been earned absent the damaging event. Section 252 BGB.

General form:

restitution in kind under Section 249 I BGB
-> monetary compensation under Sections 249 II-251 BGB where appropriate

Difference hypothesis:

damage = hypothetical situation without damaging event - actual situation

Damages Instead Of Performance Under Section 281 BGB

Use this route for non-performance or malperformance that can still be cured.

Statutory combination:

Section 280 I BGB + Section 280 III BGB + Section 281 BGB

Additional Section 281 requirements:

  • due obligation to perform;
  • non-performance or malperformance;
  • reasonable additional period for performance/cure;
  • period expires without result;
  • exceptions under Section 281 II BGB or Section 440 BGB in purchase cases;
  • responsibility for initial malperformance or expiry of the additional period.

Exclusions:

Exclusion Anchor Meaning
Partial performance still useful Section 281 I 2 BGB No damages instead of entire performance if buyer still has interest.
Insignificant defective performance Section 281 I 3 BGB No damages instead of entire performance for insignificant defects.

Small And Big Damages

Type Deck label Economic result Nearby warranty analogy
Small claim for damages Damage instead of performance, but buyer keeps item. Buyer keeps defective item and receives value difference. Similar, but not identical, to reduction.
Big claim for damages Damage instead of entire performance. Buyer returns item and receives purchase price back or damages for non-fulfilment. Similar to revocation.

Example of small claim:

Buyer keeps defective item.
Damages = value difference between defect-free item and defective item.

Example of big claim:

Buyer urgently obtains substitute goods from another supplier.
Buyer may claim covering-purchase-related damages if requirements are met.

Small Damages Versus Reduction

Small damages and reduction can look economically similar because the buyer keeps the defective item and receives money. The legal route is different.

Question Small damages Reduction
Statutory route Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB
Buyer keeps item? Yes Yes
Seller responsibility needed? Yes, under Section 280 I 2 BGB No fault requirement
Core function Compensation for the performance deficit Price adjustment to the lower value
Exam signal Buyer claims loss/value deficit as damages Buyer declares reduction or asks for refund of overpaid price

Example:

agreed price = EUR 10,000
defect-free value = EUR 10,000
defective value = EUR 7,000
value deficit = EUR 3,000

If the buyer says “I keep the machine but want compensation for the EUR 3,000 loss”, route as small damages. If the buyer says “I reduce the price because the machine is worth less”, route as reduction. The same value gap may appear, but damages require responsibility and the damages route.

Reusable exam sentence:

Although the economic result resembles reduction, the buyer is claiming compensation for the value deficit. This is small damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, and 281 BGB, so responsibility and the damages requirements must be checked.

Reduction sentence:

The buyer does not claim damages but adjusts the purchase price because the defective item is worth less. This is reduction under Sections 437 No. 2 and 441 BGB, which does not require seller responsibility.

Big Damages Versus Revocation

Big damages and revocation can also look similar because the buyer gives up the defective performance. Again, the legal route is different.

Question Big damages Revocation
Statutory route Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 ff. BGB
Buyer gives up performance? Usually yes Yes
Seller responsibility needed? Yes, under Section 280 I 2 BGB No fault requirement
Core function Compensation for non-fulfilment loss Unwind the contract and return performances
Money focus Loss such as extra cost of substitute purchase Return of purchase price / restitution

Example:

original price = EUR 10,000
seller fails to cure
buyer buys substitute machine = EUR 12,000
extra cost = EUR 2,000

If the buyer claims the EUR 2,000 extra cost of substitute performance, route as big damages. If the buyer only wants to return the defective machine and get the purchase price back, route as revocation.

Reusable exam sentence:

The buyer does not merely want to unwind the contract; she claims the loss caused by having to obtain substitute performance. This is big damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, and 281 BGB.

Revocation sentence:

The buyer wants to undo the contract and return the defective item against repayment of the purchase price. This is revocation under Sections 437 No. 2 and 323 BGB, with restitution under Sections 346 ff. BGB.

Memory rule:

Reduction/revocation = price adjustment or unwinding.
Small/big damages = compensation for loss, therefore responsibility required.

Damages Due To Impossibility

Use Sections 280 I, III, 283 BGB if performance becomes impossible after contract conclusion but before transfer of risk.

The deck links this route to Section 275 BGB:

Impossibility type Anchor Meaning
Genuine impossibility Section 275 I BGB Performance is objectively or subjectively impossible.
Practical impossibility Section 275 II BGB Performance is not literally impossible, but effort is grossly disproportionate.
Personal impossibility Section 275 III BGB Personally owed performance cannot reasonably be expected.

Effect:

debtor released from performance duty
-> damages or revocation may become possible

Initial impossibility is routed through Section 311a BGB.

Secondary Duty Damages

Sections 280 I, III, 282 BGB apply where a breach of secondary duty makes performance unacceptable.

Elements added by Section 282:

  • breach of a secondary duty under Section 241 II BGB;
  • destroyed base of trust;
  • breach relevant to the purpose of the contract;
  • weighing of interests makes further performance unacceptable.

Craftsman example from the deck:

Craftsman installs kitchen properly but acts drunk, smokes, and damages floor.
Floor damage: damages in addition to performance under Sections 280 I, 241 II BGB.
Cost of a new craftsman: damages instead of performance under Sections 280 I, III, 282 BGB.

Gas Station Example

Facts:

S sells regular fuel to B.
Due to supplier mistake, fuel has 80 octane instead of required 95.
S negligently fails to notice.
B's car breaks down and engine is damaged.
B also wants back the money spent on fuel.

Analysis:

  1. Purchase contract under Section 433 BGB.
  2. Defective fuel under Section 434 II 1 No. 2 BGB at transfer of risk.
  3. Engine damage: proper fuel delivered later would not undo engine damage.
  4. Therefore engine repair costs are damages in addition to performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB.
  5. Fuel price: defect in fuel could be cured by new conforming fuel.
  6. Therefore repayment/substitute value for fuel is damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, requiring an additional period unless an exception applies.

Exam sentence:

The engine damage is consequential damage in addition to performance; the unusable fuel itself concerns the defective performance and routes into damages instead of performance.

Reimbursement Of Futile Expenses

Section 284 BGB:

reimbursement of futile expenses instead of damages in lieu of performance

Requirements:

  • same basic requirements as damages in lieu of performance;
  • expenses in the buyer’s own interest;
  • expenses made in reliance on receiving proper performance;
  • expenses were reasonable;
  • expenses would have been recouped with due performance.

Examples:

  • transport organization costs;
  • vehicle registration costs.

Not covered:

  • expenses to avert damages;
  • expenses grossly disproportionate to the value of performance;
  • expenses made when non-performance was already foreseeable;
  • expenses that would not have been recouped for reasons unrelated to the debtor’s breach.

Relationship:

Section 284 reimbursement and damages in lieu of performance are either/or.

Warranty Rights In Works Contracts

Work contracts have a parallel but not identical warranty structure.

Decisive point:

acceptance of work under Section 640 BGB

This matters because acceptance is tied to:

  • transfer of risk under Section 644 BGB;
  • applicability of warranty rights.

Section 634 BGB is the work-contract referral provision.

Work-contract remedy Anchor Difference from purchase law
Cure Sections 634 No. 1, 635 BGB Contractor decides type of cure.
Self-help Sections 634 No. 2, 637 BGB Added work-contract remedy.
Revocation Sections 634 No. 3, 323 BGB Similar route.
Reduction Sections 634 No. 3, 638 BGB Similar idea.
Damages Section 634 No. 4 plus Sections 280 et seq. BGB Similar damages logic.
Reimbursement Section 634 No. 4 plus Section 284 BGB Similar reimbursement logic.

Exam trap: do not automatically apply purchase warranty sections to work contracts. Identify contract type first.

Visual Knowledge Map

flowchart TD
    Gateway[Section 437 No. 3] --> DamageType{Which damage?}
    DamageType -->|still exists after proper performance| AddPerf[Damages in addition: Section 280 I]
    DamageType -->|replaces missing/defective performance| Instead[Damages instead]
    Instead --> CurePossible{Performance/cure still possible?}
    CurePossible -->|yes| S281[Sections 280 I, III, 281]
    CurePossible -->|no subsequent impossibility| S283[Sections 280 I, III, 283]
    CurePossible -->|initial impossibility| S311a[Section 311a]
    AddPerf --> Elements[Obligation + breach + responsibility + causal damage]
    S281 --> Period[Additional period unless exception]
    S283 --> Impossibility[Section 275 impossibility]
    Gateway --> Reimb[Section 284 reimbursement]
    Reimb --> EitherOr[Instead of damages in lieu]
    Work[Works contract] --> S634[Section 634 remedies]

Subject Knowledge Graph

Node Meaning Exam Relevance
Damages In Addition Loss remains even if performance is later correct. Usually Section 280 I BGB.
Damages Instead Loss replaces missing/defective performance. Needs Section 281, 283, or 311a route.
Hypothetical-Performance Test Would damage remain if proper performance were rendered? Main classification tool.
Section 280 I Elements Obligation, breach, responsibility, causal damage. Basic damages skeleton.
Responsibility Intent/negligence, guarantee, attributed helper fault. Seller can escape only if not responsible.
Damage Involuntary loss measured by difference hypothesis. Defines compensation target.
Small Damages Buyer keeps defective item and claims value difference. Similar to reduction.
Big Damages Buyer gives up whole performance and claims non-fulfilment. Similar to revocation.
Section 284 Reimbursement Futile expenses instead of damages in lieu. Do not mix with damage prevention costs.
Work-Contract Warranty Section 634 remedy system. Identify contract type.
From Relationship To Why It Matters
Section 437 No. 3 routes to Sections 280 et seq. Warranty damages use general damages law.
Hypothetical-Performance Test classifies Damages In Addition / Damages Instead Prevents wrong statutory route.
Section 281 requires Additional Period Cure priority continues in damages.
Section 283 depends on Impossibility No period for impossible performance.
Section 284 replaces Damages In Lieu Either/or relationship.
Work-Contract Warranty adds Self-Help Purchase law does not have the same self-help remedy.

Real Business Examples

  • Defective fuel damages an engine: engine repair is damages in addition to performance.
  • Faulty delivered machine can be repaired, but buyer wants reduced market value: damages instead of performance under Section 281.
  • Custom-built software project is accepted and then defects appear: work-contract warranty law may be relevant, not purchase law.
  • Buyer registers and transports a car in reliance on proper delivery, but the seller fails to deliver conforming performance: reimbursement of futile expenses may be considered.

Exam Relevance

Likely prompts:

  • Distinguish damages in addition to performance and damages instead of performance.
  • State the elements of Section 280 I BGB.
  • Explain responsibility and Section 278 BGB helper attribution.
  • Classify a loss using the hypothetical-performance test.
  • Choose between Section 281 and Section 283.
  • Explain small versus big damages.
  • Distinguish damages from reimbursement of futile expenses.
  • Identify warranty remedies in work contracts.

Common traps:

  • Calling every loss “damages instead” because the good was defective.
  • Forgetting the additional period under Section 281.
  • Ignoring impossibility and using Section 281 even when cure is impossible.
  • Treating voluntary expenses as damage instead of Section 284 reimbursement.
  • Applying purchase warranty sections to a work contract without checking contract type.

High-scoring answer structure:

  1. Start with Section 437 No. 3 if the case is a defective purchase item.
  2. Classify the loss with the hypothetical-performance test.
  3. State the correct route: Section 280 I, Section 281, Section 283, Section 311a, or Section 284.
  4. Check Section 280 I elements.
  5. Add route-specific requirements, especially additional period or impossibility.
  6. State the legal consequence and business meaning.

Official Exercise Case Routes

The exercise deck uses one kitchen-machine fact pattern to train remedy selection across four subquestions.

Case 1a: Revocation For Missing Professional Equipment

Question: did C revoke the purchase contract?

Route:

  1. Legal basis: Sections 437 No. 2 Alt. 1, 323, and 346 BGB because the facts point to a defect.
  2. Purchase agreement: C and T agree on the kitchen machine “Helping Elf” with additional integrated professional equipment for EUR 1,000.
  3. Defect: the integrated professional equipment is part of the machine’s agreed quality under Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB, not merely an accessory.
  4. Transfer of risk: the equipment had to be built in from the beginning, so the defect existed at delivery.
  5. Additional period: C did not set one, but it is dispensable under Section 440 BGB because T refused both kinds of cure by saying retrofitting is impossible and he will do nothing.
  6. Declaration: C demanded cure, not revocation. No revocation declaration under Section 349 BGB has yet been made.
  7. Exclusions: not trivial under Section 323 V 2 BGB because the professional equipment was specially agreed and necessary for C’s demanding baking use; no responsibility of buyer under Section 323 VI BGB.

Result: C has a right to revoke, but still needs a revocation declaration.

Exam trap: a right to revoke and an exercised revocation are different.

Case 1b: Reduction Calculation

Question: did C reduce the purchase price and how much can she demand back?

Route:

  1. Reduction under Sections 437 No. 2 Alt. 2 and 441 BGB requires a right to revoke; Case 1a supplies it.
  2. Declaration: C demands a refund for the money paid too much, which can be a reduction declaration under Section 441 I BGB.
  3. Formula under Section 441 III BGB:
reduced price = value with defect * agreed price / value without defect
reduced price = EUR 600 * EUR 1,000 / EUR 800 = EUR 750
refund = EUR 1,000 - EUR 750 = EUR 250

Result: C effectively reduces the price to EUR 750 and can demand EUR 250 back under Section 441 IV BGB.

Exam trap: reduction is proportional value math, not automatically the repair cost or the subjective disappointment.

Case 1c: Fire Damage To Kitchen Cabinets

Question: can C demand EUR 20,000 for the burned cabinets?

Route:

  1. Legal basis: Sections 437 No. 3 Alt. 1 and 280 I BGB. The damage to cabinets would remain even if T later delivered a proper machine, so it is damages in addition to performance.
  2. Contractual obligation: purchase agreement.
  3. Breach: T had to deliver a defect-free machine and had to perform cure properly; the replacement machine had a dangerous electronics defect.
  4. Defect at transfer of risk: the electronics problem existed at delivery of the replacement machine.
  5. Responsibility: presumed under Section 280 I 2 BGB; negligence is clear because T knew of the recall campaign and mixed up the machines.
  6. Causal damage: the electronics defect caused the fire and destroyed cabinets worth EUR 20,000.
  7. Legal consequence: restitution in kind or money compensation under Section 249 BGB; C wants the value.

Result: C can claim EUR 20,000 as damages in addition to performance.

Exam trap: damage to other property caused by the defective thing is not cured by later proper performance, so route it as damages in addition.

Case 1d: Personalized Cover As Futile Expense

Question: can C claim EUR 30 for the personalized cover?

Route:

  1. Legal basis: Sections 437 No. 3 Alt. 2 and 284 BGB, in place of damages in lieu of performance.
  2. Damages-instead route must be available: purchase agreement, defective second machine, reasonable two-week period for new cure, no response by T, and responsibility.
  3. Futile expense: C voluntarily spent EUR 30 on a personalized cover in reliance on receiving usable performance.
  4. Fairness: the expense was reasonable for a EUR 1,000 kitchen machine.
  5. No exception: the purpose of the expense would have been achieved if T had performed properly.

Result: C can claim reimbursement of EUR 30 under Sections 437 No. 3 Alt. 2 and 284 BGB.

Exam trap: Section 284 is not “any cost refund”; it substitutes for damages in lieu and requires reliance on proper performance.

Retrieval Prompts

Closed-book questions:

  1. What is the hypothetical-performance test?
  2. What are the four elements of Section 280 I BGB?
  3. When do you use Section 281 instead of Section 283?
  4. What does Section 278 BGB do?
  5. What is the difference between damage and futile expense?
  6. Which additional remedy appears in work-contract warranty law?

Application prompts:

  1. Defective fuel destroys a car engine. Classify engine repair and fuel-price claim separately.
  2. Buyer keeps defective machinery and claims the value difference. Is this small or big damages?
  3. Seller cannot cure because the specific sold object was destroyed before transfer of risk. Which route is likely?
  4. Buyer paid vehicle registration costs in reliance on delivery. Damages or reimbursement?
  5. A contractor’s work is accepted, then defects appear. Which warranty gateway do you open?

Practice Tasks

  1. Build a two-column table for Section 280 I, Section 281, Section 283, Section 284, and Section 634.
  2. Write a 12-line answer to the gas station case.
  3. Invent one example of damages in addition and one example of damages instead.
  4. Explain why Section 284 is not just “damages with another name.”
  5. Compare purchase-contract cure with work-contract cure in three sentences.

Connections

Previous notes:

  • Week 08 Warranty Rights I: gateway, defect, transfer of risk, cure, revocation, reduction.
  • Week 05 Contract Law III: revocation and restitution background.
  • Week 06 Standard Business Terms: exclusions and liability limitations can be controlled by SBT rules.

Future notes:

  • Week 10 Transfer of Property: separates contract duties from ownership transfer.

Weakness Flags

  • Pending active recall: no first-pass retrieval has been completed yet.

  • High-risk issue: Section 281 additional period.
  • High-risk issue: purchase warranty versus work-contract warranty.

[W09.2] Week 09 Warranty Rights II Cheatsheet And Tricks

Source: business-law/wiki/week-09-warranty-rights-ii/week-09-warranty-rights-ii-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-09-warranty-rights-ii.md, clarification-session-2026-07-12.md

Warranty Rights II is the money-claim extension of Warranty Rights I: once Section 437 BGB opens the gateway, this week routes the buyer’s claim into damages or reimbursement rather than cure/revocation/reduction themselves.

Must-Know (exam-critical)

Concept Anchor Core rule
Hypothetical-performance test — Would the loss still exist if the seller had performed correctly at the latest possible time? Yes → damages in addition. No → damages instead.
Damages in addition to performance Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB Loss survives even correct later performance (e.g. consequential damage to other property).
Damages instead of performance, curable case Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB Non/malperformance that could still be cured; needs a reasonable additional period unless dispensable (281 II BGB, or 440 BGB in purchase cases).
Damages instead of performance, impossibility Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 283 BGB Performance became impossible after contract conclusion; no additional period needed.
Initial impossibility Section 311a BGB Performance was already impossible at contract conclusion.
Section 280 I elements Section 280 I BGB (1) obligation, (2) breach of duty, (3) responsibility (presumed, seller must disprove), (4) causal damage.
Responsibility Section 276 BGB (intent/negligence), Section 278 BGB (helper fault attributed) Guarantee assumption triggers strict liability with no fault needed; tacit guarantee has a high threshold.
Small damages Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB Buyer keeps the defective item, claims the value deficit as damages; requires seller responsibility.
Big damages Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB Buyer gives up the defective performance, claims the non-fulfilment loss (e.g. substitute-purchase extra cost); requires seller responsibility.
Section 284 reimbursement Section 284 BGB Futile-expense reimbursement instead of damages in lieu of performance; either/or with damages instead of performance.
Work-contract warranty Section 634 BGB referral, Section 640 acceptance as the decisive timing point Parallel but not identical structure to purchase law; adds self-help (Section 637 BGB).

Nice-to-Have (depth/edge cases)

  • Secondary-duty damages under Sections 280 I, III, 282 BGB: applies when a breach of a Section 241 II duty (not the main performance) destroys the base of trust and makes further performance unacceptable — the deck’s drunk-craftsman example splits floor damage (in addition) from the cost of a replacement craftsman (instead of, via 282).
  • Damage categories: material (Sections 249 ff.), immaterial (Section 253, only if statute allows), lost profit (Section 252).
  • Difference hypothesis: damage = hypothetical situation without the damaging event minus the actual situation.
  • Exclusions from Section 281 damages instead of the entire performance: partial performance still useful (281 I 2) and insignificant defective performance (281 I 3).
  • Section 284 requirements beyond “spent money”: expense was in the buyer’s own interest, made in reliance on proper performance, reasonable, and would have been recouped had performance been proper. Excludes expenses to avert damage, grossly disproportionate expenses, expenses made when non-performance was already foreseeable, or expenses that would not have been recouped for unrelated reasons.
  • Gas-station fact pattern: wrong-octane fuel — engine damage is damages in addition (would remain even after correct fuel is later supplied); the fuel price itself is damages instead (curable by conforming fuel), so one fact pattern can split into two separate routes.

Nuances And Traps

Nuance/Trap Why it’s easy to get wrong Correct handling
Treating Week 09 as “the details of revocation/reduction” The clarification session flags this as a recorded confusion — Warranty II is not a deep dive into revocation/reduction mechanics, those belong to Warranty I / Section 437 No. 2. State plainly: Week 09 routes money claims — damages in addition, damages instead, and Section 284 reimbursement — as separate branches off the same Section 437 gateway.
Confusing small damages with reduction Both leave the buyer holding the defective item and receiving money, so the economic result looks identical. Ask whether the buyer is claiming compensation for a loss (needs seller responsibility, Sections 280 I, III, 281) or adjusting the price with no fault requirement (Sections 437 No. 2, 441). Reduction is proportional value math (reduced price = value with defect × agreed price / value without defect), not damages.
Confusing big damages with revocation Both end with the buyer giving up the defective performance. Ask whether the buyer wants compensation for non-fulfilment loss (needs responsibility, e.g. substitute-purchase extra cost) or simply wants to unwind the contract and get the purchase price back with no fault requirement (Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 ff.).
Ignoring seller responsibility for damages claims Reduction and revocation do not require fault, which makes it tempting to skip the fault check for damages too. Damages (small, big, in addition, instead) always run through Section 280 I and require responsibility, presumed under 280 I 2 but rebuttable by the seller. Reduction/revocation never need this check.
Calling every loss from a defective item “damages instead” The word “defective” pulls attention to the instead-of-performance route by default. Always run the hypothetical-performance test first — consequential damage to other property (e.g. burned cabinets, damaged engine) survives correct later performance and is damages in addition, not instead.
Forgetting the additional period requirement under Section 281 The Section 437 I gateway summary makes cure sound automatic, but Section 281 has its own procedural step. Damages instead of performance for a curable defect needs a reasonable additional period that expired without result, unless dispensable under Section 281 II or Section 440 BGB (e.g. seller seriously refuses cure).
Using Section 281 when cure is actually impossible 281 and 283 sit right next to each other and look interchangeable at first glance. If cure/replacement is genuinely impossible (Section 275), route through Section 283 (no additional period needed), not Section 281. Initial impossibility (already impossible at contract conclusion) goes through Section 311a instead.
Treating a voluntary reliance expense as ordinary “damage” Both feel like money the buyer lost because of the seller’s failure. Only involuntary loss is “damage” under Sections 249 ff. Voluntary spending made in reliance on proper performance (e.g. a personalized cover, registration costs) routes through Section 284 reimbursement instead, and is either/or with damages instead of performance — never claim both for the same expense.
Applying purchase warranty sections to a work contract Purchase and works contracts share similar-looking remedy vocabulary (cure, revocation, reduction, damages). Identify contract type first. Works contracts run through Section 634 BGB’s referral system, add self-help under Section 637 (no purchase-law equivalent), and use acceptance of work (Section 640) as the decisive timing point instead of transfer of risk.
Right to revoke vs. an exercised revocation The exercise case (kitchen-machine 1a) shows a buyer who qualifies for revocation but only ever demanded cure. Meeting the substantive requirements (defect, dispensable additional period, no exclusion) only creates a right to revoke — the buyer still needs an actual revocation declaration under Section 349 BGB before the contract is unwound.

One-Line Recall Drill

hypothetical-performance test = would the loss survive correct later performance?
280 I = obligation + breach + responsibility (presumed) + causal damage
281 = curable non/malperformance + additional period (unless dispensable)
283 = subsequent impossibility, no additional period
311a = initial impossibility
282 = secondary-duty breach destroys base of trust
278 = helper fault attributed to debtor
small damages = keep item + value-deficit compensation + responsibility required
reduction = keep item + price adjustment + no fault required
big damages = give up performance + non-fulfilment compensation + responsibility required
revocation = give up performance + unwind contract + no fault required
284 = futile expense reimbursement, either/or with damages instead
634 = work-contract warranty referral; 640 = acceptance is the timing anchor; 637 = self-help, purchase law has no equivalent

[W09.3] Week 09 Warranty Rights II Practice Questions And Model Answers

Source: business-law/wiki/week-09-warranty-rights-ii/week-09-warranty-rights-ii-practice-questions-and-model-answers.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-09-warranty-rights-ii.md, week-09-warranty-rights-ii-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md Format note: 24 questions — 8 short-answer/theory, 16 case/legal-opinion (schema-based). Six case questions integrate other weeks: Week 04 Contract Law II (rescission/revocation), Week 05 Contract Law III (withdrawal-versus-warranty routing), Week 08 Warranty Rights I (cure disproportionality; reduction’s cure-first gateway), and Week 11 Trade Law (Section 377 HGB notice duty).

Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 1

Explain reimbursement of futile expenses under Section 284 BGB.

Model Answer: 1. Definition: Reimbursement of futile expenses lets a creditor claim back expenses reasonably incurred in reliance on receiving proper performance, instead of claiming damages instead of performance. 2. Statutory anchor: Section 284 BGB. 3. Requirements: (1) the general requirements for damages instead of performance are otherwise met (via Section 280 I, III with 281, 283, or 311a); (2) the expense was made in the creditor’s own interest and in reliance on receiving proper performance; (3) the expense was reasonable and would have been recouped through proper performance. 4. Example: a buyer pays vehicle registration costs anticipating delivery of a car the seller never conforms to the contract. 5. Consequence/trap: Section 284 is either/or with damages instead of performance for the same expense, and it excludes expenses incurred once non-performance was already foreseeable, or expenses grossly disproportionate to the value of performance.

Question 2

Compare damages in addition to performance and damages instead of performance.

Model Answer: Damages in addition to performance trigger when the loss would still exist even if the debtor rendered proper performance at the latest possible moment (e.g. a defective product damages other property), anchored in Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB, leading to a straightforward claim with no additional-period requirement. Damages instead of performance trigger when proper performance would have removed or avoided the loss (e.g. the defective item itself just needs fixing or replacing), anchored in Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III with 281 (curable), 283 (subsequently impossible), or 311a (initially impossible) BGB, and for the 281 route specifically require a reasonable additional period to have expired without result. Contrast example: defective fuel that both damages an engine (in addition) and itself needs replacing (instead) — one fact pattern, two separate routes. Exam trap: do not label every loss arising from a defect as “damages instead” merely because the underlying good was defective — always run the hypothetical-performance test first.

Question 3

Compare small damages and big damages.

Model Answer: Small damages trigger when the buyer keeps the defective item and claims the value deficit as compensation, anchored in Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, leading to payment of the difference between a defect-free item’s value and the defective item’s value, conditional on seller responsibility. Big damages trigger when the buyer gives up the entire defective performance and claims the non-fulfilment loss (e.g. the extra cost of a substitute purchase elsewhere), anchored in the same Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, but the payment replaces the whole performance rather than closing a value gap. Contrast example: a EUR 10,000 machine worth EUR 7,000 defective — small damages claims the EUR 3,000 gap while keeping the machine; big damages returns the machine and claims the EUR 2,000 extra cost of a EUR 12,000 replacement bought elsewhere. Exam trap: both look similar to reduction/revocation because the buyer ends up with money either way, but damages require seller responsibility while reduction and revocation do not.

Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 4 (Case)

Facts: F sells industrial lubricant to a machine shop M for EUR 500. Due to a mixing error at F’s warehouse, the lubricant delivered is corrosive rather than the ordinary type M ordered. F did not notice the mix-up. M’s technician uses it in a precision lathe; the lathe’s bearings are destroyed, costing EUR 4,000 to repair. M wants F to pay both the EUR 4,000 repair cost and refund the EUR 500 paid for the unusable lubricant. M has not yet asked F for a replacement delivery of correct lubricant.

Question: Does M have a claim against F for (a) the EUR 4,000 lathe repair and (b) the EUR 500 lubricant price, and under what legal bases?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: M could have a claim against F for damages under Section 437 No. 3 in conjunction with Section 280 I BGB for the lathe repair, and separately under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB for the lubricant price, if the requirements of these provisions are met. II. Requirements: I. Valid purchase contract (Section 433 BGB). II. Defect at transfer of risk (Section 434, 446 BGB). III. For the lathe repair: obligation, breach, responsibility, causal damage (Section 280 I elements) — damages in addition. IV. For the lubricant price: the same elements plus, for Section 281, a reasonable additional period that expired without result, unless dispensable. III. Application: I. Purchase contract: M and F concluded a purchase contract for lubricant under Section 433 BGB when M ordered and F agreed to supply it for EUR 500. II. Defect: Questionable is whether the delivered lubricant was defective. This is supported by the fact that it was corrosive rather than the ordinary type agreed, so it lacked the agreed quality under Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB. Consequently, the lubricant was defective at transfer of risk (Section 446 BGB). III. Lathe repair — damages in addition: Questionable is whether the EUR 4,000 repair is damages in addition to performance. This is supported by the hypothetical-performance test: even if F delivered conforming lubricant now, the lathe damage would remain. Against this, one could argue the damage flows directly from the defect and should follow the defect’s own route. However, consequential damage to other property caused by a defective item is not cured by later proper performance. Responsibility is presumed under Section 280 I 2 BGB and not rebutted, since F’s own mixing error caused the wrong delivery. Consequently, the lathe repair is damages in addition to performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB. IV. Lubricant price — damages instead: Questionable is whether the EUR 500 lubricant price is damages instead of performance. This is supported by the fact that conforming lubricant could still cure the defect entirely — the defect concerns the lubricant itself, not other property. However, Section 281 additionally requires a reasonable additional period for cure that expired without result, unless dispensable under Section 281 II or Section 440 BGB. The facts show M never demanded cure and F never refused it. Consequently, this requirement is not met on the facts as given. IV. Interim results: the lathe-repair claim is established (damages in addition); the lubricant-price claim is not yet established because the additional-period requirement under Section 281 has not been satisfied or dispensed with. V. Final answer: As a result, M can currently claim the EUR 4,000 lathe repair from F as damages in addition to performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB, but cannot yet claim the EUR 500 lubricant price as damages instead of performance unless M first sets F a reasonable additional period for cure (or such a period is dispensable).

Question 5 (Case)

Facts: F sold a used delivery van to bakery B for EUR 12,000. The transmission was defective at handover; a defect-free equivalent van would be worth EUR 12,000, while the van’s actual value with the defect is EUR 9,000. B keeps using the van as-is and writes to F: “I am not returning the van, and I want you to compensate me because I effectively overpaid due to the transmission problem — I hold you responsible for not disclosing this.”

Question: Should B’s claim be routed as small damages or as reduction, and what does each route require B to show?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: B’s claim could be small damages under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB or reduction under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB, depending on how B’s demand is properly classified. II. Requirements: small damages requires seller responsibility (Section 280 I 2 BGB, presumed but rebuttable) in addition to the warranty gateway; reduction requires no fault, only the warranty gateway and a reduction declaration under Section 441 I BGB. III. Application: Questionable is whether B’s letter is a demand for compensation (damages) or a price adjustment (reduction). This is supported by B’s own wording — B explicitly “holds F responsible,” asserting fault-based compensation for a loss, not merely adjusting the price to the lower value. Against this, one could argue the economic outcome (keeping the van, receiving EUR 3,000) is identical either way, so the label should not matter. However, the two routes carry different legal requirements: small damages presupposes F’s responsibility, which must be checked and could be rebutted if F neither knew nor should have known of the defect, while reduction requires none. Consequently, because B’s letter asserts fault, this is small damages, not reduction, and the responsibility requirement must be affirmatively established. IV. Interim result: the requirements for small damages are met only if F’s responsibility for the defect is shown or not rebutted; reduction would apply regardless of fault and yields the same EUR 3,000 figure through the proportional formula. V. Final answer: As a result, B’s demand as framed is small damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB for EUR 3,000, conditional on F’s responsibility being established or not rebutted; if F disproves responsibility, B would need to fall back on reduction under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB for the same amount, without needing to prove fault.

Question 6 (Case — integrates Week 09 + Week 04)

Facts: P buys a vintage racing bicycle advertised by seller Q as “an original 1985 frame, hand-built by the famous frame-builder Enzo Colnago,” paying EUR 8,000. After delivery, P has the bicycle authenticated and learns the frame is a well-made modern replica worth about EUR 1,200. Q genuinely believed the frame was authentic when selling it, relying on paperwork that later turns out to have been forged by an earlier owner in the chain of title. P wants to undo the deal and recover the EUR 8,000.

Question: Should P’s claim be pursued as rescission for an essential-characteristic mistake under Section 119 II BGB, or through the warranty route? Advise P.

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: P’s claim could be pursued through rescission for an essential-characteristic mistake (Section 119 II BGB) or through the warranty gateway (Section 437 BGB), with revocation under Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 BGB as the likely remedy if warranty law applies. II. Requirements: (I) determine whether the frame’s inauthenticity is a formation-stage mistake (119 II) or a transfer-stage material defect (434 II); (II) purchase contract; (III) defect and transfer of risk; (IV) revocation requirements, including Nachfrist and its exclusions; (V) legal consequence. III. Application: Questionable is whether Q’s own mistaken belief about the frame’s origin allows reliance on Section 119 II BGB. This is supported by the fact that authorship/origin of a collectible item is exactly the kind of “essential characteristic” Section 119 II covers in the abstract. Against this, one could argue that Section 119 II rescission is a defense available to the party who made the mistaken declaration — here Q, the seller — and does not assist P as buyer; moreover, once a purchased item is delivered and found not to match its agreed quality, that is precisely what warranty law under Section 434 BGB is designed to handle, not a mistake analysis on the buyer’s side. However, applying rescission analysis to a delivered good that turns out defective would bypass the tiered warranty-remedy system (cure first) that Section 437 specifically builds in. Consequently, P’s route is warranty law, not rescission: the frame’s actual authorship differs from the agreed quality (an authentic 1985 hand-built Colnago frame), so it lacks the agreed quality under Section 434 II 1 No. 1 BGB, and the defect existed at transfer of risk (Section 446 BGB) since the frame was never actually authentic. Revocation ordinarily requires a Nachfrist for cure, but cure — turning a replica into an authentic original — is objectively impossible, so the additional period is dispensable. No fault/responsibility is required for revocation under Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 BGB. IV. Interim result: P cannot pursue Section 119 II rescission as buyer; P’s route is the Section 437 warranty gateway, and within it, revocation is available without needing to show Q’s fault, because cure is objectively impossible. V. Final answer: As a result, P should be advised to pursue revocation of the purchase contract under Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 BGB (Nachfrist dispensable due to impossibility of cure), not rescission under Section 119 II BGB; upon a valid revocation declaration (Section 349 BGB), P returns the bicycle and recovers the EUR 8,000 purchase price under Sections 346 ff. BGB.

Question 7 (Case)

Facts: Interior fit-out company I delivers custom-built cabinetry to office tenant O for EUR 15,000. Several drawer fronts are warped due to a manufacturing defect. O immediately emails I: “This is unacceptable, I don’t want you anywhere near my office again — I am buying replacement cabinetry from someone else and will bill you the difference.” I is never given a chance to inspect or cure. Two weeks later, O buys replacement cabinetry from another supplier for EUR 17,000 and demands the EUR 2,000 difference from I as damages.

Question: Can O successfully claim the EUR 2,000 as big damages instead of performance without first setting I an additional period for cure?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: O could have a claim against I for EUR 2,000 in big damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB if the requirements, including the additional-period rule, are met. II. Requirements: (I) valid supply contract, (II) defect at transfer of risk, (III) reasonable additional period for cure that expired without result, or a dispensing exception, (IV) responsibility, (V) causal damage in the amount claimed. III. Application: Questionable is whether O needed to set I a Nachfrist before buying elsewhere.
