This is supported by the general rule that damages instead of performance under Section 281 requires exactly that — a reasonable additional period must expire unsuccessfully first, preserving the debtor’s chance to cure. Against this, one could argue O’s email was so final in tone that it functions as an implicit refusal of cure. However, the dispensability exceptions under Section 281 II BGB require a serious and definitive refusal by the debtor — here it is O, not I, who unilaterally shuts out the opportunity for cure; I never refused. Consequently, O’s own refusal to allow cure does not satisfy the exception. IV. Interim result: the additional-period requirement under Section 281 is not met and not validly dispensed with. V. Final answer: As a result, O cannot currently claim the EUR 2,000 as damages instead of performance, because O never gave I a reasonable additional period to cure and no recognized exception applies; O would first need to have set (or been excused from setting) such a period.

Question 8 (Case)

Facts: Homeowner H hires contractor K to design and build a custom walk-in wine cellar in H’s basement, including all materials and labor, for a lump sum of EUR 40,000. After H formally accepts the finished cellar, H notices the climate-control unit K installed does not maintain the agreed humidity range.

Question: Which warranty regime governs H’s claim, and what remedies — including any not found in ordinary sale-of-goods warranty law — are available to H?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: H could have a claim against K for cure, self-help, reduction, revocation, or damages under the works-contract warranty regime (Section 634 BGB and its referrals) if the requirements are met — not under the ordinary purchase warranty gateway (Section 437 BGB). II. Requirements: (I) classify the contract type, (II) confirm acceptance of the work (Section 640 BGB) as the relevant timing point, (III) confirm a defect under Section 633 BGB, (IV) select the appropriate Section 634 remedy and its own sub-requirements. III. Application: Questionable is whether the cellar project is a purchase contract or a works contract. This is supported by the fact that K did not merely deliver a pre-made item but designed and built a bespoke result — a custom wine cellar meeting a specific agreed outcome (the humidity range) — which is the hallmark of a works contract under Section 631 BGB, not a sale under Section 433 BGB. Against this, one could argue materials were also supplied, which sounds sale-like. However, where labor and a specific promised result dominate the transaction, works-contract law under Section 631 BGB and its warranty referral in Section 634 BGB applies. Consequently, this is a works contract. The decisive timing point is acceptance of the work under Section 640 BGB, already satisfied here, and the humidity-control failure means the work lacks the agreed quality under Section 633 BGB. Available remedies under Section 634 BGB are: cure (Section 634 No. 1, 635 BGB, with the contractor — not the customer — choosing the type of cure, unlike purchase law); self-help (Section 634 No. 2, 637 BGB, letting H fix it and bill K, a remedy purchase law does not have); revocation (Section 634 No. 3 with Section 323 BGB); reduction (Section 634 No. 3 with Section 638 BGB); and damages or reimbursement (Section 634 No. 4 with Sections 280 ff. or 284 BGB), following the same damages logic as this week’s purchase-law analysis. IV. Interim result: the works-contract warranty regime applies, and H has the full remedy menu under Section 634 BGB, including self-help, which purchase law does not offer. V. Final answer: As a result, H should pursue a claim under the works-contract warranty regime (Section 634 BGB), most naturally starting with a demand for cure under Sections 634 No. 1, 635 BGB (with K choosing the method), and escalating to self-help, reduction, revocation, or damages if cure fails.

Additional Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 9

Explain secondary-duty damages under Section 282 BGB, using the drunk-craftsman fact pattern to illustrate.

Model Answer: 1. Definition: Secondary-duty damages under Sections 280 I, III, 282 BGB compensate for damages instead of performance when a breach of a secondary duty (Section 241 II BGB) destroys the trust basis of the contract, making continued performance by that debtor unacceptable to the creditor. 2. Statutory anchor: Sections 280 I, III, 282 BGB, referencing Section 241 II BGB. 3. Requirements: (1) breach of a secondary duty, not the main performance duty; (2) the breach destroys the base of trust; (3) the breach is relevant to the purpose of the contract; (4) weighing of interests makes further performance by that debtor unacceptable. 4. Example: a craftsman properly installs a kitchen but works drunk, smokes, and damages the floor. The floor damage is damages in addition to performance under Sections 280 I, 241 II BGB, since it survives correct later performance; the cost of hiring a new craftsman to finish the job is damages instead of performance under Sections 280 I, III, 282 BGB, because the trust basis for continuing with this particular craftsman is destroyed. 5. Trap: Section 282 is not a catch-all for “the debtor behaved badly” — it specifically requires that the secondary-duty breach be serious enough to undermine confidence in that debtor’s ability to properly perform the main duty, not just any incidental misconduct.

Question 10

Explain when the additional-period (Nachfrist) requirement under Section 281 BGB is dispensable.

Model Answer: 1. Definition: Section 281 damages instead of performance ordinarily require a reasonable additional period for cure that expires without result; certain circumstances dispense with this requirement. 2. Statutory anchor: Section 281 II BGB (general dispensability); Section 440 BGB (purchase-law-specific dispensability). 3. Requirements/features: (1) under Section 281 II, dispensable if the debtor seriously and definitively refuses performance, or special circumstances justify immediate damages after weighing both parties’ interests; (2) under Section 440 BGB, also dispensable if both cure types fail, are refused, or are unreasonable for the buyer, mirroring revocation-dispensability logic; (3) objective impossibility of the needed cure routes around Section 281 entirely via Sections 275/283. 4. Example: a seller who states “I will never repair or replace this item” makes a serious and definitive refusal that dispenses with the Nachfrist requirement under Section 281 II. 5. Trap: the buyer’s own refusal to allow cure does not dispense with the additional-period requirement — only the debtor’s own serious refusal or an objective impossibility qualifies (see Question 7 above, where the buyer’s own refusal to let the seller cure did not count).

Question 11

Compare Section 283 BGB and Section 311a BGB damages instead of performance.

Model Answer (Compare Schema):

Section 283 damages instead of performance apply when performance becomes impossible after the contract was validly concluded, anchored in Sections 280 I, III, 283 BGB together with Section 275 BGB, and require no additional period since demanding one for genuinely impossible performance would be pointless. Section 311a damages instead of performance apply when performance was already impossible at the moment of contract conclusion, anchored in Section 311a II BGB, and additionally require that the debtor knew or should have known of the initial impossibility. Contrast example: a seller promises to deliver a specific vintage machine that is destroyed by fire the week after the contract is signed — Section 283 applies; if the same machine had already been destroyed the day before the contract was signed and neither party knew, Section 311a governs instead, and additionally asks whether the seller should have known the machine no longer existed. Exam trap: do not default to Section 283 for every “impossible” fact pattern — always fix the exact moment impossibility arose relative to contract conclusion before choosing between Sections 283 and 311a.

Question 12

Distinguish “damage” from a “futile expense,” and state the difference hypothesis.

Model Answer: 1. Definition: damage under Sections 249 ff. BGB is an involuntary loss of material or immaterial goods/interests; a futile expense under Section 284 BGB is voluntary spending made in reliance on receiving proper performance. 2. Statutory anchor: Sections 249 ff. BGB (damage); Section 284 BGB (futile expenses). 3. Requirements/features: (1) difference hypothesis formula: damage = hypothetical situation without the damaging event minus the actual situation; (2) damage categories are material (Sections 249 ff.), immaterial (Section 253, only if a statute allows compensation), and lost profit (Section 252); (3) a futile expense is not “damage” in this sense because it was spent voluntarily rather than lost involuntarily, so it needs its own gateway (Section 284) rather than Sections 249 ff. 4. Example: a buyer’s engine destroyed by defective fuel is damage (involuntary loss, difference hypothesis applies); a buyer’s voluntary vehicle-registration fee paid in reliance on receiving a conforming car is a futile expense (Section 284), not damage. 5. Trap: Section 284 and damages instead of performance are either/or for the same expense — a claimant cannot recover a given outlay as both damages instead of performance and as a Section 284 futile expense.

Additional Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 13 (Case)

Facts: Print shop P buys a used industrial printer from dealer D for EUR 20,000. The printer’s color calibration sensor is defective at handover; a properly calibrated equivalent machine is worth EUR 20,000, while the actual machine with the defect is worth EUR 16,000. P keeps using the printer for black-and-white jobs and writes to D demanding EUR 4,000 “in compensation because you are responsible for selling me a defective machine.” D responds that the sensor defect was caused by a manufacturing fault that neither D nor any reasonable dealer performing a standard pre-sale check could have detected.

Question: Can P recover the EUR 4,000 as small damages, and what does D’s response change?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: P could have a claim against D for EUR 4,000 in small damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, if D’s responsibility for the defect is established and not rebutted. II. Requirements: (I) valid purchase contract; (II) defect at transfer of risk; (III) P’s demand properly classified as damages, not reduction; (IV) D’s responsibility under Section 280 I 2 BGB, presumed but rebuttable; (V) value-deficit amount. III. Application: the printer sale is a valid purchase contract (Section 433 BGB), and the sensor defect deviates from the agreed/objective quality under Section 434 II BGB, present at handover under Section 446 BGB. P’s letter explicitly frames the demand as “compensation because you are responsible,” so, as with the fault-based wording seen elsewhere in this set, this is small damages, not reduction. Questionable is whether D can rebut the presumed responsibility under Section 280 I 2 BGB. This is supported by D’s factual claim that neither D nor any reasonable dealer performing a standard pre-sale check could have detected the manufacturing-origin defect — this speaks to an absence of negligence under Section 276 BGB. Against this, one could argue dealers bear a general risk for what they sell. However, Section 280 I 2 BGB only presumes responsibility and allows the debtor to disprove intent and negligence, and an undetectable manufacturing defect is exactly the kind of fact that rebuts negligence. Consequently, if D’s factual claim is proven, D is not responsible under Section 280 I 2 BGB. IV. Interim result: the defect and its classification as small damages are established, but D’s responsibility — the decisive requirement — is successfully rebutted on the facts given. V. Final answer: As a result, P cannot recover the EUR 4,000 as small damages because D has rebutted the presumption of responsibility; P would instead need to fall back on reduction under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB, which reaches the same EUR 4,000 figure via the proportional formula without requiring D’s fault.

Question 14 (Case — integrates Week 09 + Week 08)

Facts: Bakery B buys a commercial oven from supplier S for EUR 25,000. The oven’s door seal is defective at handover, causing heat loss; a defect-free equivalent oven is worth EUR 25,000, the actual oven with the defect is worth EUR 23,000, replacing the entire oven would cost S EUR 25,000, and repairing just the seal would cost S EUR 300. B demands S replace the entire oven. S refuses, offering only to repair the seal; B refuses that offer, sets S no further deadline, and claims EUR 2,000 as small damages.

Question: Was S entitled to refuse B’s chosen cure type, and does that affect B’s damages claim?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: whether B can claim EUR 2,000 in small damages depends first on whether S validly refused B’s chosen cure type (replacement) under Section 439 IV BGB, and second on whether B’s own refusal of the remaining valid cure option (repair) forecloses the damages claim. II. Requirements: (I) valid purchase contract; (II) defect at transfer of risk; (III) Section 439 IV disproportionality test for the refused cure type; (IV) effect of B’s refusal of the remaining cure type on the Section 281 additional-period/dispensability requirement. III. Application: the oven purchase and seal defect at handover are established (Sections 433, 434, 446 BGB). Questionable is whether S could refuse replacement under Section 439 IV BGB. This is supported by the stark cost gap: replacement costs S EUR 25,000 against a EUR 300 repair that fully resolves the defect — precisely the gross disproportion Section 439 IV lets the seller avoid, weighing defect-free value, defect significance, and whether the other cure type works without substantial disadvantage to B. Against this, one could argue B has an unqualified right to choose between the two cure types under Section 439 I BGB. However, Section 439 IV specifically limits that choice where one type is disproportionately expensive and the other remains fully effective and reasonable for the buyer — here repair fully eliminates the heat-loss defect. Consequently, S validly refused only the replacement type, not cure as such, and B remained restricted to repair. Because B then refused the very cure type S was entitled to insist on, and set no further deadline, the Section 281 additional-period requirement is not satisfied; B’s own refusal is not a dispensing “serious and definitive refusal” by the debtor S under Section 281 II, since S never refused cure altogether, only the disproportionate type. IV. Interim result: S validly limited B to the repair option under Section 439 IV BGB; B’s refusal of that valid cure option, without setting a further deadline, means the Section 281 additional-period requirement remains unmet. V. Final answer: As a result, S was entitled to refuse replacement but not repair, and B cannot currently claim the EUR 2,000 as small damages because B refused the cure option S was entitled to offer instead of setting S a deadline for it; B would first need to give S a reasonable opportunity to repair the seal.

Question 15 (Case — integrates Week 09 + Week 11)

Facts: Wholesaler W (a merchant) sells 500 packaged industrial gaskets to manufacturer M (also a merchant) for EUR 10,000, a mutual commercial purchase. An employee of M signs for the delivery, but the shipment sits unopened in M’s warehouse for three weeks due to a production slowdown. When finally opened, 200 gaskets are the wrong diameter — a defect that would have been visible on a routine visual count-and-sample check. M immediately notifies W and claims EUR 4,000 in small damages for the value deficit of the wrong-diameter gaskets.

Question: Can M successfully pursue the EUR 4,000 small-damages claim against W?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: M’s EUR 4,000 small-damages claim under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB is only viable if M first cleared the Section 377 HGB inspection-and-notice gateway that precedes any Section 437 BGB warranty claim in a mutual commercial purchase. II. Requirements: (I) mutual commercial purchase between merchants (Section 343 HGB); (II) prompt inspection and notice of defects under Section 377 HGB; (III) if that gateway is cleared, the ordinary Section 437/280 ff. small-damages requirements. III. Application: W and M are both merchants and the gasket sale is a mutual commercial purchase under Section 343 HGB, so Section 377 HGB applies before Section 437 BGB is reached. Questionable is whether M’s three-week delay in opening the shipment satisfies the “promptly” requirement of Section 377 HGB. This is supported by the fact that the wrong diameter was discoverable on a routine visual count-and-sample check — exactly the ordinary-course inspection Section 377 HGB expects a merchant buyer to perform without delay. Against this, one could argue M’s production slowdown is a legitimate business reason for the delay. However, Section 377 HGB ties the inspection duty to the ordinary course of business, not the buyer’s own scheduling convenience, and the employee’s receipt of the goods is attributed to M under Section 278 BGB regardless of who within M’s organization caused the delay. Consequently, a three-week delay in opening and inspecting a routinely checkable delivery is not prompt, and the gaskets are deemed approved under Section 377 HGB. IV. Interim result: M failed to satisfy the Section 377 HGB inspection-and-notice duty, so the goods are deemed approved. V. Final answer: As a result, M cannot pursue the EUR 4,000 small-damages claim, or any Section 437 BGB warranty remedy, against W, because the goods are deemed approved under Section 377 HGB for M’s failure to inspect and notify promptly — this bars the claim regardless of how genuine the diameter defect actually was.

Question 16 (Case)

Facts: Gallery G contracts to sell art dealer A a specific antique sculpture for EUR 50,000, to be delivered next month after G completes a scheduled restoration. Before delivery, the restoration workshop suffers a fire and the unique sculpture is destroyed. G had no direct involvement in the fire, but the workshop’s faulty wiring — which G had been warned about twice by the workshop’s own inspector and failed to have fixed — caused the blaze. A demands EUR 50,000 as damages instead of performance without ever setting G a deadline for delivery.

Question: Does A need to set a deadline, and is G responsible for the destruction?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: A’s claim is for damages instead of performance due to subsequent impossibility under Sections 280 I, III, 283 BGB, which does not require a deadline but does require G’s responsibility for the impossibility. II. Requirements: (I) valid contract for the specific sculpture; (II) performance became impossible after conclusion (Section 275 I BGB); (III) no additional period needed for the Section 283 route; (IV) responsibility for the impossibility (Section 276 BGB, presumed under Section 280 I 2 but rebuttable). III. Application: G and A concluded a valid contract for a specific, non-fungible sculpture. Performance became genuinely impossible under Section 275 I BGB once the unique sculpture was destroyed by fire before delivery. Questionable is whether A must first set G a deadline. This is supported by the general rule that Section 283, unlike Section 281, applies to subsequently impossible performance precisely because a deadline would be pointless — no amount of additional time restores a destroyed unique object. Consequently, no deadline is required. Questionable is whether G is responsible for the fire. This is supported by the fact that G was twice warned about the faulty wiring by the workshop’s own inspector and failed to have it fixed — a clear failure to exercise the care of a reasonable party under Section 276 BGB. Against this, one could argue G did not personally start the fire and did not control the workshop’s premises. However, the standard is not who lit the match but whether G’s own failure to act on a known, specific risk contributed negligently to the loss, and ignoring two direct warnings about faulty wiring is exactly that kind of negligent omission. Consequently, G is responsible for the impossibility. IV. Interim result: performance is subsequently impossible, no deadline is required under Section 283, and G’s responsibility is established through negligent disregard of known warnings. V. Final answer: As a result, A does not need to set G a deadline and can claim the EUR 50,000 as damages instead of performance under Sections 280 I, III, 283 BGB, because G is responsible for the impossibility.

Question 17 (Case)

Facts: Restaurant owner R buys a custom-built pizza oven from manufacturer P for EUR 18,000, to be installed by a specific date so R can open a new location. In reliance on timely delivery, R pays EUR 1,500 to a contractor to build a reinforced platform for the oven and pays EUR 500 for a permit specific to that oven model. P never delivers; after a reasonable additional period passes without result, R cancels and buys a comparable oven elsewhere. The platform remains usable for the substitute oven, but the EUR 500 permit was specific to P’s oven model and is now worthless.

Question: Can R recover the EUR 500 permit fee, and what about the EUR 1,500 platform cost?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: R may recover the EUR 500 permit fee as reimbursement of a futile expense under Section 284 BGB, while the EUR 1,500 platform cost is not futile and falls outside Section 284’s reach. II. Requirements: (I) the requirements for damages instead of performance are otherwise met; (II) the expense was made in R’s own interest and in reliance on proper performance; (III) the expense was reasonable; (IV) the expense would have been recouped through proper performance. III. Application: the requirements for damages instead of performance are met in the background — P failed to deliver by the deadline, a reasonable additional period expired without result, and P’s non-delivery is presumptively its responsibility under Section 280 I 2 BGB, not rebutted on the facts. Questionable is whether the EUR 500 permit fee qualifies as a futile expense under Section 284 BGB. This is supported by the fact that R paid it in reliance on receiving P’s specific oven, it was a reasonable step given the planned installation, and it would have been recouped had P delivered as promised — but because the permit is specific to P’s oven model, it is now worthless following P’s non-performance, satisfying the futility element. Questionable is whether the EUR 1,500 platform cost is also futile. This is supported by the fact that it, too, was spent in reliance on the contract. Against this, one could argue both expenses should be treated identically since both preceded the same broken promise. However, Section 284 requires that the expense have failed to achieve its purpose — the platform remains usable for the substitute oven R ultimately bought, so its purpose was still achieved. Consequently, only the permit fee lost its value because of the non-performance. IV. Interim result: the EUR 500 permit fee satisfies all Section 284 requirements and is a futile expense; the EUR 1,500 platform cost served its purpose regardless of P’s breach and is not futile. V. Final answer: As a result, R can recover the EUR 500 permit fee from P under Section 284 BGB as reimbursement of a futile expense, but cannot recover the EUR 1,500 platform cost, since that expense was not rendered futile by P’s non-performance.

Question 18 (Case — integrates Week 09 + Week 08)

Facts: Furniture retailer F sells a designer sofa to buyer C for EUR 6,000. The sofa’s fabric has a dye-batch defect visible on close inspection; a defect-free sofa of the same design is worth EUR 6,000, the actual sofa is worth EUR 4,800. Without first asking F for repair or a replacement sofa, C writes: “I’m keeping the sofa but I am reducing what I owe you — please refund the difference; I’m not blaming you for it, these things happen with dye batches.” F had already delivered and been paid in full.

Question: Is C’s demand governed by reduction or small damages, and does C need to have given F a chance to cure first?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: C’s demand, as framed, is reduction under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB, not small damages under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, and the two routes differ on whether a prior cure opportunity is required. II. Requirements: (I) valid purchase contract; (II) defect at transfer of risk; (III) proper classification of C’s demand; (IV) for reduction, a right to revoke as the gateway condition, itself requiring the ordinary cure-first sequence unless dispensable; (V) reduction formula. III. Application: the sofa purchase and dye-batch defect at handover are established (Sections 433, 434 II, 446 BGB). Questionable is whether C’s letter is reduction or small damages. This is supported by C’s own wording — C explicitly disclaims blame (“I’m not blaming you… these things happen”), the opposite framing from a fault-based compensation demand, and asks only for a price adjustment to the lower value. Against this, one could argue the economic outcome (keep sofa, get EUR 1,200) looks identical to small damages. However, as with the small-damages-versus-reduction test used elsewhere in this set, the legal route turns on whether the buyer is asserting fault-based compensation or a no-fault price adjustment, and C’s language signals the latter. Consequently, this is reduction, not small damages. Questionable is whether C needed to give F a chance to cure first. This is supported by the rule, carried over from Warranty Rights I, that reduction requires a right to revoke as its gateway (Sections 437 No. 2, 441 I BGB reference the same preconditions as revocation), which ordinarily requires cure to have first failed, been refused, or been dispensable — C never asked F for repair or replacement and points to no dispensing circumstance. However, unlike a damages claim, reduction does not additionally require fault, so once the cure-first gateway is satisfied reduction follows automatically from the value gap. Consequently, C’s demand is correctly classified as reduction, but the cure-first gateway it depends on is not yet shown to be satisfied. IV. Interim result: the demand is reduction, not small damages, but the cure-first gateway underlying the right to reduce has not yet been shown to be satisfied or dispensable. V. Final answer: As a result, C’s demand should be routed as reduction under Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB, using the formula reduced price = agreed price × actual value / defect-free value = EUR 6,000 × EUR 4,800 / EUR 6,000 = EUR 4,800, yielding a refund of EUR 1,200 — but only once C is shown to have first given F a genuine opportunity to cure (or such an opportunity is dispensable), since reduction’s gateway requires the same cure-first sequence as revocation even though reduction itself needs no fault.

Further Short-Answer / Theory Questions

Question 19

Explain how a seller’s guarantee under Section 443 BGB changes the responsibility analysis for damages claims under Section 280 I BGB.

Model Answer: 1. Definition: A guarantee (Garantie) under Section 443 BGB is a voluntary additional promise by the seller (or manufacturer) that the item has certain qualities or will retain them, layered on top of statutory warranty rights; once a genuine guarantee is given, the responsibility standard under Section 276 I BGB can be stricter than ordinary intent/negligence, so the guarantor answers for the guaranteed outcome without needing separate proof of fault. 2. Statutory anchor: Section 443 BGB (guarantee); Section 276 I BGB (permits an assumed, stricter standard of responsibility); Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I BGB (the damages claim itself). 3. Requirements/features: (1) a genuine guarantee must first be identified — express guarantees are straightforward, but a tacit (implied) guarantee is possible only where the seller’s conduct or statements clearly go beyond ordinary sales talk, and course materials flag this threshold as high; (2) once a guarantee is established, the responsibility element of Section 280 I BGB is satisfied by the guaranteed quality simply being absent — the seller cannot rebut responsibility by showing an absence of fault, unlike the ordinary Section 280 I 2 presumption; (3) Section 444 BGB reinforces this by blocking any warranty-exclusion clause where a guarantee was given. 4. Example: a seller who advertises a used generator as “guaranteed to run for 500 hours without failure” cannot escape a damages claim by proving they neither knew nor should have known about a hidden manufacturing flaw that caused failure after 100 hours — the guarantee itself, not fault, is the basis of liability. 5. Trap: do not treat every confident sales statement as a guarantee — casual assurances or ordinary advertising puffery do not meet the high threshold for a tacit guarantee, and without a genuine guarantee the seller keeps the ordinary chance to rebut the Section 280 I 2 responsibility presumption.

Further Case / Legal-Opinion Questions

Question 20 (Case)

Facts: Antique dealer A agrees to sell collector C a specific 18th-century clock that A describes from a photograph sent by a consignor. A and C sign the sale contract on 3 March. Unknown to both parties, the clock had already been destroyed in a warehouse fire on 1 March, two days before the contract was signed. C demands damages instead of performance. A protests that C never set a deadline for delivery.

Question: Does C need to have set A a deadline, and can C recover damages given that neither party knew about the fire at the time of contracting?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: C’s claim is for damages instead of performance due to initial impossibility under Section 311a II BGB, which does not require a deadline but does require that A knew or should have known of the impossibility at the time of contracting. II. Requirements: (I) a contract was concluded for a specific, non-fungible item; (II) performance was already impossible at the moment of conclusion (Section 275 I BGB, tested as of contract conclusion rather than afterward); (III) no additional period is needed for the Section 311a route; (IV) A knew or, applying reasonable care, should have known that the clock no longer existed. III. Application: A and C concluded a valid contract on 3 March for a specific clock. Questionable is whether Section 283 or Section 311a governs, since both deal with impossibility. This is supported by the fact that the clock was destroyed on 1 March, before the 3 March contract — fixing the moment of impossibility before conclusion routes the case to Section 311a, not Section 283, which only covers impossibility arising after conclusion. Consequently, no deadline is required under either route, since demanding one for a destroyed unique object would be pointless. Questionable is whether A knew or should have known of the fire. This is supported by the fact that A relied solely on a photograph sent by the consignor and never independently verified the clock’s continued existence immediately before signing. Against this, one could argue A had no realistic way to learn of a fire that happened only two days earlier in someone else’s warehouse. However, Section 311a II BGB specifically asks whether A, applying the care reasonably expected of an antique dealer transacting on a stranger’s unverified photograph, should have confirmed the item’s continued existence before contracting — the facts as given do not show A made any such basic check. Consequently, A’s failure to verify supports a finding that A should have known. IV. Interim result: the contract-conclusion-versus-impossibility timing places this under Section 311a, dispensing with any deadline requirement; A’s failure to verify the clock’s existence before contracting supports a finding that A should have known of the impossibility. V. Final answer: As a result, C does not need to have set A a deadline, and C can claim damages instead of performance under Section 311a II BGB, because the impossibility already existed at contract conclusion and A should have known of it through a basic pre-contract check.

Question 21 (Case)

Facts: Furniture maker M sells and installs a custom wardrobe for buyer K. M subcontracts the installation to an independent carpentry crew, C-Crew, whom M regularly uses for deliveries. During installation, a C-Crew worker carelessly drills through a live electrical cable in K’s wall, causing a short circuit that damages K’s home entertainment system worth EUR 2,000. M argues M personally did nothing wrong and cannot be held responsible for C-Crew’s carelessness.

Question: Is M responsible for the EUR 2,000 damage despite not personally causing it?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: K could have a claim against M for EUR 2,000 in damages under Sections 280 I, 241 II BGB for breach of a care duty during performance of the installation, with C-Crew’s negligence attributed to M under Section 278 BGB, if the requirements are met. II. Requirements: (I) a valid contract obliging M to install the wardrobe, generating an ancillary duty of care toward K’s other property (Section 241 II BGB); (II) breach of that duty; (III) responsibility, including attribution of a performance-assistant’s fault under Section 278 BGB; (IV) causal damage that would survive even correct later performance of the wardrobe installation itself. III. Application: M and K concluded a contract under which M owed proper installation of the wardrobe, carrying an ancillary duty under Section 241 II BGB not to damage K’s other property while doing so. Questionable is whether M is responsible for C-Crew’s carelessness given that M personally did nothing wrong. This is supported by Section 278 BGB, which attributes the fault of a person the debtor uses to perform their obligation to the debtor as if it were the debtor’s own fault — M chose to use C-Crew to carry out the installation M owed to K, so C-Crew acted within the scope of M’s own obligation. Against this, one could argue M exercised no direct control over how C-Crew’s individual worker handled the drill, so fault should stay with C-Crew alone. However, Section 278 BGB does not require the debtor’s own control over the helper’s methods — it is enough that the helper was used to perform the debtor’s obligation, and installation was squarely within that scope. Consequently, C-Crew’s careless drilling is attributed to M as if M had drilled through the cable personally. The cable damage to the entertainment system would remain even if the wardrobe were later installed correctly, since the harm is to separate property rather than the wardrobe itself. IV. Interim result: C-Crew’s negligence is attributed to M under Section 278 BGB, and the entertainment-system damage survives correct later performance of the installation. V. Final answer: As a result, M is responsible for the EUR 2,000 damage despite not personally causing it, because Section 278 BGB attributes C-Crew’s carelessness to M, and K can claim the EUR 2,000 under Sections 280 I, 241 II BGB.

Question 22 (Case)

Facts: Furniture retailer F sells buyer D a dining table for EUR 3,000. On delivery, D notices a single small scratch, about 2cm long, on the underside of the table, invisible unless the table is tipped over — cosmetically and functionally irrelevant to ordinary use. D immediately refuses the table entirely, buys an equivalent table elsewhere for EUR 3,200, and demands the EUR 200 price difference as big damages instead of performance, without ever asking F to touch up the scratch.

Question: Can D recover the EUR 200 as big damages instead of performance for the whole contract?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: D’s claim for EUR 200 as big damages instead of the entire performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB fails if the scratch is an insignificant defect excluded under Section 281 I 3 BGB. II. Requirements: (I) valid purchase contract; (II) a defect at transfer of risk; (III) the defect must not be insignificant, or Section 281 I 3 BGB bars damages instead of the entire performance; (IV) if not excluded, the ordinary Nachfrist and responsibility requirements. III. Application: F and D concluded a purchase contract for the table (Section 433 BGB), and the underside scratch is a deviation from the agreed/expected quality under Section 434 II BGB, present at handover. Questionable is whether D can claim big damages for the whole contract given the scratch’s minor character. This is supported by Section 281 I 3 BGB, which expressly excludes damages instead of the entire performance where the breach of duty is insignificant — a defect described as a small, cosmetically and functionally irrelevant mark on a surface never seen in ordinary use is exactly the kind of minor deviation this exclusion targets. Against this, one could argue any deviation from the agreed defect-free condition entitles the buyer to full big-damages treatment. However, Section 281 I 3 BGB specifically singles out insignificant defects to prevent buyers from using a trivial flaw to unwind an entire high-value contract, and the scratch here affects neither function nor visible appearance. Consequently, the defect is insignificant, and big damages for the whole contract are excluded regardless of whether D set a deadline. IV. Interim result: the scratch is an insignificant defect under Section 281 I 3 BGB, which bars big damages instead of the entire performance. V. Final answer: As a result, D cannot recover the EUR 200 as big damages instead of the entire performance; D would at most be limited to small damages for the value deficit caused specifically by the scratch (subject to F’s responsibility) or reduction, not a claim treating the whole delivery as rejected.

Question 23 (Case)

Facts: Boutique owner N buys a designer display cabinet from supplier V for EUR 9,000. The cabinet’s glass shelving arrives cracked, a defect V fails to cure after N sets a reasonable deadline. N writes to V: “I no longer want anything to do with this cabinet — please take it back and return my EUR 9,000.” N has not bought a replacement elsewhere and states no lost profit or extra cost.

Question: Is N’s demand big damages instead of performance or revocation, and what does the classification change?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: N’s demand, as framed, is revocation under Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 BGB, not big damages instead of performance under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB, and the two routes differ on whether V’s responsibility must be shown. II. Requirements: (I) valid purchase contract; (II) defect at transfer of risk; (III) proper classification of N’s demand as unwinding (revocation) or loss-compensation (big damages); (IV) for revocation, an expired Nachfrist and no exclusion; for big damages, the same procedural gateway plus V’s responsibility. III. Application: N and V concluded a purchase contract for the cabinet (Section 433 BGB), and the cracked shelving is a material defect under Section 434 II BGB present at handover; V failed to cure after a reasonable deadline set by N, satisfying the Nachfrist requirement common to both routes. Questionable is whether N’s letter should be read as revocation or as big damages. This is supported by N’s own wording — N asks only to return the cabinet and get the EUR 9,000 back, stating no additional loss such as a substitute-purchase price difference or lost profit; this is a pure request to unwind the exchange, not a demand for compensation of an extra loss. Against this, one could argue any request for “my money back” could be read loosely as a damages demand. However, big damages specifically compensates a non-fulfilment loss beyond the price itself (e.g. a pricier replacement), which N does not claim, while revocation simply reverses the exchange of performances — N’s letter matches the latter. Consequently, this is revocation, not big damages. IV. Interim result: N’s demand is properly classified as revocation; the Nachfrist requirement is already satisfied. V. Final answer: As a result, N can revoke the purchase contract under Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 BGB and recover the EUR 9,000 purchase price against return of the cabinet, without needing to show V’s responsibility for the defect — had N instead claimed an extra loss beyond the price (e.g. a pricier replacement), that portion would need to be routed as big damages under Sections 437 No. 3, 280 I, III, 281 BGB and would require V’s responsibility to be established or not rebutted.

Question 24 (Case — integrates Week 09 + Week 05)

Facts: Consumer P orders a wireless speaker online from retailer Q for EUR 300, a distance contract under Section 312c BGB. Q ships proper withdrawal instructions with the delivery. Twenty days after receiving the speaker, P discovers a manufacturing defect that causes intermittent audio cutouts — a material defect under Section 434 BGB present at handover. P wants to return the speaker and get a full refund with the least hassle.

Question: Is P’s 14-day consumer withdrawal right still available, and if not, what route remains open, and by when must P act?

Model Answer: I. Claim/issue sentence: P’s route to return the speaker and recover the EUR 300 could run through either consumer withdrawal under Sections 312c, 312g, 355 BGB or the warranty gateway under Section 437 BGB, but only one of the two remains available on these facts. II. Requirements: (I) for withdrawal: distance-contract status, no exclusion under Section 312g II BGB, and the 14-day period (Sections 355 II, 356 II No. 1 BGB) not yet expired; (II) for warranty: valid purchase contract, defect at transfer of risk, no exclusion, and the applicable warranty limitation period (Section 438 I No. 3 BGB, two years) not yet expired. III. Application: P ordered the speaker from Q, a distance contract under Section 312c BGB. Questionable is whether P can still withdraw. This is supported by the general 14-day withdrawal window under Section 355 II BGB. Against this, the facts state that Q shipped proper withdrawal instructions with the delivery, so the clock started running on receipt of the goods under Section 356 II No. 1 BGB and was not extended under Section 356 III BGB, which only extends the period where instructions were missing or wrong. Since P discovered the defect twenty days after receipt — six days past the 14-day mark — the withdrawal right has already lapsed, and nothing in the facts suggests P withdrew earlier. Consequently, the withdrawal route is closed. Questionable is whether the warranty route remains open. This is supported by the fact that the speaker’s intermittent audio cutouts are a material defect under Section 434 BGB present at handover (Section 446 BGB), triggering the Section 437 gateway, and the applicable limitation period for warranty claims on movable goods is two years from delivery under Section 438 I No. 3 BGB — twenty days is far inside that window. Against this, one could argue the online-distance facts should default P to withdrawal since that is a “no questions asked” route. However, where the facts emphasize a defect/performance failure, the performance route leads and withdrawal is only a fallback where its own window is still open — here withdrawal’s own 14-day window is independently expired regardless of the defect. Consequently, P must pursue the warranty route. IV. Interim result: the withdrawal right expired six days before P acted and cannot be revived by the later-discovered defect; the warranty route remains available for nearly two more years. V. Final answer: As a result, P’s 14-day withdrawal right is no longer available, but P can still pursue the warranty route under Section 437 BGB — ordinarily starting with a demand for cure under Section 439 BGB, and escalating to revocation (Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 BGB) or reduction (Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB) if cure fails or is dispensable — with up to two years from delivery under Section 438 I No. 3 BGB to act.

Quick Answer Route Summary

Question # Primary Route/Section One-line takeaway
1 Section 284 BGB Futile-expense reimbursement is either/or with damages instead of performance.
2 Sections 280 I vs. 281/283/311a BGB Hypothetical-performance test decides in addition vs. instead.
3 Sections 280 I, III, 281 BGB Small vs. big damages both need seller responsibility; the difference is keep-item vs. give-up-item.
4 Sections 280 I; 280 I, III, 281 BGB One defective delivery can split into a damages-in-addition claim and a not-yet-ripe damages-instead claim.
5 Sections 280 I, III, 281 vs. 441 BGB Fault-based wording (“I hold you responsible”) signals small damages, not reduction.
6 Section 437 gateway vs. Section 119 II BGB Buyer cannot use seller’s own mistake defensively; defect goes through warranty law, with revocation via impossible-cure dispensability.
7 Section 281 BGB Buyer’s own refusal to allow cure does not create a 281 II dispensability exception.
8 Section 634 BGB Works contracts run a parallel remedy system, including self-help, absent from purchase warranty law.
9 Section 282 BGB Secondary-duty breach destroying trust splits into in-addition (direct damage) and instead-of (replacement cost) claims.
10 Sections 281 II, 440 BGB Only the seller’s own serious refusal or objective impossibility dispenses the Nachfrist, not the buyer’s impatience.
11 Sections 283 vs. 311a BGB Fix the moment impossibility arose relative to contract conclusion before choosing the route.
12 Sections 249 ff. vs. 284 BGB Involuntary loss = damage (difference hypothesis); voluntary reliance spending = futile expense.
13 Section 280 I 2 BGB An undetectable manufacturing defect can rebut the responsibility presumption, defeating small damages but not reduction.
14 Section 439 IV BGB Seller may refuse only the disproportionate cure type; buyer’s refusal of the remaining valid cure type blocks damages.
15 Section 377 HGB Merchant buyer’s own inspection delay bars the small-damages claim before Section 437 BGB is even reached.
16 Sections 280 I, III, 283 BGB No deadline needed for subsequent impossibility; ignoring known wiring warnings establishes responsibility.
17 Section 284 BGB Only the expense whose purpose failed (permit) is futile; an expense still useful for a substitute (platform) is not.
18 Sections 437 No. 2, 441 BGB Fault-disclaiming language signals reduction, but reduction still needs the same cure-first gateway as revocation.
19 Section 443 BGB guarantee A genuine guarantee replaces the fault check — the seller cannot rebut responsibility once a guaranteed quality is missing.
20 Section 311a II BGB Impossibility before contract conclusion routes here, not Section 283; no deadline needed, but seller’s should-have-known matters.
21 Sections 280 I, 241 II, 278 BGB A subcontractor’s carelessness during performance is attributed to the debtor who used them.
22 Section 281 I 3 BGB An insignificant defect blocks big damages for the whole contract, no matter how firmly the buyer rejects it.
23 Sections 437 No. 2, 323, 346 vs. 280 I, III, 281 BGB “Take it back, refund me” with no extra loss claimed is revocation, not big damages.
24 Sections 355/356 vs. 437/438 I No. 3 BGB Proper instructions mean the 14-day withdrawal clock runs and can expire before a later-discovered defect is found — the 2-year warranty window survives it.

[W10.1] Week 10: Transfer Of Property

Source: business-law/wiki/week-10-transfer-of-property/week-10-transfer-of-property.md

Source: business-law/raw/moodle-export-business-law-950848572-s26-20260628/22.06. - Transfer of Property - Haag/Transfer or Property.pdf Course: Business Law Processed: 2026-06-28 Wiki note: business-law/wiki/week-10-transfer-of-property/week-10-transfer-of-property.md

Course direction checked against business-law/wiki/_course-logistics.md: Transfer of Property is Session 10 in the teaching outline and follows Warranty Rights II.

External statute check: statutory anchors were cross-checked against the official Gesetze-im-Internet BGB source on 2026-06-28. The official English BGB translation warns that translations may lag the current German text; use current German statutory text for exact wording.

80/20 Exam Summary

Transfer of Property explains that a purchase contract and ownership transfer are legally separate.

  • Ownership and possession are different. A thief can possess a thing without owning it.
  • Ownership is the strongest right over a thing; possession is actual control.
  • German private law uses the principle of separation: obligation contract and disposition contract are distinct legal transactions.
  • German private law also uses the principle of abstraction: invalidity of the purchase contract does not automatically invalidate the property transfer, and vice versa.
  • Transfer of movable ownership usually requires agreement, delivery, agreement at delivery, and authorization under Section 929 sentence 1 BGB.
  • Delivery is a real act, not a declaration-of-intent contract; agency rules do not apply in the same way.
  • Delivery can be replaced by constructive delivery under Section 930 BGB or assignment of the claim for possession under Section 931 BGB.
  • A non-owner can sometimes transfer ownership if the acquirer obtains ownership in good faith under Sections 929, 932 BGB.
  • No good-faith acquisition is possible for lost or stolen things under Section 935 BGB, with special handling for money.
  • Immovables require conveyance and land-register entry under Sections 873, 925 BGB.
  • Claims are transferred by assignment under Section 398 BGB, not by delivery.

Where This Fits

Warranty law asks whether the seller fulfilled the purchase contract properly. Transfer-of-property law asks who owns the thing.

Purchase agreement = obligation to transfer ownership and pay.
Transfer of ownership = separate disposition transaction.

This matters because a valid purchase contract alone does not make the buyer owner.

Clarification Router: Use Cases And Conclusions

Use transfer of property as a router. The first question is not “was there a sale?” but “what kind of right or object is moving?”

1. What is transferred?
   movable thing / land / claim?

2. Is this only the obligation contract, or also the disposition transaction?
   The purchase contract creates duties; it does not itself transfer ownership.

3. If movable:
   test Section 929 BGB:
   agreement
   + delivery or delivery replacement
   + agreement still exists at delivery
   + transferor is owner or authorized

4. If authorization is missing:
   test good-faith acquisition under Sections 932, 935 BGB.

5. Conclude:
   ownership passed / ownership did not pass / acquirer obtained ownership in good faith.

Case 1: Normal Sale Of A Movable

Facts:

S owns a laptop. S sells it to B and hands it over.

Check:

Object: movable thing.
Transfer agreement: S and B agree ownership should pass.
Delivery: S hands the laptop to B.
Agreement at delivery: yes.
Authorization: S is owner.

Conclusion:

B becomes owner under Section 929 sentence 1 BGB.

Do not write “B owns because B bought it.” Write that the Section 929 requirements are met.

Case 2: Purchase Contract But No Delivery Yet

Facts:

S owns a bike. S and B sign a purchase contract today. Delivery is planned for Friday.

Check:

Purchase contract: yes.
Delivery: no.
Property transfer: not complete.

Conclusion:

B is not owner yet. B only has a claim against S to deliver and transfer ownership.

This is the cleanest separation-principle case: contract answers “who must do what?”, property law answers “who owns what?”

Case 3: Buyer Already Possesses The Thing

Facts:

S owns a camera. B borrowed it last week. Today S sells the camera to B and says, "It is yours now."

Check:

Object: movable thing.
Transfer agreement: yes.
Physical delivery: unnecessary because B already possesses the camera.
Special route: Section 929 sentence 2 BGB.
Authorization: S is owner.

Conclusion:

B becomes owner under Section 929 sentence 2 BGB.

Case 4: Chattel Mortgage / Security Transfer

Facts:

S owns a production machine.
L lends S money.
S transfers ownership of the machine to L as collateral.
S keeps using the machine in the factory.

Check:

Object: movable thing.
Transfer agreement: S and L agree ownership should pass to L.
Physical delivery: no.
Delivery replacement: constructive delivery under Section 930 BGB.
Possession relationship: S keeps direct possession for L under the security arrangement.
Authorization: S is owner.

Conclusion:

L becomes owner, even though S still physically possesses the machine.

Mental model:

S has possession.
L has ownership.

This split creates the good-faith purchase risk.

Case 5: Good-Faith Purchase From A Non-Owner

Facts:

After the chattel mortgage, S sells the same machine to B.
B has no reason to know that L owns it.
S hands the machine to B.

Check Section 929 first:

Transfer agreement: S and B agree ownership should pass.
Delivery: S hands the machine to B.
Agreement at delivery: yes.
Authorization: no, because L is owner and L did not consent.

Then check good-faith acquisition:

Good faith: B did not know and was not grossly negligently unaware.
Legal appearance: S possessed the machine.
Section 935 block: no, because L voluntarily let S keep possession.
Distinct-party transaction: yes, S and B.

Conclusion:

B acquires ownership in good faith under Sections 929, 932 BGB.
L loses ownership.

The result does not depend on L consenting to the sale. Good-faith acquisition is a statutory exception. If L voluntarily created the risk by leaving possession with S, the law can protect B’s reliance on S’s possession.

Case 6: Stolen Thing

Facts:

T steals O's watch and sells it to B.
B honestly believes T is owner.

Check:

Transfer agreement and delivery: yes.
Authorization: no, T is not owner.
Good faith: maybe yes.
Legal appearance: T possesses the watch.
Section 935 block: yes, O lost possession involuntarily.

Conclusion:

B does not become owner. O remains owner.

Section 935 BGB is the owner-protection limit to good-faith acquisition.

Case 7: Land

Facts:

S sells land to B.

Do not use Section 929 BGB. Land follows the immovable route:

Purchase contract: notarial form, Section 311b BGB.
Ownership transfer: conveyance plus land-register entry, Sections 873 and 925 BGB.

Conclusion:

B becomes owner only after the real-property transfer requirements are met, especially land-register entry.

Case 8: Claim

Facts:

A is owed EUR 5,000 by D. A transfers this claim to C.

Claims are not physical things, so there is no delivery under Section 929 BGB.

Check:

Object: claim/right.
Transfer route: assignment under Section 398 BGB.
Agreement: assignor A and assignee C agree to transfer the claim.
Debtor participation: D does not need to consent in the basic assignment case.

Conclusion:

C becomes the new creditor of D.

Ownership Versus Possession

Concept Meaning Example Exam use
Ownership Legal right to control/exclude others regarding a thing. Owner of a bike. Ask who has the right.
Possession Actual power over a thing plus will to possess. Thief holding the bike. Ask who physically controls it.

Memory hook:

ownership = legal right
possession = actual control

Ownership:

  • protected by Article 14 German Basic Law;
  • strongest right over a thing;
  • includes utilization and exclusion functions;
  • can be acquired by transfer or statutory acquisition.

Possession:

  • governed by Sections 854 et seq. BGB;
  • acquired by actual power;
  • legal right to possession is not required for possession itself;
  • can be direct, indirect, or fictive possession;
  • creates presumptions, especially Section 1006 BGB.

Principle Of Separation

Execution of a purchase agreement involves at least three transactions:

1. Purchase agreement under Section 433 BGB.
2. Disposition contract transferring ownership of the good.
3. Disposition contract transferring ownership of the money.

Bakery example:

Everyday perception: one unitary exchange.
Legal structure: purchase contract + transfer of bread + transfer of money.

Exam sentence:

The purchase agreement obliges transfer of ownership, but it does not itself transfer ownership.

Principle Of Abstraction

Abstraction builds on separation.

obligation contract validity and disposition contract validity are independent

Consequences:

  • invalid purchase contract does not automatically invalidate the ownership transfer;
  • invalid transfer does not automatically invalidate the purchase contract;
  • reversal may require restitution, especially Sections 985 or 812 I 1 alternative 1 BGB.

Exception: identity of the flaw.

Examples from the deck:

Facts Result
Mentally ill B concludes purchase and receives transfer. Both declarations may be invalid under Sections 104 No. 2, 105 I BGB.
Deceit/duress under Section 123 I BGB affects both transactions. Rescission of obligation and disposition contract can be possible.
Price typo under Section 119 I BGB affects only purchase price. Disposition contract may remain valid because transfer agreement does not concern the price.

Exam trap: do not reverse ownership automatically just because the sales contract is invalid. Ask whether the transfer transaction is also invalid or whether restitution is needed.

Things And Movables

Section 90 BGB:

Only corporeal objects are things.

Important exclusions/clarifications:

  • humans are not things;
  • animals are not things, but similar rules apply under Section 90a BGB;
  • immaterial rights and claims are not things;
  • software as data is not a thing, but a physical data carrier can be;
  • movables differ from immovables.

Transfer Of Movables Under Section 929 Sentence 1 BGB

Regular acquisition of a movable:

1. Agreement.
2. Delivery / handover.
3. Agreement at handing over.
4. Authorization.

1. Agreement

The transfer agreement is a normal contract at the disposition level.

General declaration-of-intent rules apply:

  • agency;
  • rescission;
  • invalidity;
  • conditions under Section 158 BGB.

Principle of determination:

an objective third party must be able to identify the concrete object being transferred

Examples:

  • pointing to a specific machine;
  • naming machine #1;
  • “all items manufactured in January 2023.”

2. Delivery

Delivery is a real act and publicity act, not a contract.

Consequences:

  • declaration-of-intent rules do not apply directly to delivery;
  • no agency under Sections 164 et seq. BGB for the real act itself;
  • an agent in possession under Section 855 BGB can matter, such as an employee holding firm goods.

Delivery requirements:

  • acquirer obtains possession through the transferor;
  • transferor loses possession;
  • third parties can objectively discern the transfer.

3. Agreement At Handing Over

The agreement must still exist when delivery occurs.

Before delivery, the disposition agreement is freely revocable at the property-law level.
Contractual penalties or damages may exist at the obligation-contract level.

4. Authorization

In principle, only the owner can transfer ownership.

Possible restrictions:

  • insolvency law, especially Section 81 InsO;
  • family law restrictions protecting family economic basis.

Authorized non-owner:

  • owner consent under Section 185 I BGB;
  • statutory power of disposition, such as insolvency administrator under Section 80 I InsO.

Unauthorized non-owner:

  • may still transfer ownership through good-faith acquisition.

Delivery Replacements

Mode Anchor Logic Example
Acquirer already possesses Section 929 sentence 2 BGB Delivery unnecessary. Buyer already has borrowed item.
Constructive delivery Section 930 BGB Delivery replaced by possession relationship. Chattel mortgage; seller remains possessor for buyer.
Assignment of claim for possession Section 931 BGB Transferor assigns claim against current possessor. Thing held by a third party.

Good-Faith Acquisition Of Movables

Good-faith acquisition solves legal traffic cases where the seller possesses the thing but is not owner.

Requirements under Sections 929 sentence 1, 932 I 1 BGB:

1. All Section 929 sentence 1 requirements except authorization.
2. Good faith of acquirer.
3. Legal appearance due to possession, Section 1006 BGB.
4. Thing not lost or stolen, Section 935 BGB.
5. Legal transaction between two distinct parties.

Good faith is defined negatively:

acquirer is not in good faith if aware, or grossly negligently unaware, that the seller is not owner

Section 935 BGB:

No good-faith acquisition if the thing was lost, stolen, or otherwise involuntarily lost by the owner.

Exam trap: possession creates legal appearance, but Section 935 protects owners who involuntarily lost possession.

Chattel Mortgage Case

Facts:

S needs EUR 100,000.
L lends money and wants collateral.
S wants to keep machine #1 for production.
S and L agree to transfer ownership of machine #1 as chattel mortgage and conclude a security purpose agreement.

Issue:

Who owns machine #1?

Analysis:

  1. S was initially owner.
  2. S and L agreed to transfer ownership of machine #1.
  3. No physical delivery occurred.
  4. Delivery is replaced by constructive delivery under Sections 929, 930 BGB.
  5. The chattel mortgage/security purpose agreement supplies the possession relationship.
  6. Agreement persisted and S was authorized as owner.

Conclusion:

S lost ownership to L under Sections 929 sentence 1, 930 BGB, while S kept possession.

Business meaning:

S can keep using the machine, but L owns it as collateral.

Good-Faith Purchase Case

Facts:

After transferring ownership to L as collateral, S sells machine #1 to B.
B cannot know the machine is owned by L.
S gives the machine to B, who transports it to his premises.

Issue:

Who owns machine #1?

Analysis:

  1. L was owner.
  2. S and B agreed to transfer ownership.
  3. Delivery occurred when B received and transported the machine.
  4. Agreement persisted until handover.
  5. S was not authorized because S was no longer owner and L did not consent.
  6. Good-faith acquisition under Sections 929 sentence 1, 932 BGB:
    • B was in good faith under Section 932 II BGB.
    • S’s possession created legal appearance under Section 1006 BGB.
    • Machine was not lost or stolen under Section 935 BGB.
    • Legal transaction occurred between two distinct parties.

Conclusion:

B acquires ownership in good faith. L loses ownership to B.

Statutory Acquisition Of Movables

The deck lists statutory acquisition modes:

Mode Anchor
Acquisition by prescription, 10 years Section 937 BGB
Combination with plot of land Section 946 BGB
Combination with another movable Section 947 BGB
Intermixture / mingling Section 948 BGB
Processing into a new thing Section 950 BGB
Acquisition of products/components Sections 953 et seq. BGB
Acquisition of ownerless movables Section 958 BGB

Exam use: mention these only if facts fit. Most exam facts in this deck focus on Section 929 and good-faith acquisition.

Transfer Of Immovables

Transfer of immovables is stricter.

Transfer of movables Transfer of immovables
Sections 929 et seq. BGB Sections 873, 925 BGB
Agreement Agreement / conveyance
Delivery Entry in land register
Agreement at delivery Agreement at entry
Authorization or good-faith acquisition Authorization or good-faith acquisition

Immovable agreement:

  • called conveyance under Section 925 BGB;
  • special form: authentication by public notary;
  • real property purchase agreement must also be notarized under Section 311b I BGB.

Good faith:

land register creates strong legal appearance;
positive knowledge of incorrectness blocks good-faith acquisition.

Transfer Of Claims

Claims are not corporeal things, so they are not transferred under Section 929 BGB.

Core distinction:

purchase of rights = obligation contract under Section 453 BGB
assignment of claim = disposition under Section 398 BGB

Assignment requirements:

  1. disposition contract under Section 398 sentence 1 BGB;
  2. claim exists;
  3. claim is identifiable;
  4. claim is transferable.

No debtor participation is required, though notification is advisable.

Important limits:

  • no good-faith acquisition of non-existing claims generally;
  • future claims may be assigned if identifiable;
  • statutory or contractual exclusions can block transferability.

Business examples:

  • factoring;
  • bank takes salary claim as collateral;
  • supplier assigns future purchase-price claims.

Visual Knowledge Map

flowchart TD
    Start[Property question] --> OwnPoss[Ownership vs possession]
    OwnPoss --> Separation[Principle of separation]
    Separation --> Obligation[Purchase agreement: Section 433]
    Separation --> Disposition[Disposition contract]
    Disposition --> Abstraction[Principle of abstraction]
    Disposition --> Movables[Movables]
    Movables --> S929[Section 929: agreement + delivery + authorization]
    S929 --> Replacements[Delivery replacements: 929 II / 930 / 931]
    S929 --> Auth{Owner authorized?}
    Auth -->|yes| OwnerTransfer[Regular transfer]
    Auth -->|no| GoodFaith[Good-faith acquisition: Section 932]
    GoodFaith --> S935[No lost/stolen thing: Section 935]
    Disposition --> Immovables[Immovables: 873 / 925 + land register]
    Disposition --> Claims[Claims: assignment under Section 398]

Subject Knowledge Graph

Node Meaning Exam Relevance
Ownership Legal right over a thing. Determines who can transfer.
Possession Actual control over a thing. Creates legal appearance and transfer starting point.
Principle Of Separation Obligation and disposition contracts are separate. Purchase contract does not transfer ownership.
Principle Of Abstraction Validity of obligation and disposition are independent. Invalid sales contract does not automatically undo ownership transfer.
Movable Transfer Agreement, delivery, agreement at delivery, authorization. Main Section 929 test.
Constructive Delivery Delivery replacement under Section 930 BGB. Chattel mortgage cases.
Good-Faith Acquisition Ownership transfer from non-owner under strict conditions. Protects legal traffic.
Lost/Stolen Exclusion Section 935 BGB barrier. Protects owners who involuntarily lost possession.
Immovable Transfer Conveyance plus land-register entry. Real property rules.
Assignment Transfer of claims under Section 398 BGB. Claims are not delivered.
From Relationship To Why It Matters
Purchase Agreement obliges Transfer Of Ownership Contract creates duty, not ownership.
Principle Of Separation separates Obligation / Disposition Prevents one-step thinking.
Principle Of Abstraction separates validity of Obligation / Disposition Reversal needs separate analysis.
Possession creates Legal Appearance Basis for good-faith acquisition.
Section 935 BGB blocks Good-Faith Acquisition Stolen/lost property protection.
Section 930 BGB replaces Delivery Collateral without physical handover.
Assignment transfers Claim Different from transfer of things.

Real Business Examples

  • A company sells machinery but keeps it as collateral through a chattel mortgage.
  • A buyer purchases equipment from a possessor who is no longer owner; good-faith acquisition becomes decisive.
  • A real property transaction requires notarial steps and land-register entry, not simple handover.
  • A supplier sells receivables to a factoring company; the claim is assigned, not physically delivered.

Exam Relevance

Likely prompts:

  • Distinguish ownership and possession.
  • Explain separation and abstraction.
  • Apply Section 929 sentence 1 BGB.
  • Explain when delivery is dispensable or replaced.
  • Analyze good-faith acquisition from a non-owner.
  • Apply Section 935 BGB to stolen/lost property.
  • Compare transfer of movables and immovables.
  • Explain assignment of claims under Section 398 BGB.

Common traps:

  • Saying the purchase contract transfers ownership.
  • Treating possession as ownership.
  • Forgetting agreement at the time of delivery.
  • Applying agency rules directly to delivery as a real act.
  • Allowing good-faith acquisition despite stolen property.
  • Forgetting that claims are not things and require assignment.

High-scoring answer structure for movables:

  1. Identify initial owner.
  2. Test transfer under Section 929 sentence 1 BGB.
  3. Check agreement and determination of the object.
  4. Check delivery or replacement.
  5. Check agreement at delivery.
  6. Check authorization.
  7. If authorization fails, test good-faith acquisition under Section 932 and Section 935.
  8. State who owns the thing.

Clarification checkpoint:

Contract answers: who must do what?
Property law answers: who owns what?

If the transferor is a non-owner, do not stop at “no authorization.” Continue into the statutory exception: good-faith acquisition under Sections 932 and 935 BGB.

Retrieval Prompts

Closed-book questions:

  1. What is the difference between ownership and possession?
  2. What are the principles of separation and abstraction?
  3. What are the four requirements of Section 929 sentence 1 BGB?
  4. Why is delivery a real act?
  5. What does Section 930 BGB replace?
  6. What blocks good-faith acquisition under Section 935 BGB?
  7. How are claims transferred?

Application prompts:

  1. S sells and hands over a bike to B. Build the Section 929 test.
  2. S transfers machine ownership to L as collateral but keeps the machine. Which delivery replacement applies?
  3. S later sells the same machine to good-faith B. Does B acquire ownership?
  4. Thief T sells stolen jewelry to good-faith B. What does Section 935 BGB do?
  5. C assigns a future salary claim to a bank. Which requirements matter?

Practice Tasks

  1. Draw the three transactions involved in buying bread with cash.
  2. Explain abstraction using a void purchase contract but valid handover.
  3. Write a mini-case answer for the chattel mortgage machine case.
  4. Write a mini-case answer for good-faith acquisition from S to B.
  5. Compare transfer of movables and immovables in a four-row table.

Connections

Previous notes:

  • Week 03 Contract Law I: general declaration-of-intent and contract rules apply to agreement but not delivery.
  • Week 07 Agency: agency can affect agreement, but delivery is a real act.
  • Week 08 Warranty Rights I: Section 433 seller duty includes transfer of ownership free from defects.
  • Week 09 Warranty Rights II: remedies are separate from ownership transfer and restitution.

Future notes:

  • Trade Law and Company Law will build on commercial transactions and representation.

Cross-course links:

  • Finance: collateral and assignment of claims are legal tools behind secured lending and factoring.

Weakness Flags

  • Pending active recall: no first-pass retrieval has been completed yet.

  • High-risk issue: good-faith acquisition and Section 935.
  • High-risk issue: claims are assigned, not delivered.

[W10.2] Week 10 Transfer Of Property Cheatsheet And Tricks

Source: business-law/wiki/week-10-transfer-of-property/week-10-transfer-of-property-cheatsheet-and-tricks.md

Course: Business Law Exam date: 2026-07-28 Source: week-10-transfer-of-property.md, clarification-session-2026-07-15.md

Must-Know (exam-critical)

Rule Anchor Backbone reason
Ownership and possession are different things Sections 854 ff. (possession), Article 14 GG (ownership) A thief has possession without ownership — every case opens on this split.
Object router: movable / land / claim decides the whole route n/a (case-classification step) Wrong object type means the wrong statute block from the start.
Principle of separation: obligation contract and disposition contract are distinct Section 433 BGB (obligation) vs. disposition A purchase contract only creates a duty to transfer; it never transfers ownership itself.
Principle of abstraction: validity of the obligation and disposition contracts is independent n/a (doctrinal principle) An invalid sales contract does not automatically undo an already-completed ownership transfer, and vice versa.
Movable transfer test (four cumulative elements) Section 929 sentence 1 BGB This is the core route almost every movable-property case runs: agreement + delivery (or replacement) + agreement still existing at delivery + authorization.
Delivery is a real act, not a declaration of intent n/a Agency rules (Sections 164 ff.) do not apply directly to the handover itself, only to the agreement.
Delivery replacements Section 929 sentence 2 (acquirer already possesses), Section 930 (constructive delivery), Section 931 (assignment of claim for possession) Physical handover is not mandatory — these three routes substitute for it, especially in collateral/chattel-mortgage facts.
Good-faith acquisition from a non-owner Sections 929 sentence 1, 932 BGB Only route available once “authorization” fails — do not stop the analysis at “no authorization.”
Lost/stolen block Section 935 BGB Kills good-faith acquisition even for a completely honest buyer if the true owner lost possession involuntarily.
Immovable transfer needs conveyance plus land-register entry Sections 873, 925 BGB; notarial form under Section 311b I BGB for the underlying contract Section 929 never applies to land — different statute family entirely.
Claims transfer by assignment, not delivery Section 398 BGB Claims are not corporeal things (Section 90 BGB), so there is no “handover” step at all.

Nice-to-Have (depth/edge cases)

  • Statutory (non-transactional) acquisition modes: prescription after 10 years (Section 937), combination with land (Section 946), combination with another movable (Section 947), intermixture (Section 948), processing into a new thing (Section 950), acquisition of products/components (Sections 953 ff.), acquisition of ownerless movables (Section 958). Mention only if the facts actually fit — most exam facts stay on Section 929 and good-faith acquisition.
  • Section 90a BGB: animals are not “things” but similar rules apply to them anyway.
  • Software as pure data is not a thing; a physical data carrier can be.
  • Principle of determination for the transfer agreement: an objective third party must be able to identify the concrete object (pointing at a specific machine, naming “machine #1,” or “all items manufactured in January 2023” all satisfy this).
  • Assignment does not require debtor participation/consent, though notification is practically advisable; future claims can be assigned if identifiable, and statutory/contractual clauses can block transferability.
  • Business framings worth name-dropping if the question invites it: chattel mortgage as secured lending, factoring as claim assignment, bank taking a salary claim as collateral.

Nuances And Traps

Nuance/Trap Why it’s easy to get wrong Correct handling
“B owns it because B bought it” Sounds intuitive but merges the two separate legal layers. Never write ownership as a consequence of the purchase contract alone — always run the Section 929 test and state which of its four elements are met.
Assuming a signed purchase contract already means the buyer owns the good Everyday intuition treats signing as the transaction; German private law treats it as only the first of three transactions (goods contract, transfer of the good, transfer of the money). If delivery has not happened yet, the buyer only has a claim against the seller — state explicitly “B is not owner yet.”
Thinking good-faith acquisition needs the true owner’s consent The clarification session flags this as the central confusion: how can L lose ownership to B without L ever agreeing to S’s resale? Good-faith acquisition is a statutory exception that overrides the authorization requirement — it runs on the acquirer’s good faith and the seller’s possession-based legal appearance (Section 1006 BGB), not on the true owner’s consent.
Treating every “possessor sold it to someone else” fact pattern the same way The outcome flips entirely depending on whether the true owner lost possession voluntarily or involuntarily. Always ask “did the true owner give up possession voluntarily (e.g., left it with S as collateral) or involuntarily (theft, loss)?” Voluntary loss → good-faith acquisition can succeed. Involuntary loss → Section 935 blocks it regardless of the buyer’s honesty.
Forgetting the “agreement still exists at delivery” element It is easy to check only agreement + delivery + authorization and skip the third element. The disposition agreement is freely revocable at the property-law level before delivery — explicitly confirm it was still in force when delivery happened, especially in multi-step or delayed-delivery facts.
Applying agency rules to the delivery act itself Delivery looks like an act a representative could perform, so students import Sections 164 ff. directly. Agency rules govern the agreement (a declaration of intent); delivery is a real/factual act, not a declaration — an agent’s possession is instead analyzed under Section 855 BGB (possession through an agent in possession).
Missing the special constructive-delivery route in collateral/chattel-mortgage facts These facts describe the seller keeping the object physically, which looks like “no delivery happened” and therefore “no transfer happened.” Recognize the security-purpose agreement as supplying Section 930 constructive delivery — ownership passes to the lender even though the borrower keeps physical possession the whole time.
Using Section 929 for land or Section 398 language for movables Object misclassification carries the wrong statute block through the entire answer. Fix the object type first: movable → Section 929 family; land → Sections 873/925 plus notarial Section 311b I; claim → Section 398 assignment, no delivery concept at all.
Assuming abstraction always shields the disposition contract from the obligation contract’s invalidity Some flaws (e.g., Section 104 No. 2 / 105 I incapacity, Section 123 deceit/duress) can taint both transactions identically (“identity of the flaw”), while others (e.g., a Section 119 I price typo) usually only hit the purchase contract. Check the specific defect against both transactions separately — do not assume abstraction automatically saves the disposition contract in every case.

One-Line Recall Drill

929 I = agreement + delivery + agreement-at-delivery + authorization
929 II = acquirer already possesses, no handover needed
930 = constructive delivery, security/collateral facts
931 = assignment of the claim for possession
932 = good-faith acquisition from a non-owner
935 = lost/stolen block, kills good faith even if honest
1006 = possession creates legal appearance
873 + 925 = land: conveyance + register entry
311b I = notarial form for land purchase contract
398 = assignment of a claim, not delivery
90 = only corporeal objects are things
separation = contract creates duty, disposition transfers ownership
abstraction = validity of the two transactions is independent

[W10.3] Week 10 Transfer Of Property Practice Questions And Model Answers

Source: business-law/wiki/week-10-transfer-of-property/week-10-transfer-of-property-practice-questions-and-model-answers.md
